docs.title: Inspect / verify

kubectl get all,pdb,hpa,networkpolicy -l app=hello-prod
kubectl describe pdb hello-prod
kubectl describe hpa hello-prod
kubectl describe networkpolicy hello-prod

# Check pods spread across nodes / zones

docs.title: Test PDB protection
docs.text:
# Drain a node — PDB blocks if disruption would violate it
kubectl drain kind-worker --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
kubectl uncordon kind-worker

docs.title: Verify securityContext
docs.text:
kubectl get pod -l app=hello-prod -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.securityContext}'
kubectl exec -it -l app=hello-prod -- id          # uid != 0
kubectl exec -it -l app=hello-prod -- touch /test # read-only root FS -> denied

docs.title: Verify NetworkPolicy
docs.text:
kubectl get netpol
kubectl describe netpol hello-prod

# From an unauthorized pod — should be blocked
kubectl run test --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- \
  curl -s --max-time 3 http://hello-prod/ || echo BLOCKED

docs.title: Cheat Sheet (Hot Context)
docs.text:
• Pod = smallest unit, one or more containers sharing net+storage
  • Deployment = ReplicaSet manager with rollout history
  • Service = stable virtual IP and DNS in front of pods
  • ConfigMap = non-secret key/value, mountable
  • Secret = base64 key/value, mountable, RBAC-restricted
  • PVC = request for storage, bound to a PV
  • Ingress = HTTP/S router into the cluster
  • HPA = autoscaler based on metrics
  • RBAC = who can do what to which resource

docs.title: Architect-Level Q&A — Kubernetes Core
docs.text: 60+ questions you should be able to answer cold in a senior design review. Grouped by topic.

docs.title: Q1. When do you choose hard multi-tenancy over soft?
docs.text: Hard tenancy (separate clusters or virtual clusters via vcluster/Capsule) when tenants are mutually distrusting, have regulatory boundaries (PCI, HIPAA), or wildly divergent SLOs. Soft tenancy (namespaces + RBAC + NetworkPolicy + ResourceQuota) when tenants are internal teams with comparable trust levels.

docs.title: Q2. What are the four enforcement layers in soft multi-tenancy?
docs.text:
1. RBAC for API access scoping
  2. NetworkPolicy for east-west traffic
  3. ResourceQuota and LimitRange for resource fairness
  4. PodSecurity admission for workload isolation

docs.title: Q3. Why is kube-system a tenancy risk?
docs.text: Cluster-scoped controllers run there with cluster-admin. A tenant who gets pod-exec into a privileged daemonset escapes namespace isolation. Always pin tenant workloads to dedicated node pools and use admission to block hostPath, hostNetwork, and privileged.

docs.title: Q4. How do you handle DNS noisy-neighbor in shared clusters?
docs.text: NodeLocal DNSCache eliminates per-pod conntrack churn against kube-dns. For very high QPS tenants, set per-namespace CoreDNS rate limiting via the rewrite plugin and monitor SERVFAIL by namespace.

docs.title: Q5. Should you give tenants their own ingress controller?
docs.text: Yes when SLA isolation matters. Run per-tenant ingress-nginx in its own namespace with --ingress-class=tenant-a. Shared ingress is fine for read-mostly low-RPS tenants.

docs.title: Q6. How do you bill tenants accurately?
docs.text: OpenCost or Kubecost emits per-namespace cost using node prices, allocation, and idle. Augment with custom labels (team=, cost-center=) enforced by Kyverno admission so untagged pods are rejected.

docs.title: Q7. What is the practical etcd object limit per cluster?
docs.text: Recommended max DB size is 8 GiB. In practice you start hurting around 4 GiB with slow LIST calls and watch lag. Object count target is under 200k for healthy operation.

docs.title: Q8. How do you size etcd disks?
docs.text: NVMe SSDs only. Sustained write IOPS budget of 50 MB/s minimum, p99 fsync under 10 ms. Use etcdctl check perf and watch etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds.

docs.title: Q9. What is the etcd memory rule of thumb?
docs.text: Plan for 8 GB RAM minimum, 16 GB for clusters with 1000+ nodes. The full keyspace lives in memory.

docs.title: Q10. How frequently should etcd be defragmented?
docs.text: When etcd_mvcc_db_total_size_in_use_in_bytes divided by etcd_mvcc_db_total_size_in_bytes falls below 0.5. Typically weekly on busy clusters, rolling one member at a time.

docs.title: Q11. What is the failure mode of an etcd write quorum loss?
docs.text: API server goes read-only-ish (mutating calls fail). Existing pods keep running because kubelet uses local cache. Restore from snapshot, never from a single member.

docs.title: Q12. How big should etcd snapshots be and where stored?
docs.text: Full DB plus 10% overhead. Store in object storage in two regions, encrypted, with daily lifecycle. Snapshot every 30 minutes for production.

docs.title: Q13. Stacked vs external etcd topology?
docs.text: Stacked is simpler and cheaper, suitable up to 500 nodes. External etcd gives independent scaling and isolated failure domains, mandatory above 1000 nodes.

docs.title: Q14. How do you handle etcd compaction lag?
docs.text: Set --auto-compaction-mode=periodic --auto-compaction-retention=8h. Without it the keyspace grows unbounded.

docs.title: Q15. What metric tells you etcd is the bottleneck?
docs.text: etcd_server_proposals_failed_total increasing, etcd_disk_backend_commit_duration_seconds p99 above 25 ms, or apiserver_request_duration_seconds p99 above 1s for LIST.

docs.title: Q16. How do you safely add a fourth etcd member?
docs.text: Add as learner first. Wait for it to catch up. Promote. Never jump from 3 to 5 in one step.

docs.title: Q17. Do you use etcd encryption at rest?
docs.text: Yes. Use KMS provider with envelope encryption. Rotate KEK quarterly. Test decryption path during DR drills.

docs.title: Q18. What is the impact of large secrets on etcd?
docs.text: Each Secret read pulls full payload through API server. Many large secrets in LIST operations balloon memory. Cap secret size to 256 KB.

docs.title: Q19. Minimum production control-plane topology?
docs.text: Three API servers behind an L4 LB, three etcd members, two scheduler and two controller-manager replicas with leader election, spread across three AZs.

docs.title: Q20. Why three and not two control-plane nodes?
docs.text: Two cannot form quorum if one fails. Three tolerates one failure. Five tolerates two but doubles write latency.

docs.title: Q21. How do you upgrade a control plane without downtime?
docs.text: Upgrade etcd first (one member at a time). Then API servers (one at a time, drain LB). Then scheduler and controller-manager. Then nodes. Never skip minor versions.

docs.title: Q22. What does the API server LB need to do?
docs.text: TCP passthrough on 6443. Health check /livez. Sticky-by-source-ip is fine but not required. SNI passthrough for kubelet client cert auth.

docs.title: Q23. How do you protect against API server overload?
docs.text: APF (API Priority and Fairness) flow schemas. Dedicate priority levels for system-leader-election, node-high (kubelet), workload-low (CI bots).

docs.title: Q24. What is the default scheduler throughput?
docs.text: About 100 pods per second on a tuned 5000-node cluster. Raw scoring is bounded by the number of nodes scored.

docs.title: Q25. How does percentageOfNodesToScore help?
docs.text: Below this percentage of feasible nodes, scheduler stops scoring further. Default is adaptive (5% at 5000 nodes). Lower values trade quality for speed.

docs.title: Q26. When do you write a custom scheduler?
docs.text: For batch workloads with gang scheduling (Volcano, Kueue), spot-aware bin packing, or topology-aware placement beyond what TopologySpreadConstraints offers.

docs.title: Q27. What is the difference between affinity and topology spread?
docs.text: Affinity is hard or soft preference between pods. Topology spread enforces even distribution across a topology key with skew tolerance. Spread is the right primitive for HA.

docs.title: Q28. How do PodTopologySpreadConstraints scale?
docs.text: O(pods x nodes) in worst case. At 5000 nodes with thousands of spread pods, scheduler latency spikes. Mitigate with matchLabelKeys and per-namespace selectors.

docs.title: Q29. How does the scheduler handle preemption?
docs.text: Identifies victims with lower priority that, if removed, would let the pending pod fit. Adds a 30s grace nomination. Disable on tenant clusters to prevent noisy neighbors abusing priority.

docs.title: Q30. What is the cache invalidation cost on scheduler restart?
docs.text: Full re-list of nodes and pods. At 5000 nodes this is multi-minute. Run two scheduler replicas with leader election and stagger restarts.

docs.title: Q31. How do you debug scheduler latency?
docs.text: Enable scheduler verbosity=4 briefly. Check scheduler_e2e_scheduling_duration_seconds. The PreFilter and Score plugins are usually the culprits — InterPodAffinity at scale is the worst offender.

docs.title: Q32. What is the theoretical pod-per-node limit?
docs.text: 110 pods per node default, raisable to 250 with kubelet --max-pods. Above 250, conntrack and IP exhaustion bite.

docs.title: Q33. What runs out first as you push density?
docs.text:
1. CIDR IPs (each pod needs one)
  2. Conntrack entries
  3. cgroup memory accounting overhead
  4. PLEG relist time (kubelet performance)

docs.title: Q34. How do you budget node CPU for system overhead?
docs.text: Reserve 100m + (10m per pod) for kubelet, plus 100m for kube-proxy, plus runtime overhead. On a 32-core node hosting 110 pods that is roughly 1.5 cores reserved.

docs.title: Q35. What is PLEG and why does it fail?
docs.text: Pod Lifecycle Event Generator. Kubelet polls container runtime to detect state changes. With many pods or slow runtime it exceeds the 3-minute threshold and node goes NotReady.

docs.title: Q36. How does the IPv4 ENI limit affect AWS density?
docs.text: Each EC2 instance type has a max ENI count and IPs per ENI. Use ENI prefix delegation or IPv6 to increase pod density on small nodes.

docs.title: Q37. Calico vs Cilium tradeoffs?
docs.text: Calico: mature, simple BGP, iptables or eBPF dataplane, strong policy. Cilium: eBPF native, identity-based policy, Hubble observability, service mesh capabilities, steeper learning curve.

docs.title: Q38. When would you not use a CNI overlay?
docs.text: When pods need real routable IPs (legacy firewall integration), when overlay encapsulation overhead matters (sub-microsecond latency), or in baremetal with BGP.

docs.title: Q39. What does kube-proxy do and what replaces it?
docs.text: Implements Service VIP via iptables or IPVS. Cilium kube-proxy replacement uses eBPF for lower latency and no iptables churn. Required at high service counts.

docs.title: Q40. NetworkPolicy default-deny pattern?
docs.text: Deploy a default-deny ingress and egress per namespace, then allow specific flows. Without default-deny, NetworkPolicy is additive-only and tenants can talk freely.

docs.title: Q41. When is NodePort acceptable?
docs.text: Internal traffic, lab clusters. Production should use LoadBalancer or Ingress. NodePort exposes random high ports and complicates firewall rules.

docs.title: Q42. What is the cost of LoadBalancer-per-Service?
docs.text: One cloud LB per Service. At 100 services that is 100 LBs. Use a single Ingress controller or Gateway API instead.

docs.title: Q43. How do you tier storage for cost and performance?
docs.text: Premium SSD (databases), standard SSD (logs and general), HDD (cold backups). Define StorageClasses per tier with volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer for topology-aware provisioning.

docs.title: Q44. Static vs dynamic provisioning?
docs.text: Dynamic for stateless and most stateful. Static for pre-existing volumes (legacy NFS shares, snapshot restores).

docs.title: Q45. What is the impact of ReadWriteMany?
docs.text: Most block storage cannot do RWX. Forces NFS, CephFS, EFS, or cloud filesystems with higher latency. Avoid unless required.

docs.title: Q46. How do you do volume backups at scale?
docs.text: Velero with CSI snapshots. Schedule per namespace. Test restore in a sandbox cluster monthly. Snapshots are not backups until restored.

docs.title: Q47. What happens when a PVC outgrows its PV?
docs.text: With allowVolumeExpansion: true on the StorageClass, edit PVC spec.resources.requests.storage. CSI driver expands. Some filesystems require pod restart for online resize.

docs.title: Q48. How do you handle stuck PVCs after node deletion?
docs.text: Force delete the VolumeAttachment, then the PVC. Cleanup orphaned cloud disks via cloud CLI. Automate via a controller for large clusters.

docs.title: Q49. Namespace per team or per app?
docs.text: Per app for production, per team for dev. App-per-namespace gives clean RBAC and quota boundaries. Team-per-namespace simplifies dev sandbox cleanup.

docs.title: Q50. What belongs in a NamespaceTemplate?
docs.text: ResourceQuota, LimitRange, default NetworkPolicy (deny-all), default ServiceAccount with minimal RBAC, image pull secret. Use Kyverno or HNC to apply.

docs.title: Q51. How do you handle cross-namespace references?
docs.text: Avoid. Services can be referenced as service.namespace.svc.cluster.local but Secrets and ConfigMaps cannot cross namespaces. Use ExternalSecrets or replicate via controller.

docs.title: Q52. What is the pod count per namespace ceiling?
docs.text: Soft ceiling around 5000 for kubectl usability. Hard ceiling is etcd size. Split namespaces when LIST takes more than 2 seconds.

docs.title: Q53. Argo CD vs Flux?
docs.text: Argo CD: UI-first, multi-tenancy via projects, application-of-applications pattern. Flux: CLI-first, GitOps Toolkit composable, Kustomize-native, OCI artifact support. Pick based on team UI preference.

docs.title: Q54. Push vs pull deployment?
docs.text: Pull (GitOps) is the default. Cluster-internal agent reconciles from Git. Push (CI deploys) is simpler but exposes kubeconfig and breaks audit. Use push only for short-lived ephemeral envs.

docs.title: Q55. How do you handle secrets in GitOps?
docs.text: SealedSecrets, External Secrets Operator with Vault/SM, or SOPS. Never plaintext in Git. Sealed secrets are cluster-scoped which complicates DR.

docs.title: Q56. App-of-apps vs ApplicationSet?
docs.text: App-of-apps for static known set. ApplicationSet for templated dynamic generation (one app per cluster, per environment).

docs.title: Q57. How do you do progressive delivery with GitOps?
docs.text: Argo Rollouts or Flagger sidecar to GitOps. The CRD lives in Git, the controller manages canary or blue-green steps.

docs.title: Q58. Drift detection and auto-heal — when do you disable?
docs.text: Disable auto-heal during incident response so you can hotfix in-cluster. Re-enable after Git is updated. Always keep drift detection.

docs.title: Q59. What is the multi-cluster GitOps pattern?
docs.text: Hub-and-spoke: one Argo CD or Flux instance manages many clusters via cluster registration. Or one instance per cluster for stronger blast radius isolation.

docs.title: Q60. How do you avoid Helm value drift?
docs.text: Single source of truth: values.yaml in Git. PRs only. Use helm diff in CI. Block kubectl edit via RBAC for production namespaces.

docs.title: Q61. When do you split a cluster?
docs.text: At etcd 4 GiB, 5000 nodes, or when blast radius of a single failure exceeds tolerated impact. Earlier if multi-region or regulatory.

docs.title: Q62. What is the right VPA + HPA combination?
docs.text: VPA for memory (right-sizing), HPA for CPU and custom metrics. Never both on the same metric or they fight.

docs.title: Q63. Cluster autoscaler vs Karpenter?
docs.text: CA: node-group based, slow (minutes). Karpenter: just-in-time provisioning, instance-type aware, faster, AWS-only mature support but expanding.

docs.title: Q64. How do you do zero-downtime cluster upgrades?
docs.text: Blue-green clusters with traffic shift via DNS or Gateway. Or in-place rolling, draining nodes one AZ at a time, with PodDisruptionBudgets enforced.

docs.title: Q65. What is the single most important production safety net?
docs.text: PodDisruptionBudget on every critical workload. Without it, a node drain can take down all replicas.

docs.title: End

docs.title: Kubernetes for 10-year-olds (PhD edition)
docs.text: Each section: analogy, real explanation, mermaid diagram, kubectl steps to see it.

docs.title: 1. Pod — Team of friends in one tent
Analogy
docs.text: A Pod is like a small group of best friends camping in one tent. They share the same tent (network), the same cooler (storage), and if the tent moves, they all move together. They cannot be separated.

docs.title: Real explanation
docs.text: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. It groups one or more containers that share a Linux network namespace (same IP, same port space) and optionally shared volumes. Containers in a Pod are always co-scheduled to the same node and live and die together.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    A[Pod] --> B[Container 1]
    A --> C[Container 2]
    A --> D[Shared Network]
    A --> E[Shared Volume]

docs.title: Try it live
docs.text:
kubectl run mypod --image=nginx
kubectl get pods
kubectl describe pod mypod
kubectl exec -it mypod -- sh
kubectl delete pod mypod

docs.title: 2. Deployment — A baker that makes 5 cookies and replaces eaten ones
Analogy
docs.text: The Deployment is a baker. You tell the baker: I always want 5 chocolate-chip cookies on the plate. If a kid eats one, the baker bakes another. If you say change to oatmeal, the baker swaps them out one at a time so the plate is never empty.

docs.title: Real explanation
docs.text: A Deployment manages a ReplicaSet, which manages Pods. It guarantees the desired replica count, performs rolling updates with configurable surge and unavailable, and keeps revision history for rollback. It is the standard primitive for stateless workloads.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart TB
    A[Deployment] --> B[ReplicaSet]
    B --> C[Pod 1]
    B --> D[Pod 2]
    B --> E[Pod 3]

docs.title: Try it live
docs.text:
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx --replicas=5
kubectl get deploy,rs,pods
kubectl set image deploy/web nginx=nginx:1.25
kubectl rollout status deploy/web
kubectl rollout undo deploy/web

docs.title: 3. Service — The school office that knows where every student is
Analogy
docs.text: The Service is the school office. Students (Pods) move classrooms all the time, but if you call the office and ask for "Sarah from grade 4", the office routes your call. You never need to know which classroom Sarah is in today.

docs.title: Real explanation
docs.text: A Service is a stable virtual IP and DNS name that load-balances to a dynamic set of Pods selected by labels. It abstracts pod IP churn. Types: ClusterIP (in-cluster), NodePort (port on every node), LoadBalancer (cloud LB), ExternalName (DNS CNAME).

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    A[Client] --> B[Service VIP]
    B --> C[Pod 1]
    B --> D[Pod 2]
    B --> E[Pod 3]

docs.title: Try it live
docs.text:
kubectl expose deploy/web --port=80 --target-port=80
kubectl get svc web
kubectl run tester --rm -it --image=busybox -- wget -qO- web
kubectl get endpoints web

docs.title: Analogy
docs.text: The ConfigMap is the recipe sheet pinned on the fridge. Anyone in the kitchen can read it. Change the sheet, and next time you cook the dish you use the new recipe. The recipe is not secret.

docs.title: Real explanation
docs.text: A ConfigMap stores non-confidential key-value pairs. Pods consume it as environment variables, command-line args, or mounted files. Updates to mounted ConfigMaps propagate to running Pods after a sync delay (env vars do not update without pod restart).

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    A[ConfigMap] --> B[Pod env]
    A --> C[Pod volume]
    B --> D[App reads var]
    C --> E[App reads file]

docs.title: Try it live
docs.text:
kubectl create configmap appcfg --from-literal=COLOR=blue
kubectl get cm appcfg -o yaml
kubectl run demo --image=busybox --env="COLOR=$(kubectl get cm appcfg -o jsonpath='{.data.COLOR}')" -- env
kubectl describe cm appcfg

docs.title: Analogy
docs.text: The Secret is a locked recipe sheet inside the safe. Only people with the safe key can open it. The recipe is the same kind of thing as the ConfigMap, but the contents are sensitive (passwords, API keys).

docs.title: Real explanation
docs.text: A Secret holds sensitive data (passwords, tokens, certificates). Stored base64-encoded in etcd (encrypt at rest with KMS in production). RBAC controls access. Mountable as env vars or files like ConfigMaps. Types include Opaque, kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson, kubernetes.io/tls.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    A[Secret] --> B[etcd encrypted]
    A --> C[Pod env]
    A --> D[Pod volume]
    C --> E[App uses token]

docs.title: Try it live
docs.text:
kubectl create secret generic dbpw --from-literal=PASSWORD=s3cret
kubectl get secret dbpw -o yaml
kubectl get secret dbpw -o jsonpath='{.data.PASSWORD}' | base64 -d
kubectl describe secret dbpw

docs.title: Analogy
docs.text: The PVC is your locker at school. You ask the office for a locker of a certain size. They assign one. Your stuff stays there even if you go home for the night. Next morning your stuff is still inside.

docs.title: Real explanation
docs.text: A PersistentVolumeClaim is a Pod-friendly request for storage with a size and access mode. It binds to a PersistentVolume (provisioned dynamically by a StorageClass or pre-created). Data survives Pod restarts and reschedules.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    A[PVC] --> B[StorageClass]
    B --> C[Provisioner]
    C --> D[PV]
    D --> E[Pod mount]

docs.title: Try it live
docs.text:
kubectl get sc
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: mydata
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
EOF
kubectl get pvc,pv
kubectl describe pvc mydata

docs.title: Analogy
docs.text: The Ingress is the front gate of the school. Visitors from outside check in there. The guard looks at who they want to see and points them to the right office (Service), which then points to the right student (Pod).

docs.title: Real explanation
docs.text: An Ingress is an HTTP/HTTPS L7 router. It defines hostnames, paths, and TLS, and forwards requests to backend Services. Requires an Ingress Controller (nginx, traefik, ALB) running in the cluster. Gateway API is the modern successor.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    A[Internet] --> B[Ingress Controller]
    B --> C[Ingress Rule]
    C --> D[Service]
    D --> E[Pod]

docs.title: Try it live
docs.text:
kubectl get ingressclass
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  rules:
  - host: web.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: web
            port:
              number: 80
EOF
kubectl get ingress web
kubectl describe ingress web

docs.title: Analogy
docs.text: A Namespace is a classroom. Each classroom has its own desks (resources), its own teacher's rules (RBAC), and its own supply cabinet (quotas). Sarah in Room A is different from Sarah in Room B.

docs.title: Real explanation
docs.text: Namespaces are virtual clusters within a cluster. They scope names, RBAC, ResourceQuotas, NetworkPolicies, and most resources. Cluster-scoped resources (Nodes, PVs, ClusterRoles) are not namespaced.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart TB
    A[Cluster] --> B[Namespace dev]
    A --> C[Namespace prod]
    B --> D[Pods]
    C --> E[Pods]

docs.title: Try it live
docs.text:
kubectl create namespace dev
kubectl run hello --image=nginx -n dev
kubectl get pods -n dev
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces
kubectl delete namespace dev

docs.title: 9. Bonus — Node as a school building
Analogy
docs.text: A Node is a school building. It has classrooms (Pods), a janitor (kubelet) who keeps things tidy, and a security guard (kube-proxy) at the door routing visitors. The principal (control plane) decides which kid goes in which building.

docs.title: Real explanation
docs.text: A Node is a worker machine (VM or physical) running kubelet, container runtime, and kube-proxy. The scheduler places Pods on Nodes based on resource requests, taints, affinity, and topology constraints.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart TB
    A[Node] --> B[kubelet]
    A --> C[Container Runtime]
    A --> D[kube-proxy]
    A --> E[Pods]

docs.title: Try it live
docs.text:
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl describe node NODE_NAME
kubectl top node
kubectl get pods -o wide --all-namespaces | grep NODE_NAME

docs.text: Object Analogy Real role Pod Tent of friends Smallest deployable unit Deployment Baker replacing cookies Manages stateless replicas Service School office Stable VIP for pods ConfigMap Recipe sheet Non-secret config Secret Locked recipe Sensitive config PVC School locker Persistent storage request Ingress Front gate HTTP router Namespace Classroom Virtual cluster scope Node School building Worker machine

docs.title: Visual Flows — Kubernetes Core
docs.text: 12 simple mermaid flowcharts of the most important runtime paths. Max 6 nodes each.

docs.title: Flow 1 — Pod Scheduling
docs.text:
The scheduler picks a node for a pending Pod.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    A[Pod Pending] --> B[Scheduler]
    B --> C[Filter Nodes]
    C --> D[Score Nodes]
    D --> E[Bind Pod to Node]
    E --> F[Kubelet Starts Pod]

Notes: Filter eliminates nodes that cannot fit (resources, taints, affinity). Score ranks remaining nodes (least loaded, image locality). Binding writes the chosen node into the Pod spec.

docs.title: Flow 2 — kubectl apply Path
docs.text:
What happens when you apply a YAML.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    A[kubectl apply] --> B[API Server]
    B --> C[Auth and Admission]
    C --> D[etcd Write]
    D --> E[Controllers React]
    E --> F[Resources Created]

Notes: Authentication checks who you are. Authorization (RBAC) checks what you can do. Admission webhooks mutate or validate. etcd is the source of truth.

docs.title: Flow 3 — Service Routing to Backend
docs.text:
How traffic reaches a Pod via a Service.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    A[Client Pod] --> B[Service VIP]
    B --> C[kube-proxy iptables]
    C --> D[Endpoint IP]
    D --> E[Backend Pod]

Notes: kube-proxy programs iptables (or IPVS) to DNAT the VIP to a real pod IP. Endpoints (or EndpointSlices) keep the live list updated.

docs.title: Flow 4 — ConfigMap into Env
docs.text:
How a ConfigMap value lands in the container's environment.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    A[ConfigMap] --> B[Pod Spec envFrom]
    B --> C[Kubelet Reads CM]
    C --> D[Container Env Set]
    D --> E[App Reads VAR]

Notes: Env vars are evaluated at container start. Changes to the ConfigMap do not propagate to running containers via env (only via mounted volumes).

docs.title: Flow 5 — PVC Binding
docs.text:
How a PVC becomes a usable mounted volume.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    A[PVC Created] --> B[StorageClass Provisioner]
    B --> C[Cloud Disk Created]
    C --> D[PV Object]
    D --> E[PVC Bound]
    E --> F[Pod Mount]

Notes: Dynamic provisioning is triggered by the StorageClass. The CSI driver creates the underlying disk. Binding is exclusive (one PVC to one PV).

docs.title: Flow 6 — Deployment Rollout
docs.text:
How a Deployment performs a rolling update.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    A[Update Image] --> B[New ReplicaSet]
    B --> C[Scale Up New]
    C --> D[Scale Down Old]
    D --> E[Old RS Zero]
    E --> F[Rollout Complete]

Notes: Surge and maxUnavailable control concurrency. ReadinessProbe must pass before old replicas are removed. Old ReplicaSets are kept for rollback.

docs.title: Flow 7 — RBAC Check
docs.text:
How an API request is authorized.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    A[API Request] --> B[Authentication]
    B --> C[Authorization RBAC]
    C --> D[Role Bindings]
    D --> E[Allow or Deny]

Notes: Multiple authorizers can be chained (RBAC, Node, Webhook). First allow wins. Default is deny.

docs.title: Flow 8 — HPA Scale-Up
docs.text:
How the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler reacts to load.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    A[Metrics Server] --> B[HPA Controller]
    B --> C[Compare to Target]
    C --> D[Calc Desired Replicas]
    D --> E[Patch Deployment]
    E --> F[More Pods Run]

Notes: Default sync period is 15s. Scale-up is fast, scale-down has a stabilization window (5 min default) to avoid flapping.

docs.title: Flow 9 — Pod Termination
docs.text:
What happens when you delete a Pod.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    A[Delete Pod] --> B[API Marks Terminating]
    B --> C[PreStop Hook]
    C --> D[SIGTERM to Container]
    D --> E[Grace Period Wait]
    E --> F[SIGKILL if Needed]

Notes: Default grace period is 30s. Endpoints removal happens in parallel; in-flight traffic may still hit the pod briefly.

docs.title: Flow 10 — Image Pull
docs.text:
How a container image arrives on a node.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    A[Pod Scheduled] --> B[Kubelet Pull]
    B --> C[Registry Auth]
    C --> D[Image Layers Download]
    D --> E[Container Created]
    E --> F[Container Started]

Notes: Image pull policy IfNotPresent is default for tagged images, Always for :latest. Use imagePullSecrets for private registries.

docs.title: Flow 11 — Liveness Probe Failure
docs.text:
What happens when liveness fails repeatedly.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    A[Probe Fails] --> B[Failure Counter Up]
    B --> C[Threshold Hit]
    C --> D[Container Killed]
    D --> E[Restart Policy Apply]
    E --> F[New Container Up]

Notes: Restart policy Always is default for Deployments. Backoff is exponential capped at 5 min. Excessive restarts mark Pod CrashLoopBackOff.

docs.title: Flow 12 — Ingress Request Path
docs.text:
How an external HTTPS request reaches a Pod.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    A[User Browser] --> B[Cloud LB]
    B --> C[Ingress Controller]
    C --> D[Service]
    D --> E[Backend Pod]

Notes: TLS terminates at the Ingress Controller (or LB). Host and path rules pick the backend Service. Service then routes to a Pod.

docs.title: Cross-Reference
docs.text: Flow Related architect-qa Related eli10 1 Scheduling Q24-Q31 Pod, Node 2 Apply Q19-Q23 All 3 Service Q39-Q42 Service 4 ConfigMap env n/a ConfigMap 5 PVC Q43-Q48 PVC 6 Rollout Q21 Deployment 7 RBAC Q2 n/a 8 HPA Q62 n/a 9 Termination Q65 Pod 10 Image pull Q5 Pod 11 Liveness n/a Pod 12 Ingress Q42 Ingress

docs.title: Reading Tips
docs.text:
• Read flows top-to-bottom in the order above; they roughly follow the lifecycle of a workload (create, route, observe, scale, terminate).
  • Pair each flow with the matching ELI10 section and architect Q&A for full coverage.
  • Whiteboard each flow from memory as practice.

docs.title: Common Pitfalls Highlighted by Flows
docs.text:
• Flow 2: Skipping admission means no policy enforcement. Always run validating webhooks (Kyverno, OPA).
  • Flow 3: kube-proxy iptables rules grow O(services). At 5k services, switch to IPVS or eBPF.
  • Flow 4: Env vars are static. Use volumes for live config reload.
  • Flow 5: WaitForFirstConsumer prevents cross-AZ binding mistakes.
  • Flow 6: Without readiness probes, rollout declares success too early.
  • Flow 7: Default deny — never grant cluster-admin to humans long-term.
  • Flow 8: HPA without resource requests means division by zero — set requests.
  • Flow 9: Apps must trap SIGTERM; otherwise SIGKILL after 30s loses in-flight requests.
  • Flow 10: Pull credentials per namespace via imagePullSecrets.
  • Flow 11: Liveness too aggressive causes restart storms. Use startupProbe for slow-starting apps.
  • Flow 12: TLS at LB vs Ingress — pick one for cert management sanity.

docs.title: Quick reference — strategy selector
docs.text: Strategy Downtime Risk Extra infra When to use Recreate Yes Low None Batch jobs, DB migrations RollingUpdate None Low None Default web services Blue-Green None Low 2× cost Need instant rollback Canary None Medium Ingress / mesh Gradual user exposure A/B Testing None Medium Mesh + session User cohort experiments Shadow None Very Low Mesh Validate v2 risk-free Feature Flags None Very Low Flag service Decouple deploy/release Flagger None Very Low Mesh + Prometheus Auto-gated promotion Argo Rollouts None Very Low Argo controller Step-based CI/CD Rollback Depends — None Incident recovery

docs.title: 1. Recreate
docs.text:
🧭 Reason

Why this exists. Your PostgreSQL migration adds a NOT NULL column. v1 pods cannot run alongside v2 — they will crash the moment v2 writes to the schema. You need every v1 pod dead before v2 starts. Recreate is the only Kubernetes-native strategy that guarantees this. Pretending you can avoid downtime for a schema migration is how on-call engineers get paged at 03:00.

🧠 Thinking

Mental model. Recreate is a two-phase hard-stop. All running replicas are terminated first, then the new replicas start. No overlap, no race condition.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Running_v1 : initial state
    Running_v1 --> Terminating : kubectl set image / helm upgrade
    Terminating --> Gap : all v1 pods deleted\n⚠ DOWNTIME WINDOW
    Gap --> Pending_v2 : new ReplicaSet created
    Pending_v2 --> Running_v2 : image pulled, containers ready
    Running_v2 --> [*] : stable

Key facts: - Kubernetes sets spec.strategy.type: Recreate — that's it. No tuning parameters. - The Deployment controller scales the old ReplicaSet to 0, waits for all pods to reach Terminating, then creates the new ReplicaSet. - Downtime = pod termination time + image pull time + container startup time + readiness probe delay. Budget 30–120 seconds for typical workloads. - Acceptable because batch jobs, workers, and migrating services are downstream of a queue — callers retry automatically.

⚡ Execution

Run it yourself.

# Deploy v1 with Recreate strategy
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: hello
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 4
  strategy:
    type: Recreate            # <-- the only required field
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: hello
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: hello
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: hello
        image: gcr.io/google-samples/hello-app:1.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 3
EOF

# Watch in a separate terminal while you trigger the update
kubectl get pods -w --field-selector=metadata.name!=dummy

# Trigger the upgrade (runs schema migration job first in real life)
kubectl set image deployment/hello hello=gcr.io/google-samples/hello-app:2.0

# Verify rollout complete
kubectl rollout status deployment/hello

# Confirm version
kubectl exec -it $(kubectl get pod -l app=hello -o name | head -1) \
  -- wget -qO- http://localhost:8080

🔮 Simulation — what you'll see

$ kubectl get pods -w
# NAME                     READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
# hello-7d8c9b4f6-2xkpq   1/1     Running   0          2m
# hello-7d8c9b4f6-5lmrd   1/1     Running   0          2m

🌍 Real-world use case

At Booking.com, the payments team runs nightly fare-recalculation batch workers as Recreate deployments. The strategy guarantees that a mid-flight worker running old fare logic never conflicts with the new pricing schema applied at 01:00 UTC. Downtime is measured in seconds during low-traffic overnight windows, and the CronJob that triggers the batch simply retries if it starts during the gap.

docs.text: v1: 100% · 4 pods v2: 0% · 0 pods schema: old

docs.title: 2. RollingUpdate
docs.text:
🧭 Reason

Why this exists. Your API service has 10 pods serving live traffic. You want to ship a bug fix without a maintenance window. RollingUpdate replaces pods incrementally — Kubernetes never takes down more than maxUnavailable pods at once, and never adds more than maxSurge pods above your desired count. The math determines your blast radius if the new version is broken.

🧠 Thinking

Mental model. RollingUpdate is a sliding window across your ReplicaSet. The two knobs are maxSurge (how much over capacity you'll temporarily run) and maxUnavailable (how many pods can be down simultaneously).

flowchart LR
    subgraph "replicas: 10, maxSurge: 2, maxUnavailable: 1"
        direction LR
        S1["Step 1\nv1×10"] -->|"surge +2\nterminate 1"| S2["Step 2\nv1×9 + v2×2\n= 11 pods"]
        S2 -->|"terminate 2\nsurge +2"| S3["Step 3\nv1×7 + v2×4\n= 11 pods"]
        S3 -->|"..."| SN["Step N\nv1×0 + v2×10"]
    end

Key facts: - maxSurge: 2 means Kubernetes will start 2 new v2 pods before removing old ones — you temporarily pay for 12 pods. - maxUnavailable: 1 means at most 1 pod is unhealthy at any moment. With 10 replicas, 90% capacity is always available. - The readiness probe is your traffic gate. A pod only receives traffic after its readiness probe passes. Set it correctly or you'll route requests to a pod still warming up. - Surge capacity cost: if pods cost $0.02/hour each, 2 surge pods = $0.04/hour during rollout (~10 minutes) = $0.007 per deploy. Negligible. - Default values are maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 25% — fine for most apps. High-traffic services should use maxUnavailable: 0 to guarantee full capacity.

Math: 

minimum available = replicas - maxUnavailable
maximum running   = replicas + maxSurge

⚡ Execution

Run it yourself.

kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: hello-rolling
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 10
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 2          # 12 pods max during rollout
      maxUnavailable: 1    # 9 pods always available
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: hello-rolling
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: hello-rolling
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: hello
        image: gcr.io/google-samples/hello-app:1.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 3
          failureThreshold: 3   # fail 3× before marking not-ready
EOF

# Watch rolling progress in real time
kubectl rollout status deployment/hello-rolling --watch

# Trigger the update
kubectl set image deployment/hello-rolling \
  hello=gcr.io/google-samples/hello-app:2.0

# Observe pod-by-pod replacement (run in parallel terminal)
kubectl get pods -l app=hello-rolling -L version --watch

# Verify zero downtime with a continuous probe (separate terminal)
while true; do
  curl -s http://$(kubectl get svc hello-rolling -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].ip}')/
  sleep 0.5
done

# Rollback if the new image is broken
kubectl rollout undo deployment/hello-rolling

# Cleanup
kubectl delete deployment hello-rolling

🔮 Simulation — what you'll see

$ kubectl get pods -l app=hello-rolling -L version --watch
# NAME                         READY  STATUS     VERSION
# hello-rolling-abc-r1         1/1    Running    v1
# hello-rolling-abc-r2         1/1    Running    v1
# ... (10 total v1 pods)
#
# --- update triggered ---
#
# hello-rolling-xyz-n1         0/1    Pending    v2      ← surge pod 1
# hello-rolling-xyz-n2         0/1    Pending    v2      ← surge pod 2
# hello-rolling-xyz-n1         1/1    Running    v2      ← readiness passed
# hello-rolling-abc-r1         1/1    Terminating v1
# hello-rolling-xyz-n3         0/1    Pending    v2
# ... (repeats until 10×v2)
#
$ kubectl rollout status deployment/hello-rolling
# Waiting for deployment "hello-rolling" rollout to finish: 4 out of 10 new replicas updated...
# Waiting for deployment "hello-rolling" rollout to finish: 5 out of 10 new replicas updated...
# deployment "hello-rolling" successfully rolled out

✅ Output — state change

→ →

🌍 Real-world use case

At Spotify, the backend-for-frontend team ships 40–60 deployments per day across their microservice fleet. They standardised on maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 for all HTTP services. This ensures 100% capacity throughout every rollout — critical during active listening sessions where a dropped request triggers a client retry storm. The maxUnavailable: 0 constraint adds ~90 seconds per rollout (one extra pod cycle) but eliminated all rollout-related latency spikes from their SLO dashboards.

docs.text: v1: 100% · 10 pods v2: 0% · 0 pods capacity: 10/10

docs.title: Mid-rollout
docs.text: v1: 50% · 5 pods v2: 50% · 5 pods capacity: 11/10 (surge +1) zero-downtime: YES

docs.title: After
docs.text: v1: 0% · 0 pods v2: 100% · 10 pods capacity: 10/10 zero-downtime: YES

docs.title: 3. Blue-Green
docs.text:
🧭 Reason

Why this exists. Your e-commerce checkout service cannot tolerate even a partial canary failure during Black Friday. You need the ability to flip all traffic in one atomic operation and, if something is wrong, flip it back in under 10 seconds without waiting for a rolling update to drain. Blue-Green gives you exactly that: two full environments running in parallel, with a single label selector change routing all traffic between them.

🧠 Thinking

Mental model. Two identical Deployments — blue (current) and green (new) — run side by side. The Service's selector points at one set at a time. Traffic flip is instantaneous.

flowchart LR
    LB[Load Balancer\nService]

    subgraph "Blue — v1 (live)"
        B1[pod v1] & B2[pod v1] & B3[pod v1]
    end

    subgraph "Green — v2 (idle → live)"
        G1[pod v2] & G2[pod v2] & G3[pod v2]
    end

    LB -->|"selector: slot=blue\n100% traffic"| B1
    LB -.->|"after patch:\nselector: slot=green\n100% traffic"| G1

    style B1 fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B2 fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style B3 fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff
    style G1 fill:#27ae60,color:#fff
    style G2 fill:#27ae60,color:#fff
    style G3 fill:#27ae60,color:#fff

Key facts: - Cost: 2× pod count during the transition period. For large deployments this is expensive — budget for it. - Flip time: kubectl patch service takes < 1 second. The Service endpoint controller propagates the change to kube-proxy on all nodes in ~1–5 seconds. - Rollback time: re-patch the selector back to blue. Just as fast. - Warm-up: run load against the green environment (behind a test header or internal URL) before the flip. Cold starts in green during peak traffic cause latency spikes. - Database compatibility: blue and green must be able to share the same DB schema. Use expand/contract migrations.

⚡ Execution

Run it yourself.

# --- Deploy BLUE (v1) ---
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: hello-blue
  labels:
    slot: blue
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: hello
      slot: blue
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: hello
        slot: blue
        version: v1
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: hello
        image: gcr.io/google-samples/hello-app:1.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: { path: /, port: 8080 }
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: hello
spec:
  selector:
    app: hello
    slot: blue        # <-- points at blue
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8080
EOF

# --- Deploy GREEN (v2) — traffic not yet routed ---
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: hello-green
  labels:
    slot: green
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: hello
      slot: green
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: hello
        slot: green
        version: v2
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: hello
        image: gcr.io/google-samples/hello-app:2.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: { path: /, port: 8080 }
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
EOF

# --- Wait for green to be fully ready ---
kubectl rollout status deployment/hello-green

# --- Smoke test green directly (optional pre-flight) ---
kubectl port-forward deployment/hello-green 9090:8080 &
curl -s http://localhost:9090/
kill %1

# --- FLIP: point Service at green ---
kubectl patch service hello \
  -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"hello","slot":"green"}}}'

# --- Verify ---
kubectl get endpoints hello
# All endpoint IPs should now be green pods

# --- Rollback in < 5 seconds ---
# kubectl patch service hello \
#   -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"hello","slot":"blue"}}}'

# --- Cleanup after confidence ---
kubectl delete deployment hello-blue hello-green
kubectl delete service hello

🔮 Simulation — what you'll see

$ kubectl get pods -L slot,version
# NAME                          READY   SLOT    VERSION
# hello-blue-6b9f7c-p1          1/1     blue    v1
# hello-blue-6b9f7c-p2          1/1     blue    v1
# hello-blue-6b9f7c-p3          1/1     blue    v1
# hello-green-7d4a2b-q1         1/1     green   v2
# hello-green-7d4a2b-q2         1/1     green   v2
# hello-green-7d4a2b-q3         1/1     green   v2

$ kubectl patch service hello -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"slot":"green"}}}'
# service/hello patched

$ kubectl get endpoints hello
# NAME    ENDPOINTS
# hello   10.244.1.12:8080,10.244.2.7:8080,10.244.3.4:8080
#  ↑ all three IPs belong to green pods now

✅ Output — state change

→ →

🌍 Real-world use case

At Amazon, the Prime Day team uses blue-green deployments for the checkout path. In 2022, a payments service bug was caught 4 minutes after the green flip via Canary CloudWatch alarms. The selector was flipped back to blue in under 3 seconds — before a single customer order failed. The green deployment sat idle for 2 hours while the bug was patched, then the flip was re-attempted successfully. The 2× cost of idle green pods during the 2-hour window was immaterial compared to preventing a Prime Day outage.

docs.text: blue: 100% · 3 pods (live) green: 0% · 3 pods (idle, warm) traffic: → blue only cost: 2× pod count

docs.title: Flip (~2s)
docs.text: Service selector patching endpoint propagation in progress both slots running in-flight requests finish on blue

docs.title: After flip
docs.text: blue: 0% · 3 pods (standby 30min) green: 100% · 3 pods (live) zero-downtime: YES rollback: patch selector back

docs.title: 4. Canary
docs.text:
🧭 Reason

Why this exists. You are not confident enough for a full Blue-Green flip. You want 5% of real production requests to hit v2 so your monitoring can tell you whether error rates, latency p99, and business metrics (conversion rate, add-to-cart) are healthy before you expose the rest. If v2 is bad, only 5% of users were affected. The name comes from canaries in coal mines — early warning at minimal cost.

🧠 Thinking

Mental model. Traffic splits by pod count ratio. A Service with selector: app=hello will round-robin across all matching pods regardless of which Deployment owns them. You control the ratio by controlling replica counts.

flowchart LR
    subgraph "Traffic split by replica ratio"
        LB[Service\napp=hello] -->|"90% → 9 pods"| D1[Deployment v1\n9 replicas]
        LB -->|"10% → 1 pod"| D2[Deployment v2\n1 replica]
    end

    subgraph "Promotion steps"
        P0["0% v2"] --> P10["10% v2\n1 pod"] --> P30["30% v2\n3 pods"]
        P30 --> P50["50%\n5 pods"] --> P100["100% v2\nscale v1 → 0"]
    end

Key facts: - Traffic ratio = v2 replicas / (v1 replicas + v2 replicas). With 9+1=10 pods total, 1 v2 pod = 10%. - You need both Deployments to share the same Service selector — only the version label differs. - Readiness gate: the new pod must pass its readiness probe before it enters the endpoint pool. A failing v2 pod gets removed from rotation automatically. - Header-based canary: more precise targeting — Nginx Ingress canary-by-header: X-Canary: always routes that user to v2 regardless of pod count. Use this for internal QA. - Metrics gate: after each step, check your SLO dashboard. Automate this with Flagger (concept 8).

⚡ Execution

Run it yourself.

# --- Stable v1 with 9 replicas ---
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: hello-stable
spec:
  replicas: 9
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: hello-canary
      track: stable
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: hello-canary
        track: stable
        version: v1
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: hello
        image: gcr.io/google-samples/hello-app:1.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: { path: /, port: 8080 }
          initialDelaySeconds: 3
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: hello-canary
spec:
  selector:
    app: hello-canary     # matches BOTH stable and canary
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8080
EOF

# --- Canary v2 — starts at 1 replica (10%) ---
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: hello-canary
spec:
  replicas: 1             # 1/(9+1) = 10%
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: hello-canary
      track: canary
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: hello-canary
        track: canary
        version: v2
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: hello
        image: gcr.io/google-samples/hello-app:2.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: { path: /, port: 8080 }
          initialDelaySeconds: 3
EOF

# --- Observe split ---
kubectl get pods -l app=hello-canary -L track,version

# --- Promote: 30% canary ---
kubectl scale deployment hello-canary --replicas=4   # 4/(6+4)=40%
kubectl scale deployment hello-stable --replicas=6

# --- Promote: 50% canary ---
kubectl scale deployment hello-canary --replicas=5
kubectl scale deployment hello-stable --replicas=5

# --- Full promotion: 100% canary ---
kubectl scale deployment hello-stable --replicas=0
kubectl scale deployment hello-canary --replicas=9

# --- Rollback: bump stable back, kill canary ---
# kubectl scale deployment hello-stable --replicas=9
# kubectl scale deployment hello-canary --replicas=0

# Cleanup
kubectl delete deployment hello-stable hello-canary
kubectl delete service hello-canary

🔮 Simulation — what you'll see

$ kubectl get pods -l app=hello-canary -L track,version
# NAME                        READY  TRACK    VERSION
# hello-stable-6bc-s1         1/1    stable   v1
# hello-stable-6bc-s2         1/1    stable   v1
# hello-stable-6bc-s3         1/1    stable   v1
# hello-stable-6bc-s4         1/1    stable   v1
# hello-stable-6bc-s5         1/1    stable   v1
# hello-stable-6bc-s6         1/1    stable   v1
# hello-stable-6bc-s7         1/1    stable   v1
# hello-stable-6bc-s8         1/1    stable   v1
# hello-stable-6bc-s9         1/1    stable   v1
# hello-canary-9df-c1         1/1    canary   v2   ← 10% traffic
#
# After scale: 5 stable + 5 canary
# hello-stable-6bc-s1..5      1/1    stable   v1   ← 50%
# hello-canary-9df-c1..5      1/1    canary   v2   ← 50%

✅ Output — state change

→ →

🌍 Real-world use case

At Netflix, the streaming team runs canary deployments for every change to the video playback service. They start at 1% (roughly 1.4 million requests/hour at peak). Their "canary analysis" framework — open-sourced as Kayenta — compares error rate, latency distributions, and business metrics (play-start success rate, rebuffer ratio) between canary and baseline using Mann-Whitney U tests. If the canary's p99 latency exceeds baseline + 10ms over a 30-minute window, the canary is automatically killed and the on-call engineer receives a Slack alert with the specific metric that failed.

docs.text: v1: 0% · 0 pods v2: 100% · 9 pods zero-downtime: YES affected on failure: max 10%

docs.title: 5. A/B Testing vs Canary
docs.text:
🧭 Reason

Why this exists. A canary releases v2 to a random slice of traffic to validate stability. An A/B test releases a variant to a specific user cohort to measure a business outcome. The question changes from "is v2 broken?" to "does this checkout button colour increase conversion by 3%?". Confusing these two patterns causes you to either over-complicate a stability check or under-instrument a business experiment.

🧠 Thinking

Mental model. The routing key changes from "random 10% of requests" to "user ID hash mod N" or "header cookie matches cohort ID". Session stickiness is mandatory — a user must stay in the same variant for the duration of the experiment.

flowchart LR
    subgraph "Canary (random traffic slice)"
        CR[Client Request] --> IGW[Ingress\n10% → v2\n90% → v1]
        IGW -->|random| V1A[v1 pod]
        IGW -->|random| V2A[v2 pod]
    end

    subgraph "A/B Test (deterministic cohort)"
        ABR[Client Request\n+ user_id cookie] --> ABGW[Mesh / Ingress\nuser_id hash\nmod 2]
        ABGW -->|"cohort A\nuser_id % 2 = 0"| V1B[v1 Checkout A]
        ABGW -->|"cohort B\nuser_id % 2 = 1"| V2B[v2 Checkout B]
    end

Key facts: - Canary: validates infrastructure/code safety. Metric = error rate, latency, crash rate. - A/B test: validates product hypothesis. Metric = conversion, revenue per user, engagement. - Session stickiness: set nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-by-cookie: "abtest-group". Users without the cookie are assigned a group and the cookie is set on first response. All subsequent requests from that user hit the same variant. - Sample size: use a power analysis before starting. With 0.5% expected conversion lift, you need ~50k users per group. A 1% canary slice on low-traffic services runs experiments for months. - Istio approach: VirtualService with match.headers routing. Supports exact, regex, prefix on any header or cookie. - Concurrent experiments: use Unleash or LaunchDarkly to manage experiment assignment centrally rather than encoding it in your Ingress config.

⚡ Execution

Run it yourself.

# Prerequisites: Nginx Ingress controller installed
# kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/controller-v1.10.0/deploy/static/provider/cloud/deploy.yaml

# --- Deploy both variants ---
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
# Variant A — control
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: checkout-a
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: checkout, variant: a }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: checkout, variant: a }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: checkout
        image: gcr.io/google-samples/hello-app:1.0
        ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: checkout-a
spec:
  selector: { app: checkout, variant: a }
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 8080 }]
---
# Variant B — treatment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: checkout-b
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: checkout, variant: b }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: checkout, variant: b }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: checkout
        image: gcr.io/google-samples/hello-app:2.0
        ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: checkout-b
spec:
  selector: { app: checkout, variant: b }
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 8080 }]
EOF

# --- Primary Ingress (variant A — default) ---
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: checkout-primary
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/ingress.class: nginx
spec:
  rules:
  - host: checkout.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: checkout-a
            port: { number: 80 }
EOF

# --- Canary Ingress (variant B — cookie-based cohort) ---
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: checkout-canary-b
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/ingress.class: nginx
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-by-cookie: "ab-group"
    # Users with cookie ab-group=always → variant B
    # Users with cookie ab-group=never  → variant A
spec:
  rules:
  - host: checkout.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: checkout-b
            port: { number: 80 }
EOF

# --- Test assignment ---
# Assign user to variant B
curl -s -H "Cookie: ab-group=always" \
  http://checkout.example.com/

# Force variant A
curl -s -H "Cookie: ab-group=never" \
  http://checkout.example.com/

# Cleanup
kubectl delete ingress checkout-primary checkout-canary-b
kubectl delete deployment checkout-a checkout-b
kubectl delete service checkout-a checkout-b

🔮 Simulation — what you'll see

$ curl -s -H "Cookie: ab-group=always" http://checkout.example.com/
# Hello, world!
# Version: 2.0.0  ← variant B confirmed

$ curl -s -H "Cookie: ab-group=never" http://checkout.example.com/
# Hello, world!
# Version: 1.0.0  ← variant A confirmed

$ # No cookie = random assignment (50/50 by default)
$ for i in $(seq 1 6); do
    curl -s http://checkout.example.com/ | grep Version
  done
# Version: 1.0.0
# Version: 2.0.0
# Version: 1.0.0
# Version: 1.0.0
# Version: 2.0.0
# Version: 2.0.0

✅ Output — state change

→ →

🌍 Real-world use case

At Facebook, the Ads team runs over 1,000 simultaneous A/B experiments at any given time using their internal "GateKeeper" system (the public equivalent is LaunchDarkly). When they changed the call-to-action button on the Ads Manager, they ran a cohort experiment on 2% of advertisers for 14 days. The experiment used user-ID-based consistent hashing so each advertiser always saw the same UI. The variant increased campaign creation rates by 7.2%, an effect that would have been invisible in a random-traffic canary because the signal was in repeat-session behaviour, not first-request error rate.

docs.title: Experiment running (2 weeks)

docs.title: Variant B wins

docs.title: 6. Shadow / Mirror Traffic
docs.text:
🧭 Reason

Why this exists. You are rewriting a payment processing service in Rust. Before you route a single real charge to it, you want to run every production request through it in parallel — seeing how it handles real load, real edge cases, real malformed inputs — without risking a single customer transaction. Shadow traffic lets you validate v2 with 100% production fidelity and zero user impact.

🧠 Thinking

Mental model. The service mesh (Istio) duplicates every inbound request: one copy goes to v1 (primary, user-facing), the other goes to v2 (shadow). Responses from v2 are discarded. The user only ever sees the v1 response.

flowchart LR
    Client --> VS[Istio VirtualService]
    VS -->|"100% primary\nresponse → user"| V1[Service v1\nlive]
    VS -.->|"100% mirror\nresponse discarded"| V2[Service v2\nshadow]

    V2 --> DB2[(Shadow DB\nor read-only replica)]
    V1 --> DB1[(Production DB)]

    subgraph "Observability"
        V2 --> PROM[Prometheus\nlatency / errors\nv2 only]
    end

Key facts: - Responses from the shadow service are always discarded — Istio does not wait for them. If v2 crashes, v1 and the user are completely unaffected. - Shadow requests carry the same headers, body, and timing as the originals. - DB isolation: if v2 writes to a real DB, those writes are real. You must route v2 to a shadow DB or use read-only mode. This is the hardest part of shadow deployments. - Rate limiting: at peak, shadow doubles your backend load. Use mirror_percent: 10 to sample 10% of traffic instead of 100%. - Istio VirtualService field: spec.http[].mirror + spec.http[].mirrorPercentage. - Stripe uses this for payment gateway rewrites — they mirror 5% of production payment requests to the new gateway and compare response payloads.

⚡ Execution

Run it yourself.

# Prerequisites: Istio installed
# istioctl install --set profile=demo -y
# kubectl label namespace default istio-injection=enabled

kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
# v1 — primary service
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: payments-v1
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: payments, version: v1 }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: payments, version: v1 }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: payments
        image: gcr.io/google-samples/hello-app:1.0
        ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
---
# v2 — shadow service (Rust rewrite)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: payments-v2
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: payments, version: v2 }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: payments, version: v2 }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: payments
        image: gcr.io/google-samples/hello-app:2.0
        ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: payments
spec:
  selector: { app: payments }
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 8080 }]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: payments-shadow
spec:
  selector: { app: payments, version: v2 }
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 8080 }]
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: payments
spec:
  hosts: [payments]
  http:
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: payments
        subset: v1
      weight: 100
    mirror:
      host: payments-shadow   # shadow receives copy
    mirrorPercentage:
      value: 100.0            # mirror 100% of traffic
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: payments
spec:
  host: payments
  subsets:
  - name: v1
    labels: { version: v1 }
  - name: v2
    labels: { version: v2 }
EOF

# Send test traffic
kubectl run curl-test --image=curlimages/curl --rm -it \
  -- curl -s http://payments/

# Watch shadow logs (v2 receives mirrored requests)
kubectl logs -l version=v2 -f --tail=20

# Check v2 error rate in Prometheus (if installed)
# rate(istio_requests_total{destination_app="payments-shadow",response_code!~"2.."}[5m])

# Cleanup
kubectl delete -f - # (the above YAML)

🔮 Simulation — what you'll see

$ kubectl logs -l version=v2 -f --tail=20
# 2026-04-27T10:15:32Z GET /api/payment 200 12ms shadow-req-id=a1b2c3
# 2026-04-27T10:15:32Z GET /api/payment 200 14ms shadow-req-id=d4e5f6
# 2026-04-27T10:15:33Z POST /api/charge  200 45ms shadow-req-id=g7h8i9
# 2026-04-27T10:15:33Z POST /api/charge  500 3ms  shadow-req-id=j0k1l2
# ↑ v2 is throwing 500s on POST /charge — caught with zero user impact

$ # Meanwhile, v1 is serving all users correctly:
$ kubectl logs -l version=v1 --tail=5
# 2026-04-27T10:15:33Z POST /api/charge  200 48ms req-id=j0k1l2
# ↑ Same request, v1 succeeded. User saw 200. v2 500 was discarded.

✅ Output — state change

→ →

🌍 Real-world use case

At Stripe, the payments infrastructure team spent 18 months rewriting their charge-routing service in Go (from Ruby). Before enabling a single real transaction on the new service, they mirrored 5% of production charge requests to it for 90 days. During this period they identified 14 edge cases — including a currency-rounding bug for JPY transactions that only appeared at high decimal precision — that were invisible in their test suite. Every one of these bugs was caught without a customer ever seeing a failed payment. Shadow traffic was the difference between a risky cutover and a confident one.

docs.title: Shadow active
docs.text: v1: 100% · 3 pods (users see this) v2: 100% mirrored · 3 pods (shadow) user impact: zero v2 errors visible in metrics

docs.title: Bug found, fixed, promoted
docs.text: v1: 0% · 0 pods (decommissioned) v2: 100% · 3 pods (promoted safely) zero-downtime: YES confidence: battle-tested at prod load

docs.title: 7. Feature Flags
docs.text:
🧭 Reason

Why this exists. You deploy code 20 times a day but release features once a week. Feature flags decouple those two actions. You ship the new checkout flow to production behind a flag: new-checkout=false on Tuesday. On Thursday, you flip the flag for 1% of users. Monday, you flip it for everyone. If anything goes wrong, the rollback is a flag toggle — no redeploy, no kubectl, no downtime. The code is already there; the flag controls whether users see it.

🧠 Thinking

Mental model. The flag service is a real-time configuration layer. Your application SDK calls the flag service on each request (with local caching) to determine which code path to execute.

flowchart LR
    subgraph "Flag-controlled code path"
        R[Request] --> SDK[SDK.isEnabled\n'new-checkout'\nuserId]
        SDK -->|"cache miss"| FS[Flag Service\nLaunchDarkly\nFlagsmith\nUnleash]
        SDK -->|"cache hit\n<100ms"| LP[Local cache\nTTL: 30s]
        FS --> EVAL{Evaluate\ntargeting rules}
        EVAL -->|"user in\nrollout 10%"| NC[New Checkout\nv2 code path]
        EVAL -->|"user not\nin rollout"| OC[Old Checkout\nv1 code path]
        LP --> EVAL
    end

Key facts: - LaunchDarkly: SaaS, 30ms p99 flag evaluation, streaming updates. $10k+/year for large orgs. - Flagsmith: open-source, self-hostable on Kubernetes. helm install flagsmith flagsmith/flagsmith. - Unleash: open-source, enterprise version, battle-tested at GitLab. helm install unleash unleash/unleash. - Flag types: boolean (on/off), multivariate (A/B/C), percentage rollout, user targeting, segment targeting. - Stale flags are technical debt: enforce a TTL policy. Every flag gets a removal_date in the flag service. Facebook calls unremoved flags "flag debt" and runs quarterly cleanup sprints. - Runtime config vs feature flag: feature flags are for user-facing features. Runtime config (feature flags for infrastructure) should use ConfigMaps or cloud parameter stores, not a feature flag service.

⚡ Execution

Run it yourself.

# --- Deploy Unleash (self-hosted open-source) ---
helm repo add unleash https://docs.getunleash.io/helm-charts
helm repo update

kubectl create namespace unleash

helm install unleash unleash/unleash \
  --namespace unleash \
  --set postgresql.auth.password=unleash123 \
  --set unleash.auth.adminPassword=admin123 \
  --wait

# --- Port-forward Unleash UI ---
kubectl port-forward -n unleash svc/unleash 4242:4242 &
# Open http://localhost:4242 — login: admin / admin123

# --- Create a feature flag via API ---
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:4242/api/admin/features \
  -H "Authorization: *:*.unleash-insecure-api-token" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "new-checkout",
    "description": "New checkout flow",
    "type": "release",
    "enabled": false,
    "strategies": [
      {
        "name": "gradualRolloutUserId",
        "parameters": {
          "percentage": "10",
          "groupId": "new-checkout"
        }
      }
    ]
  }'

# --- SDK usage in your application (Python example) ---
cat > /tmp/flag_demo.py << 'PYEOF'
from UnleashClient import UnleashClient

client = UnleashClient(
    url="http://localhost:4242/api",
    app_name="checkout-service",
    custom_headers={"Authorization": "*:*.unleash-insecure-api-token"}
)
client.initialize_client()

# Evaluate flag for user
user_id = "user-12345"
if client.is_enabled("new-checkout", {"userId": user_id}):
    print(f"[{user_id}] → new checkout flow")
else:
    print(f"[{user_id}] → old checkout flow")
PYEOF
# pip install UnleashClient && python /tmp/flag_demo.py

# --- Enable flag for 100% of users ---
curl -s -X POST \
  http://localhost:4242/api/admin/features/new-checkout/toggles/on \
  -H "Authorization: *:*.unleash-insecure-api-token"

# --- Instant rollback: disable flag ---
curl -s -X POST \
  http://localhost:4242/api/admin/features/new-checkout/toggles/off \
  -H "Authorization: *:*.unleash-insecure-api-token"

# Cleanup
helm uninstall unleash -n unleash
kubectl delete namespace unleash
kill %1

🔮 Simulation — what you'll see

$ # Flag at 10% rollout — testing with different user IDs
$ python /tmp/flag_demo.py  # user-12345
# [user-12345] → old checkout flow   (in 90% bucket)

$ # Test with user in 10% bucket
# [user-98765] → new checkout flow   (in 10% bucket)

$ # After toggling flag ON for all users:
# [user-12345] → new checkout flow
# [user-98765] → new checkout flow

$ # After emergency rollback (toggle OFF):
# [user-12345] → old checkout flow   (instant, no redeploy)
# SDK cache TTL: 30s until all instances reflect the change

✅ Output — state change

→ →

🌍 Real-world use case

At Facebook, the feature flag system ("GK" — GateKeeper) controls virtually every user-facing change. When they redesigned the News Feed ranking algorithm in 2023, the new algorithm was deployed to all servers weeks before any user saw it. The rollout started at 0.01% (roughly 30k users), stayed there for 72 hours for automated metric collection, then progressed in 5% weekly increments. When engagement metrics dipped below threshold at 35% rollout, GateKeeper automatically paused the rollout and paged the team — no engineer had to manually monitor dashboards. The entire rollout took 6 weeks; the code deploy took 2 hours.

docs.text: new-checkout: 100% users flag: scheduled for removal deploy: unchanged zero-downtime: YES

docs.title: 8. Progressive Delivery with Flagger
docs.text:
🧭 Reason

Why this exists. Manual canary promotions require an engineer watching dashboards and running kubectl scale commands every 30 minutes. At Monzo, with 1,500 microservices, that human cost is unsustainable. Flagger — created by Weaveworks — automates this loop: it runs the canary, queries Prometheus for your SLOs, promotes automatically if metrics pass, and rolls back automatically if they fail. You define the policy once; Flagger runs every deployment after that.

🧠 Thinking

Mental model. Flagger installs a controller that watches Canary CRDs. When you change a Deployment's image, Flagger intercepts it, creates a shadow primary Deployment, and incrementally shifts traffic using weighted VirtualServices while polling Prometheus.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Initializing : Canary CRD created
    Initializing --> Waiting : primary healthy
    Waiting --> Progressing : new image detected
    Progressing --> Progressing : weight +10% every 60s\nif SLO ok
    Progressing --> Succeeded : weight == 100%\nall metrics green
    Progressing --> Failed : metric threshold breached\nor max iterations exceeded
    Failed --> Waiting : traffic shifted back\nv1 restored
    Succeeded --> Waiting : primary updated\ncanary deleted

Key facts: - Flagger supports Istio, Linkerd, Contour, Nginx, App Mesh, Gloo as traffic providers. - Metric templates: you define a MetricTemplate pointing at your Prometheus query. Flagger calls it every interval and checks it against threshold. - stepWeight: traffic increment per analysis iteration (default 10%). - maxWeight: maximum canary traffic (default 50% — half your users). - iterations: number of checks before promotion. iterations * interval = total analysis time. - Webhooks can trigger load tests, run e2e tests, or notify Slack before/during/after promotion. - Weaveworks coined the term "progressive delivery" to describe this automated, metric-gated release pattern.

⚡ Execution

Run it yourself.

# Prerequisites: Istio + Prometheus installed
# helm repo add flagger https://flagger.app
helm repo add flagger https://flagger.app
helm repo update

# Install Flagger for Istio
helm upgrade -i flagger flagger/flagger \
  --namespace=istio-system \
  --set crd.create=true \
  --set meshProvider=istio \
  --set metricsServer=http://prometheus:9090

# --- Deploy the app ---
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: hello
  labels:
    app: hello
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: hello
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: hello
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: hello
        image: gcr.io/google-samples/hello-app:1.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: { path: /, port: 8080 }
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: hello
spec:
  selector: { app: hello }
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 8080 }]
EOF

# --- Create Flagger Canary resource ---
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: flagger.app/v1beta1
kind: Canary
metadata:
  name: hello
spec:
  targetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: hello
  service:
    port: 80
    targetPort: 8080
  analysis:
    interval: 60s          # check every 60 seconds
    threshold: 5           # max 5 failed metric checks before rollback
    maxWeight: 50          # promote up to 50% traffic max
    stepWeight: 10         # increment by 10% per step
    metrics:
    - name: request-success-rate
      thresholdRange:
        min: 99            # success rate must be > 99%
      interval: 1m
    - name: request-duration
      thresholdRange:
        max: 500           # p99 latency must be < 500ms
      interval: 30s
    webhooks:
    - name: load-test
      url: http://flagger-loadtester/
      timeout: 5s
      metadata:
        cmd: "hey -z 1m -q 10 -c 2 http://hello/"
EOF

# --- Trigger canary by updating the image ---
kubectl set image deployment/hello \
  hello=gcr.io/google-samples/hello-app:2.0

# --- Watch Flagger progress ---
kubectl get canary hello --watch
kubectl describe canary hello

# --- Check events ---
kubectl get events --field-selector=reason=Synced

# Cleanup
kubectl delete canary hello
kubectl delete deployment hello
kubectl delete service hello

🔮 Simulation — what you'll see

$ kubectl get canary hello --watch
# NAME    STATUS        WEIGHT  LASTTRANSITIONTIME
# hello   Initialized   0       2026-04-27T10:00:00Z
# hello   Progressing   10      2026-04-27T10:01:00Z
# hello   Progressing   20      2026-04-27T10:02:00Z
# hello   Progressing   30      2026-04-27T10:03:00Z
# hello   Progressing   40      2026-04-27T10:04:00Z
# hello   Progressing   50      2026-04-27T10:05:00Z
# hello   Succeeded     0       2026-04-27T10:06:00Z
#  ↑ primary updated, canary cleaned up

$ # If v2 has errors:
# hello   Progressing   20      10:02:00Z
# hello   Progressing   20      10:03:00Z  ← metric failed, no increment
# hello   Failed        0       10:07:00Z  ← 5 failures → rollback
# hello   Waiting       0       10:07:05Z  ← back to v1

✅ Output — state change

→ →

🌍 Real-world use case

At Monzo, the UK challenger bank runs over 1,500 microservices. Before Flagger, promoting a canary required an engineer to sit at a dashboard for 30 minutes per service. After adopting Flagger with Linkerd in 2020, they automated canary promotions for all non-critical services. Their MetricTemplate checks a single SLO: success rate > 99.9% at each 1-minute interval. In their first year, Flagger automatically rolled back 23 deployments that would have otherwise required on-call intervention — each rollback took under 2 minutes, compared to a 15-minute mean manual rollback time.
