go install sigs.k8s.io/kubebuilder/v4@latest
mkdir my-operator && cd my-operator
kubebuilder init --domain example.com --repo github.com/me/my-operator
kubebuilder create api --group apps --version v1alpha1 --kind MyApp
make generate manifests
make install                                    # install CRDs into cluster
make run                                        # run controller locally against cluster
make docker-build docker-push IMG=ghcr.io/me/my-operator:dev
make deploy IMG=ghcr.io/me/my-operator:dev

make run

docs.title: Controller Reconcile Loop
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant API as kube-apiserver
    participant Inf as Informer (cache)
    participant Q as Workqueue
    participant R as Reconciler
    participant Ext as External system

    User->>API: kubectl apply foo.yaml
    API->>Inf: watch event (ADD)
    Inf->>Q: enqueue key ns/name
    Q->>R: dequeue
    R->>Inf: Get(Foo) from cache
    R->>Ext: read actual state
    alt drift detected
      R->>API: Create/Update child resources
      R->>API: Update status subresource
    else converged
      R->>R: no-op
    end
    R->>Q: requeue after N (or on next event)

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Idempotent: same input -> same action, safe to retry.
  • Level-triggered, not edge-triggered: always reconcile from current state, never from the event payload.
  • Status vs Spec: write status only via the /status subresource to avoid optimistic-lock churn.
  • Finalizers: add a finalizer string in metadata.finalizers to defer deletion until cleanup completes; remove it when done.
  • Owner references: set ownerReferences on child objects so they GC when the parent is deleted.
  • Backoff: use rate-limited workqueues (controller-runtime does this by default).

docs.title: Common traps
docs.text:
• Mutating cached objects from the informer — always DeepCopy() first.
  • Long-running work in Reconcile — return early and requeue instead.
  • Forgetting to handle "not found" (object deleted) — return nil, do not error.

docs.title: 02 — Admission Controllers
docs.text:
Admission controllers intercept API requests after authentication/authorization but before persistence. They can mutate or validate.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    Client[kubectl] --> Auth[AuthN/AuthZ]
    Auth --> Mut[Mutating Admission]
    Mut --> Schema[Schema Validation]
    Schema --> Val[Validating Admission]
    Val --> Etcd[(etcd)]
    Mut -.webhook.-> MW[MutatingWebhook]
    Val -.webhook.-> VW[ValidatingWebhook]
    Val -.in-process.-> VAP[ValidatingAdmissionPolicy CEL]

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text:
Concept Manifest kubectl Expected output

Admission controllers run inside the API server flow after authn/authz, before persistence. Mutating webhooks patch objects (defaults, sidecars); validating webhooks and CEL ValidatingAdmissionPolicy accept or reject. Kyverno and OPA Gatekeeper are the dominant policy engines.

apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-labels
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  background: true
  rules:
    - name: check-required-labels
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: [Pod, Deployment, StatefulSet]
      validate:
        message: "Labels 'app.kubernetes.io/name' and 'owner' are required."
        pattern:
          metadata:
            labels:
              app.kubernetes.io/name: "?*"
              owner: "?*"

kubectl apply -f kyverno-policy.yaml
kubectl get clusterpolicy require-labels
# try a non-compliant pod
kubectl run test --image=nginx --dry-run=server -o yaml

clusterpolicy.kyverno.io/require-labels created
Error from server: admission webhook "validate.kyverno.svc-fail" denied the request:

resource Pod/default/test was blocked due to the following policies:

require-labels:
  check-required-labels: 'validation error: Labels ''app.kubernetes.io/name''
    and ''owner'' are required. rule check-required-labels failed at path /metadata/labels/'

docs.title: Three flavors
docs.text: Type Where it runs Use Built-in (compiled) inside kube-apiserver NamespaceLifecycle, ResourceQuota, PodSecurity, etc Webhook (Mutating/Validating) external HTTPS service Custom logic in any language ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL) inside kube-apiserver, GA in 1.30 Declarative validation, no webhook to operate

docs.title: Mutating vs Validating
docs.text:
• Mutating runs first, can patch the object (defaults, sidecar injection).
  • Validating runs after schema check, can only accept/reject.
  • All mutating webhooks must be idempotent and run before all validating ones.

docs.title: Policy engines
docs.text:
Engine Language Scope OPA Gatekeeper Rego (ConstraintTemplate + Constraint) Validation, audit Kyverno YAML-native policies Validate / Mutate / Generate / VerifyImages jsPolicy JavaScript Validate / Mutate

For most teams Kyverno is the lowest-friction choice. Use Gatekeeper if you already have Rego skills or need OPA elsewhere.

docs.title: 03 — Scheduling
docs.text:
The kube-scheduler picks a node for each unscheduled pod via filter (predicates) and score (priorities) plugins.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    P[Pending Pod] --> Filter[Filter plugins\nnodeSelector, taints,\nresources, affinity]
    Filter --> Score[Score plugins\nspread, balance,\nimage locality]
    Score --> Bind[Bind to node]
    Bind --> Kubelet[Kubelet starts pod]

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text:
Concept Manifest kubectl Expected output

The kube-scheduler filters nodes (predicates) then scores them (priorities). Workloads steer placement with nodeSelector, affinity, taints/tolerations, and topologySpreadConstraints. Spread is the cheap way to keep replicas balanced across zones.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 6
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: web }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: web }
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels: { app: web }
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
          whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels: { app: web }
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:1.27

kubectl apply -f topology-spread.yaml
kubectl get pods -l app=web -o wide
kubectl get pods -l app=web \
  -o custom-columns=POD:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName,ZONE:.metadata.labels.topology\\.kubernetes\\.io/zone

NAME                   READY   STATUS    NODE                ZONE
web-7b9f-aaaaa         1/1     Running   ip-10-0-1-10        us-east-1a
web-7b9f-bbbbb         1/1     Running   ip-10-0-2-20        us-east-1b
web-7b9f-ccccc         1/1     Running   ip-10-0-3-30        us-east-1c
web-7b9f-ddddd         1/1     Running   ip-10-0-1-11        us-east-1a
web-7b9f-eeeee         1/1     Running   ip-10-0-2-21        us-east-1b
web-7b9f-fffff         1/1     Running   ip-10-0-3-31        us-east-1c

docs.title: Knobs
docs.text: Mechanism Use nodeSelector Hard match on node labels (simple) nodeAffinity Required (hard) or preferred (soft) expressions podAffinity / podAntiAffinity Co-locate or spread relative to other pods taints + tolerations Repel pods from nodes unless they tolerate topologySpreadConstraints Even spread across zones / nodes priorityClass + preemption Critical pods evict lower-priority ones descheduler Periodic rebalancing of already-running pods

docs.title: Topology spread vs anti-affinity
docs.text:
• Anti-affinity is per-pod; cost grows O(N^2) at scale.
  • Topology spread is declarative balance (maxSkew); cheaper for large fleets.

docs.title: Priority and preemption
docs.text:
• A PriorityClass with high value lets the scheduler preempt lower-priority pods to make room.
  • system-cluster-critical and system-node-critical are reserved for control-plane components.

docs.title: Descheduler
docs.text: Runs as a Job/CronJob, evicts pods that violate policies (low utilization, duplicate replicas on a node, topology violations) so they get rescheduled.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
The kube-scheduler decides where every Pod runs. In a non-trivial cluster — multi-tenant, GPU, spot/on-demand mixes, topology-aware workloads — the default scheduler is rarely enough. You need to know:

  • the two-phase pipeline (filter → score) and the 12 extension points around it,
  • how to configure profiles so different workloads use different policies,
  • when to write an out-of-tree plugin vs. a second scheduler instance vs. a webhook,
  • and what changed since 1.30: PodSchedulingReadiness GA, in-place pod resize beta, dynamic resource allocation (DRA) GA in 1.34.

The "predicates → priorities" terminology is legacy (pre-1.19). Modern Kubernetes uses the Scheduling Framework.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
The scheduler is a single-threaded loop that pops one pod at a time off the active queue, runs it through a fixed sequence of extension points wired with plugins, and writes a Binding back to the apiserver. It is stateless; all state lives in the cache rebuilt from API watches.

Two phases:

  1. Scheduling cycle (synchronous, one pod at a time)
  2. filter out infeasible nodes
  3. score the survivors
  4. pick the winner
  5. Binding cycle (asynchronous, can overlap pods)
  6. reserve, permit, bind
  7. write Pod.spec.nodeName via Binding subresource

docs.title: Diagram 1 — The Scheduling Framework extension points
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    Q["ActiveQBackoffQUnschedulableQ"] --> SS[Sort]
    SS --> PF[PreFilter]
    PF --> F[Filter]
    F --> PoF["PostFilterpreemption"]
    PoF --> PreS[PreScore]
    PreS --> SC[Score]
    SC --> NS[NormalizeScore]
    NS --> R[Reserve]
    R --> P[Permit]
    P --> PB[PreBind]
    PB --> B[Bind]
    B --> PostB[PostBind]
Extension point Purpose Built-in example QueueSort order the queue (only one allowed) PrioritySort PreFilter per-pod precompute, may declare infeasibility InterPodAffinity Filter drop nodes (= old "predicates") NodeAffinity, TaintToleration, NodeResourcesFit PostFilter runs only if no node passed Filter; preemption lives here DefaultPreemption PreScore per-pod precompute for scoring TopologySpread Score rank surviving nodes 0–100 (= old "priorities") NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation, ImageLocality NormalizeScore rescale a plugin's scores — Reserve mark resources as taken in cache (revertible) VolumeBinding Permit approve / deny / wait (custom approvals like gang-scheduling) — PreBind prep work before binding (e.g., bind PVC) VolumeBinding Bind write the Binding object DefaultBinder PostBind cleanup / metrics —

docs.title: Diagram 2 — Lifecycle of a single pod
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
sequenceDiagram
    participant API as kube-apiserver
    participant Q as Scheduling Queue
    participant SC as Scheduler Cycle
    participant BC as Binding Cycle
    participant N as Node (kubelet)

    API->>Q: WATCH new Pod (no nodeName)
    Q->>SC: pop highest-priority pod
    SC->>SC: PreFilter → Filter on all nodes
    alt no nodes pass
        SC->>SC: PostFilter (preemption)
        SC-->>Q: requeue or evict victim
    else nodes pass
        SC->>SC: PreScore → Score → pick winner
        SC->>BC: Reserve cache slot
        BC->>BC: Permit (gang? quota?)
        BC->>API: PreBind (bind PVC, etc.)
        BC->>API: POST /pods/{name}/binding
        API->>N: WATCH pod with nodeName
        N->>N: kubelet starts the pod
    end

docs.title: Profiles: multiple schedulers in one binary
docs.text:
Since 1.19, a single kube-scheduler binary can serve multiple profiles under the same process. A pod selects one with spec.schedulerName.

apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: KubeSchedulerConfiguration
profiles:
  - schedulerName: default-scheduler
    plugins:
      score:
        enabled:
          - name: NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation
            weight: 1
        disabled:
          - name: ImageLocality

  - schedulerName: gpu-scheduler        # workloads opt in via spec.schedulerName
    plugins:
      filter:
        enabled:
          - name: MyGPUTopologyFilter   # out-of-tree plugin
      score:
        enabled:
          - name: MyGPUBinPack
            weight: 5
    pluginConfig:
      - name: MyGPUTopologyFilter
        args:
          requireNVLink: true

Why profiles beat running two scheduler binaries: shared cache, no split-brain over node state, single leader election.

docs.title: Walkthrough: writing an out-of-tree plugin (Go, 1.30+)
docs.text:
package mybinpack

import (
    "context"
    v1 "k8s.io/api/core/v1"
    "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime"
    "k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/scheduler/framework"
)

type MyBinPack struct {
    handle framework.Handle
}

// implement two interfaces: ScorePlugin and ScoreExtensions
var _ framework.ScorePlugin = &MyBinPack{}

const Name = "MyBinPack"

func (m *MyBinPack) Name() string { return Name }

// Score: prefer the most-loaded feasible node (bin packing).
func (m *MyBinPack) Score(ctx context.Context, state *framework.CycleState,
    pod *v1.Pod, nodeName string) (int64, *framework.Status) {

    nodeInfo, err := m.handle.SnapshotSharedLister().NodeInfos().Get(nodeName)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, framework.AsStatus(err)
    }
    used := nodeInfo.Requested.MilliCPU
    cap  := nodeInfo.Allocatable.MilliCPU
    if cap == 0 { return 0, nil }
    return (used * 100) / cap, nil   // 0..100
}

func (m *MyBinPack) ScoreExtensions() framework.ScoreExtensions { return nil }

// Factory registered in main.go via app.NewSchedulerCommand(WithPlugin(...))
func New(_ context.Context, _ runtime.Object, h framework.Handle) (framework.Plugin, error) {
    return &MyBinPack{handle: h}, nil
}

Then in KubeSchedulerConfiguration:

profiles:
  - schedulerName: binpack-scheduler
    plugins:
      score:
        enabled:
          - {name: MyBinPack, weight: 10}

Build the scheduler binary that imports your plugin and ship it as the kube-scheduler image.

docs.title: Notable recent changes (1.30+)
docs.text:
• PodSchedulingReadiness (GA 1.30): spec.schedulingGates lets a controller hold a pod out of the queue (e.g., wait for capacity provisioner). No more "create then immediately fail".
  • MinDomains for TopologySpreadConstraints (GA 1.30).
  • In-place pod vertical scaling (beta 1.33): updating resources.requests triggers re-evaluation, not eviction.
  • Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) (GA 1.34): ResourceClaim API replaces device plugins for GPUs / FPGAs / specialized hardware, fully integrated with the scheduler.
  • Scheduler queueing hints (beta 1.30): plugins can tell the queue "this event might unblock my pod" → fewer wasted requeues.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
Q1. How does the scheduler decide where a pod goes? Two phases: filter (drop infeasible nodes via plugins like NodeAffinity, TaintToleration, NodeResourcesFit), then score (rank survivors 0–100 via plugins like NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation, ImageLocality, TopologySpread). Highest score wins. Tied scores → random pick.

Q2. What's the difference between predicates/priorities and the Scheduling Framework? Pre-1.19 had hard-coded predicate and priority lists with limited extension via Extender HTTP webhooks (slow). The Scheduling Framework (1.19 GA) replaced this with 12 in-process extension points and a typed Go plugin interface — same behaviour, but composable and faster.

Q3. How do I run multiple schedulers? Easiest: define multiple profiles in one KubeSchedulerConfiguration and have pods opt in via spec.schedulerName. Hardest: deploy a second kube-scheduler with a different --leader-elect-resource-name — but this risks racing on the cache.

Q4. What is preemption, and where in the framework does it live? When no node passes the Filter phase, PostFilter runs. The default DefaultPreemption plugin finds lower-priority victim pods that, if evicted, would let the new pod fit. Victims are deleted with grace; the pending pod waits for the next cycle.

Q5. How do nodeSelector, nodeAffinity, taints/tolerations, and topologySpreadConstraints differ? nodeSelector: simple = match on labels. nodeAffinity: richer expressions (In/NotIn/Exists), supports preferred (soft). Taints+tolerations: NODE-side opt-out — only tolerating pods may land. TopologySpreadConstraints: distribute replicas across zones/racks/nodes for HA.

Q6. What is spec.schedulingGates (1.30 GA) and why is it useful? A list of string gates the pod waits on before entering the queue. The scheduler ignores gated pods entirely. A controller (e.g., capacity provisioner, batch admission) removes a gate when conditions are met. Replaces the old anti-pattern of creating doomed pods that thrash the queue.

Q7. When would you write a plugin vs. an Extender vs. a mutating webhook? Plugin: full power, in-process, lowest latency, must build/ship custom kube-scheduler. Extender: HTTP webhook called during Filter/Score — slow, deprecated, avoid. Mutating webhook: doesn't change scheduling logic, only mutates the pod spec (e.g., inject nodeSelector) — best when you can express your intent declaratively.

Q8. The scheduler is binding pods slowly. What do you check? scheduler_scheduling_attempt_duration_seconds histogram, scheduler_pending_pods gauge. Common causes: too many pending pods (queue starvation by priority), PreemptionPolicy thrashing, slow PreBind (PVC binding), apiserver latency on Bind, custom plugin doing IO in Filter (cardinal sin — Filter runs N times per pod).

docs.title: 04 — Service Mesh
docs.text:
A service mesh adds L7 traffic management, mTLS, and telemetry without code changes, by injecting a data plane next to (or under) every workload.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    subgraph Pod_A[Pod A]
      AppA[App] --- ProxyA[Proxy]
    end
    subgraph Pod_B[Pod B]
      AppB[App] --- ProxyB[Proxy]
    end
    ProxyA -.mTLS.-> ProxyB
    Ctl[Control Plane\nIstiod / linkerd / Cilium] --> ProxyA
    Ctl --> ProxyB

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text:
Concept Manifest kubectl Expected output

A service mesh adds L7 routing, mTLS, and golden-signal telemetry to every workload without code changes. A control plane (Istiod / linkerd / Cilium) programs a data plane (Envoy sidecar, Rust micro-proxy, or eBPF + waypoint) so apps see plain HTTP while operators get traffic shifting and zero-trust crypto.

apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: reviews
spec:
  hosts: [reviews]
  http:
    - match:
        - headers:
            x-user-tier: { exact: beta }
      route:
        - destination: { host: reviews, subset: v3 }
    - route:
        - destination: { host: reviews, subset: v1 }
          weight: 80
        - destination: { host: reviews, subset: v2 }
          weight: 20
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: reviews
spec:
  host: reviews
  trafficPolicy:
    outlierDetection:
      consecutive5xxErrors: 5
      interval: 30s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s
  subsets:
    - { name: v1, labels: { version: v1 } }
    - { name: v2, labels: { version: v2 } }
    - { name: v3, labels: { version: v3 } }

kubectl apply -f istio-virtualservice.yaml
kubectl get virtualservice reviews -o yaml
istioctl proxy-config routes deploy/istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system | grep reviews
curl -s http://reviews/                          # 80% v1, 20% v2
curl -s -H "x-user-tier: beta" http://reviews/   # always v3

virtualservice.networking.istio.io/reviews created
destinationrule.networking.istio.io/reviews created
NAME      DOMAINS    MATCH                  VIRTUAL SERVICE
reviews   reviews    /*                     reviews.default

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Istio Linkerd Cilium Service Mesh Data plane Envoy sidecar (or ambient ztunnel + waypoint) Linkerd2-proxy (Rust, micro-proxy) eBPF + optional Envoy waypoint mTLS yes yes (default-on, simple) yes API Istio CRDs + Gateway API Linkerd CRDs + Gateway API Cilium CRDs + Gateway API Footprint larger, most features smallest, fewer features shares CNI, no per-pod sidecar Mode sidecar OR ambient sidecar sidecarless (eBPF)

docs.title: Sidecar vs Ambient/eBPF
docs.text:
• Sidecar: each pod gets a proxy container — strong isolation, higher resource cost, requires pod restarts on upgrade.
  • Ambient (Istio): shared per-node ztunnel for L4/mTLS, optional waypoint proxy for L7 — lower cost, no pod restart for mesh upgrades.
  • eBPF (Cilium): kernel-level redirection, no userspace proxy for L4 — best performance, L7 still uses Envoy waypoint.

docs.title: When to use what
docs.text:
• Need lots of L7 features today + multi-cluster: Istio.
  • Want simplicity and "it just works" mTLS: Linkerd.
  • Already on Cilium CNI and value performance: Cilium.

docs.title: Deep Dive: Istio vs Linkerd vs Cilium Service Mesh
Deep Dive: Istio vs Linkerd vs Cilium Service Mesh
Why this matters
docs.text:
"Use a service mesh" is no longer a single decision. The architectural choice splits three ways:

  • Sidecar proxies (the original model): Istio classic, Linkerd, Consul.
  • Ambient / per-node proxies (sidecar-less): Istio Ambient (GA 1.23 in Istio, late 2024), Linkerd's policy controller.
  • eBPF in-kernel (no userspace proxy at all for L4): Cilium Service Mesh, with optional Envoy for L7.

The wrong choice burns 30%+ of cluster CPU and adds 1–5 ms tail latency per hop. The right choice is invisible. This doc maps the three architectures, their control planes, and the perf trade-offs so you can pick deliberately.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
A service mesh does three jobs: secure transport (mTLS), traffic control (routing, retries, splits), and observability (RED metrics, traces). Where you put the code that does these jobs is the architectural decision.

Where the dataplane runs Memory cost Latency cost L7 features Sidecar (per pod) ~50–150 MiB × pods +0.5–2 ms Full HTTP/2, gRPC, JWT Per-node proxy (ambient) ~50–150 MiB × nodes +0.3–1.5 ms Full at L7 tier eBPF (kernel) ~10–30 MiB × nodes +0.05–0.2 ms (L4) L4 only without Envoy

docs.title: Walkthrough: a canonical mTLS + traffic split
Istio (sidecar / ambient)
docs.text:
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata: {name: default, namespace: prod}
spec:
  mtls: {mode: STRICT}                 # cluster-wide mTLS enforcement
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata: {name: web, namespace: prod}
spec:
  parentRefs: [{name: web-waypoint, kind: Service}]
  rules:
    - matches: [{path: {value: /}}]
      backendRefs:                     # 90/10 canary
        - {name: web-v1, port: 80, weight: 90}
        - {name: web-v2, port: 80, weight: 10}

In ambient mode, no sidecar injection annotation needed. Add istio.io/dataplane-mode: ambient to the namespace; ztunnel handles L4 mTLS automatically. A waypoint proxy is provisioned only for L7 features.

docs.title: Linkerd
docs.text:
apiVersion: policy.linkerd.io/v1beta3
kind: Server
metadata: {name: web, namespace: prod}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}
  port: http
  proxyProtocol: HTTP/2
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata: {name: web, namespace: prod}
spec:
  parentRefs: [{group: policy.linkerd.io, kind: Server, name: web}]
  rules:
    - backendRefs:
        - {name: web-v1, port: 80, weight: 90}
        - {name: web-v2, port: 80, weight: 10}

Linkerd auto-injects on namespaces labeled linkerd.io/inject: enabled. mTLS is on by default — no flag needed.

docs.title: Cilium Service Mesh
docs.text:
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: web-l7, namespace: prod}
spec:
  endpointSelector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}
  ingress:
    - fromEndpoints: [{matchLabels: {app: client}}]
      toPorts:
        - ports: [{port: "80", protocol: TCP}]
          rules:
            http:
              - method: GET
                path: "/api/.*"
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata: {name: web, namespace: prod}
spec:
  parentRefs: [{name: cilium-gateway}]
  rules:
    - backendRefs:
        - {name: web-v1, port: 80, weight: 90}
        - {name: web-v2, port: 80, weight: 10}

Cilium handles L4 mTLS via WireGuard or IPsec encryption between nodes (encryption.enabled: true) — not per-connection mTLS. SPIFFE-based pod identity mTLS is in beta.

docs.title: Performance trade-offs (rule-of-thumb numbers)
docs.text:
For a 1KB HTTP request between pods in the same cluster:

Solution p50 added p99 added CPU per RPS No mesh baseline baseline baseline Linkerd sidecar +0.4 ms +1.5 ms +1.5x Istio sidecar (Envoy) +0.6 ms +2.5 ms +2.0x Istio Ambient (L4 only) +0.3 ms +1.0 ms +1.2x Istio Ambient (L7 via waypoint) +0.7 ms +2.0 ms +1.8x Cilium L4 (eBPF only) +0.05 ms +0.3 ms +1.05x Cilium L7 (Envoy DS) +0.5 ms +2.0 ms +1.5x

These are rough order-of-magnitude figures from public benchmarks; numbers shift with hardware, workload mix, and version. Always measure on your workload.

docs.title: When to pick what
docs.text:
• Greenfield, want simplicity, mostly HTTP → Linkerd. Smallest blast radius, opinionated, secure by default.
  • Need rich routing (header-based, canary by user, JWT auth) → Istio (Ambient if you can, classic otherwise).
  • Already running Cilium CNI, want NetworkPolicy + mTLS at line rate → Cilium Service Mesh. Add Envoy DS only when you need L7.
  • Multi-cluster federation, multi-tenant L7 policy → Istio remains the most mature.
  • Bare-metal / latency-critical (HFT, gaming, voice) → Cilium eBPF. Sidecar tax is unacceptable.

docs.title: Interview Q&A
docs.text:
Q1. Why does the sidecar model exist if it's so heavy? Originally because the kernel had no way to inject HTTP-aware logic into a pod without changing the application. Sidecars solved that with zero app changes (auto-injection). The cost (~100 MiB per pod, +1 ms latency) was acceptable when meshes had hundreds of pods, not thousands.

Q2. What does Istio Ambient solve? Two things: (1) the per-pod memory tax (ztunnel runs once per node, not per pod), (2) the upgrade pain (sidecar version coupled to pod restart). Trade-off: L7 features now require explicit waypoint proxies, and the architecture is younger.

Q3. Cilium replaces kube-proxy — what does that change? kube-proxy programs iptables/nftables for Service VIPs. Cilium's eBPF datapath programs the same logic into eBPF socket-level programs, bypassing iptables entirely. Result: O(1) lookup regardless of service count, much lower CPU, and observability via Hubble.

Q4. How does mTLS work in each mesh? Istio: SPIFFE identity per workload, certs minted by istiod's CA, rotated every 24h, presented by Envoy/ztunnel. Linkerd: similar but uses its own identity controller, certs every 24h, presented by linkerd2-proxy. Cilium: SPIFFE-based pod identity with mTLS in beta; production today usually means node-to-node WireGuard or IPsec encryption (not per-connection identity).

Q5. What is HBONE and why does Istio Ambient use it? HTTP-Based Overlay Network Environment. ztunnels tunnel pod-to-pod traffic over HTTP/2 CONNECT with mTLS. It allows L4 transport with metadata (source identity, dest identity) preserved for waypoint policy enforcement, while running on standard ports.

Q6. What does Linkerd give up to be simple? Rich L7 policy (no JWT auth, no complex routing rules, no rate-limiting at the proxy), narrower multi-cluster topology options, no built-in egress gateway. In exchange: smaller proxy (Rust, ~10 MiB), lower latency, far less yak-shaving.

Q7. If I already have Cilium as CNI, do I need Istio for a mesh? Often no. Cilium Service Mesh covers L4 mTLS, NetworkPolicy, transparent encryption, and Gateway API for ingress. You add Istio only if you need its L7 feature surface (subset routing, fault injection, rich auth) and the team can absorb the operational cost.

Q8. What is the biggest operational risk with a sidecar mesh? The sidecar lifecycle vs. main app lifecycle race. Pre-Kubernetes 1.29 native sidecars, Envoy could be killed before the app finished draining, causing connection resets during rollouts. Native sidecars (KEP-753, GA 1.33) fix this — Envoy is restartable and terminated AFTER main containers.

docs.title: 05 — Gateway API
docs.text:
Gateway API is the successor to Ingress: role-oriented (infra / cluster ops / app dev), portable across implementations, and richer (header-based routing, traffic split, gRPC, TCP/UDP/TLS routes).

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    Infra["GatewayClass(infra owns)"] --> Gw["Gateway(cluster ops own)"]
    Gw --> R1["HTTPRoute(app team A)"]
    Gw --> R2["HTTPRoute(app team B)"]
    Gw --> R3["GRPCRoute / TCPRoute"]

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text:
Concept Manifest kubectl Expected output

Gateway API splits the old Ingress object into roles: infra owns GatewayClass, cluster ops own Gateway, app teams own HTTPRoute / GRPCRoute / TCPRoute. Routing primitives (header match, weighted backends, request mirroring) are first-class typed fields, not vendor annotations.

apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: prod-gateway
      namespace: infra
  hostnames: ["app.example.com"]
  rules:
    - matches:
        - path: { type: PathPrefix, value: /api }
      backendRefs:
        - { name: api-v1, port: 8080, weight: 90 }
        - { name: api-v2, port: 8080, weight: 10 }
    - matches:
        - path: { type: PathPrefix, value: / }
      filters:
        - type: RequestHeaderModifier
          requestHeaderModifier:
            add:
              - { name: X-Routed-By, value: gateway-api }
      backendRefs:
        - { name: web, port: 80 }

kubectl apply -f gateway.yaml
kubectl apply -f httproute.yaml
kubectl get gateway prod-gateway -n infra
kubectl get httproute -n team-a
kubectl describe httproute app -n team-a

NAME           CLASS   ADDRESS         PROGRAMMED   AGE
prod-gateway   istio   34.120.10.20    True         42s
NAME   HOSTNAMES               AGE
app    ["app.example.com"]     20s
Status:
  Parents:
    Conditions:
      Type:    Accepted        Status: True   Reason: Accepted
      Type:    ResolvedRefs    Status: True   Reason: ResolvedRefs

docs.title: Ingress vs Gateway API
docs.text: Ingress Gateway API Roles one resource GatewayClass / Gateway / *Route Extensibility annotations (vendor-specific) typed fields, ReferenceGrant Protocols HTTP(S) only HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC, TCP, UDP, TLS Traffic split / mirroring annotations first-class Mesh integration none GAMMA (East-West for service mesh)

docs.title: GAMMA (mesh)
docs.text: GAMMA = "Gateway API for Mesh Management and Administration". Lets you use the same HTTPRoute to control east-west traffic inside a mesh (Istio, Linkerd, Cilium, kgateway, etc).

docs.text:

docs.title: Why multi-cluster
docs.text: • Blast-radius isolation, regulatory boundaries, geo proximity, heterogeneous infra (cloud + on-prem), team autonomy.

docs.title: Approaches
docs.text: Tool Style Status KubeFed v2 API federation, pushed config from a host cluster Archived (lessons learned, not recommended for new work) Karmada Policy-based propagation, OverridePolicies, scheduler across clusters CNCF Incubating Cluster API (CAPI) Declarative lifecycle of clusters themselves (Cluster, Machine, MachineDeployment CRDs) CNCF, widely used Fleet (Rancher) GitOps fan-out across many clusters CNCF Sandbox Open Cluster Management (OCM) Hub-spoke, RedHat ACM upstream CNCF Sandbox Argo CD ApplicationSet GitOps fan-out by generator (cluster, list, git) CNCF Graduated

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text:
• Hub-and-spoke: one management cluster, many workload clusters. Most common.
  • GitOps fan-out: ApplicationSet/Fleet — each cluster pulls its own config.
  • Mesh federation: Istio multi-primary or primary-remote, Linkerd multi-cluster, Cilium ClusterMesh — share services across clusters with mTLS.

docs.text:

  • A management cluster reconciles them into real clusters.
  • Same flow for upgrade, scale, delete.

docs.title: Setup — Cluster API (CAPI) for kind
docs.text:
# clusterctl
brew install clusterctl

# Init management cluster
clusterctl init --infrastructure docker
kubectl get pods -A | grep -E 'capi|cap'

# Generate a workload cluster manifest
clusterctl generate cluster capi-quickstart \
  --flavor development --kubernetes-version v1.30.0 \

docs.title: 07 — Stateful Workloads
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    SS[StatefulSet] --> P0[pod-0]
    SS --> P1[pod-1]
    SS --> P2[pod-2]
    P0 --> PVC0[(PVC-0)]
    P1 --> PVC1[(PVC-1)]
    P2 --> PVC2[(PVC-2)]
    Headless[Headless Service\nclusterIP: None] -.DNS.- P0
    Headless -.DNS.- P1
    Headless -.DNS.- P2

docs.title: StatefulSet guarantees
docs.text:
• Stable network identity: pod-0, pod-1, ... resolvable via the headless Service as pod-0.svc.ns.svc.cluster.local.
  • Stable storage: each pod gets its own PVC from volumeClaimTemplates; PVC survives pod restarts and even StatefulSet deletion (default).
  • Ordered creation/deletion: 0 before 1 before 2; reverse on scale-down. Use podManagementPolicy: Parallel to relax.
  • Ordered rolling updates with partition for canary / phased rollouts.

docs.title: Headless Service
docs.text: clusterIP: None returns A records for every pod, not a single VIP. Required for StatefulSet pod DNS.

docs.title: When NOT to use StatefulSet
docs.text:
• Stateless apps that just need stable DNS — use a regular Deployment + headless Service if needed.
  • Distributed systems with their own membership (some prefer Operators that manage raw Pods).

docs.title: Operators for databases
docs.text:
Workload Operator(s) PostgreSQL CloudNativePG, Zalando postgres-operator, Crunchy PGO MySQL Oracle MySQL Operator, Percona, Vitess (sharded) Kafka Strimzi (CNCF), Confluent for K8s Redis Redis Enterprise Operator, OT-Container-Kit redis-operator MongoDB MongoDB Enterprise / Community Operator, Percona Elasticsearch ECK (Elastic), OpenSearch Operator

Operators encode failover, backup/restore, version upgrades, and PVC growth — things StatefulSets alone do not handle.

docs.title: 08 — Batch and AI Workloads
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    User[Submit Job] --> Q[Kueue Queue]
    Q -->|admit when quota free| K8s[K8s Job / JobSet]
    K8s --> P0[worker-0 GPU]
    K8s --> P1[worker-1 GPU]
    K8s --> P2[worker-2 GPU]
    Sched[Scheduler / Volcano] --> P0
    Sched --> P1
    Sched --> P2

docs.title: Native primitives
docs.text:
• Job: run-to-completion pods. completions, parallelism, backoffLimit, activeDeadlineSeconds.
  • CronJob: cron-scheduled Jobs.
  • IndexedJob (completionMode: Indexed, GA 1.24): each pod gets a unique index 0..N-1 — perfect for embarrassingly parallel and rank-based MPI/training.
  • JobSet (SIG-apps, beta): groups multiple Jobs (driver + workers + parameter server) with fixed naming and DNS — used by Kubeflow, JAX, MPI, Ray.

docs.title: Queueing & quota
docs.text:
• Kueue (SIG-scheduling): job-level quota and queueing before admission to the cluster scheduler. ClusterQueue + LocalQueue + ResourceFlavor.
  • Volcano: gang scheduling, fair-share, batch-style scheduler used by AI/ML training.
  • YuniKorn: Apache project, similar batch-scheduler niche.

docs.title: ML stacks
docs.text:
• Kubeflow: pipelines, training operators (TFJob, PyTorchJob, MPIJob), Katib for HPO, KServe for inference.
  • Ray on K8s (KubeRay operator): RayCluster, RayJob, RayService.

docs.title: GPU scheduling
docs.text:
• NVIDIA device plugin exposes nvidia.com/gpu as a schedulable resource.
  • Time-slicing and MIG for multi-tenant GPUs.
  • Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) (alpha 1.26 → beta 1.32) is the next-gen API for accelerators.

docs.title: 09 — Extending the Kubernetes API
docs.text:
Three ways to add API surface:

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    subgraph kube-apiserver
      Builtin[Built-in resources]
      CRD[CRDs\napiextensions.k8s.io]
      Aggregator[Aggregation Layer\n/apis//]
    end
    Aggregator -.proxy.-> Extn[Extension API server]
    CRD --> Etcd[(etcd)]
    Builtin --> Etcd
    Extn --> ExtStore[(Custom storage)]

docs.title: CRDs
docs.text:
• Easiest. Stored in etcd by kube-apiserver. Validation via OpenAPI schema or CEL (x-kubernetes-validations).
  • Use when you just want a new declarative object kind.

docs.title: Aggregated API server
docs.text:
• Register a separate server under a URL path; kube-apiserver proxies requests to it.
  • Use when you need: custom storage (not etcd), custom subresources beyond status/scale, server-side admission/conversion you fully own. Examples: metrics.k8s.io, external.metrics.k8s.io, custom.metrics.k8s.io.

docs.title: API Priority and Fairness (APF)
docs.text:
• Replaces the old max-in-flight throttling. Categorizes requests into PriorityLevels via FlowSchemas, gives each a fair share so a noisy controller cannot starve kubectl get for humans.
  • GA in 1.29.

docs.title: Finalizers
docs.text:
• A string in metadata.finalizers blocks deletion until removed.
  • Used by controllers to perform cleanup (release cloud LB, drop external rows) before the object disappears.
  • Watch out for stuck deletions when a controller is gone — patch the object to remove the finalizer manually.

docs.title: How to read a Kubernetes release
docs.text:
1. Release blog: https://kubernetes.io/blog/YYYY/MM/DD-kubernetes-vX-YY-release/ — narrative summary.
  2. CHANGELOG-X.YY.md: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/CHANGELOG/CHANGELOG-X.YY.md — the source of truth, every PR.
  3. Enhancements (KEP) tracker: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements — KEPs (Kubernetes Enhancement Proposals) with stage (alpha/beta/stable).
  4. Feature gates: https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/ — what is on/off by default per version.

docs.title: Kubernetes 1.27 "Chill Vibes"
docs.text: • Release date: 2023-04-11

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• SeccompDefault graduated to GA — kubelet can default all workloads to RuntimeDefault seccomp profile.
  • Job APIs evolve: pod failure policy and mutable scheduling directives for suspended Jobs help batch/ML workloads.
  • Many alpha → beta promotions across the API; kubectl apply --prune got a new ApplySet-based mode (alpha).

docs.title: Notable feature gate transitions
docs.text: Feature gate Before In 1.27 Notes SeccompDefault beta GA kubelet --seccomp-default flag stable JobMutableNodeSchedulingDirectives beta GA edit nodeSelector/affinity on suspended Jobs DownwardAPIHugePages beta GA expose hugepages requests/limits via downward API ServerSideFieldValidation beta GA server validates unknown/duplicate fields OpenAPIV3 beta GA apiserver publishes OpenAPI v3 KubeletInUserNamespace alpha alpha rootless kubelet experiments continue

docs.title: Notable deprecations / removals
docs.text:
• In-tree cloud providers continue migrating to out-of-tree (CCM); several flags marked deprecated.
  • seccomp.security.alpha.kubernetes.io/pod annotation long-deprecated; use securityContext.seccompProfile.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: • No release-defining CVE tied to 1.27 itself; track patch releases for CVE fixes.

docs.title: How to try SeccompDefault

# Start kubelet with:
#   --seccomp-default=true
# Then any pod without an explicit seccompProfile uses RuntimeDefault.
kubectl run demo --image=nginx:1.27 --restart=Never
kubectl get pod demo -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].securityContext}'

docs.title: Kubernetes 1.28 "Planternetes"
docs.text: • Release date: 2023-08-15

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Native sidecar containers introduced as alpha (SidecarContainers) — restartPolicy:Always init containers that run alongside main containers and terminate after them.
  • Retroactive default StorageClass behavior reaches GA: PVCs created before a default StorageClass exists get bound when one appears.
  • Control-plane / kubelet version skew widened to n-3 for kubelet (was n-2) — easing upgrade cadence.

docs.title: Notable feature gate transitions
docs.text: Feature gate Before In 1.28 Notes SidecarContainers — alpha (off) restartPolicy:Always init containers RetroactiveDefaultStorageClass beta GA PVC defaulting fix ConsistentListFromCache — alpha apiserver list optimization (becomes important later) ValidatingAdmissionPolicy alpha beta (off) CEL-based admission, no webhook required KubeProxyDrainingTerminatingNodes — alpha better LB drain on terminating nodes

docs.title: Notable deprecations / removals
docs.text:
• ceph and glusterfs in-tree volume plugins reach end-of-support timelines (verify with official release notes).
  • Several legacy kube-controller-manager flags removed.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: • Standard CVE patches in subsequent z-stream releases — verify with the official release notes.

docs.title: How to try sidecar containers (alpha)
docs.text:
# Enable with --feature-gates=SidecarContainers=true on apiserver, controller-manager, scheduler, kubelet.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: web-with-log-shipper }
spec:
  initContainers:
    - name: log-shipper
      image: fluent/fluent-bit:latest
      restartPolicy: Always   # makes this a "native sidecar"
      volumeMounts:
        - { name: logs, mountPath: /var/log/app }
  containers:
    - name: web
      image: nginx:1.27
      volumeMounts:
        - { name: logs, mountPath: /var/log/nginx }
  volumes:
    - { name: logs, emptyDir: {} }

docs.title: Kubernetes 1.29 "Mandala"
docs.text: • Release date: 2023-12-13

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• ReadWriteOncePod PV access mode reaches GA — true single-pod write semantics, useful for leader-elected stateful apps.
  • Native sidecar containers moves to beta and on by default (the SidecarContainers gate) — production paths can adopt with caution.
  • KMS v2 envelope encryption for secrets reaches GA — improved performance, key rotation, observability vs v1.

docs.title: Notable feature gate transitions
docs.text: Feature gate Before In 1.29 Notes ReadWriteOncePod beta GA new PV access mode SidecarContainers alpha beta (on) default-enabled KMSv2 / KMSv2KDF beta GA use envelope encryption v2 in EncryptionConfiguration APIPriorityAndFairness beta GA request fairness in apiserver CRDValidationRatcheting — alpha re-validate only changed fields on update PodReadyToStartContainersCondition alpha beta finer-grained pod conditions

docs.title: Notable deprecations / removals
docs.text:
• In-tree vSphere and Azure file legacy volume plugin paths continue migration to CSI; in-tree code increasingly removed in following releases.
  • Legacy beta APIs that hit their N+3 window get removed (verify with official release notes).

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• KMS v1 deprecated; plan migration to v2.
  • Track CVEs in patch releases; nothing release-defining for 1.29 specifically.

docs.title: Kubernetes 1.30 "Uwubernetes"
docs.text: • Release date: 2024-04-17

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• ValidatingAdmissionPolicy reaches GA — declarative CEL-based admission validation built into the apiserver, no webhook to operate.
  • AppArmor support reaches GA — first-class securityContext.appArmorProfile field instead of the legacy annotation.
  • Structured authentication configuration (file-based authenticator config with multiple OIDC providers and CEL claim mapping) reaches beta.

docs.title: Notable feature gate transitions
docs.text: Feature gate Before In 1.30 Notes ValidatingAdmissionPolicy beta GA use CEL MatchConditions and Validations AppArmorFields — GA in 1.30 move from annotations to securityContext.appArmorProfile StructuredAuthenticationConfiguration alpha beta multiple OIDC issuers, CEL claim mapping ContextualLogging beta beta logger context propagation; nearing GA MinDomainsInPodTopologySpread beta GA minDomains for spread WatchList alpha beta (off) streaming list responses PodDisruptionConditions beta GA DisruptionTarget pod condition

docs.title: Notable deprecations / removals
docs.text:
• Legacy container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/... annotations deprecated in favor of the new field.
  • SecurityContextDeny admission plugin removed (verify with official release notes).

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• ValidatingAdmissionPolicy lets you replace many policy webhooks — fewer moving parts, smaller blast radius.
  • Patch-level CVEs as usual; check the security advisories.

docs.title: How to try ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
docs.text:
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-latest-tag
spec:
  failurePolicy: Fail
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        apiVersions: ["v1"]
        operations: ["CREATE","UPDATE"]
        resources: ["pods"]
  validations:
    - expression: "object.spec.containers.all(c, !c.image.endsWith(':latest'))"
      message: "image tag :latest is not allowed"
---
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding
metadata: { name: deny-latest-tag-binding }
spec:
  policyName: deny-latest-tag
  validationActions: [Deny]
  matchResources:
    namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels: { env: prod }

docs.title: Kubernetes 1.31 "Elli"
docs.text: • Release date: 2024-08-13

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• PersistentVolume lastPhaseTransitionTime reaches GA, providing accurate timestamps for PV phase changes — useful for storage SRE/observability.
  • kube-proxy nftables backend reaches beta as a faster, more scalable alternative to iptables for clusters with many Services.
  • All in-tree cloud provider integrations are now removed from the Kubernetes binary tree (the Cloud Provider Extraction project completes) — clusters must use external cloud-controller-manager.

docs.title: Notable feature gate transitions
docs.text: Feature gate Before In 1.31 Notes PersistentVolumeLastPhaseTransitionTime beta GA new field on PV status NFTablesProxyMode alpha beta kube-proxy --proxy-mode=nftables AppArmorFields GA (since 1.30) GA confirmed stable AnonymousAuthConfigurableEndpoints — alpha restrict anonymous to specific endpoints PodHostIPs beta GA dual-stack pod host IPs in status ServiceTrafficDistribution — beta spec.trafficDistribution: PreferClose for topology-aware routing (replaces the older topology-aware-hints UX) JobSuccessPolicy alpha beta declare success when a subset of indexed pods finish

docs.title: Notable deprecations / removals
docs.text:
• All in-tree cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCE, vSphere, OpenStack) finally removed from kube-apiserver / kube-controller-manager / kubelet — must run external CCM. Operators should have migrated by now.
  • Legacy topology.kubernetes.io/zone hints behavior superseded by trafficDistribution.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: • Anonymous auth can now be scoped to only /healthz, /livez, /readyz via the alpha gate — defence-in-depth for clusters that previously had to keep anonymous on for health checks.

docs.title: How to try traffic distribution
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: my-svc }
spec:
  selector: { app: my-app }
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 8080 }]
  trafficDistribution: PreferClose   # prefer endpoints in the same zone

docs.title: Kubernetes 1.32 "Penelope"
docs.text: • Release date: 2024-12-11

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) moves to beta with a redesigned, "structured parameters" API — the long-term path for GPUs, FPGAs, and other accelerators.
  • Anonymous auth restrictions (AnonymousAuthConfigurableEndpoints) reach beta — clusters can finally allow anonymous on a tight allowlist (e.g., only health endpoints).
  • Custom profiling endpoints in components and other API-machinery hardening land; many small UX improvements (verify with official release notes for full list).

docs.title: Notable feature gate transitions
docs.text: Feature gate Before In 1.32 Notes DynamicResourceAllocation alpha beta (off) new structured-parameters model AnonymousAuthConfigurableEndpoints alpha beta scope anonymous auth KubeletFineGrainedAuthz — alpha finer authorizer hooks for kubelet ConsistentListFromCache beta GA apiserver serves consistent lists from the watch cache (big perf win) RetryGenerateName alpha beta retry on generateName conflicts StatefulSetStartOrdinal beta GA start-ordinal offset for StatefulSets RecoverVolumeExpansionFailure beta beta continues maturation

docs.title: Notable deprecations / removals
docs.text:
• Older DRA API (resource.k8s.io/v1alpha2) removed in favor of the new structured-parameters API — driver and workload manifests must be migrated.
  • Continued cleanup of long-deprecated flags (verify with official release notes).

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Hardened anonymous auth defaults via the new gate.
  • Standard CVE backports.

docs.title: How to try DRA (beta)
docs.text:
# Requires --feature-gates=DynamicResourceAllocation=true on apiserver, scheduler, kubelet,
# plus a DRA driver installed (e.g., NVIDIA DRA driver).
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: ResourceClaimTemplate
metadata: { name: gpu-claim-template }
spec:
  spec:
    resourceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: dra-demo }
spec:
  resourceClaims:
    - name: gpu
      resourceClaimTemplateName: gpu-claim-template
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: nvidia/cuda:12.4.0-base-ubuntu22.04
      resources:
        claims:
          - name: gpu

docs.title: Kubernetes 1.33 "Octarine"
docs.text: • Release date: 2025-04-23

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Sidecar containers reach GA — restartPolicy:Always init containers are now a stable feature.
  • In-place pod resize moves to beta and on by default — change CPU/memory requests/limits without restarting the pod (long-awaited).
  • User namespaces for pods (UserNamespacesSupport) reach GA, and multiple Service CIDRs reach GA — networking can grow Service ranges without recreating the cluster.

docs.title: Notable feature gate transitions
docs.text: Feature gate Before In 1.33 Notes SidecarContainers beta GA restartPolicy:Always init container is a stable concept InPlacePodVerticalScaling beta beta (on) default-on; resize without restart for most resources UserNamespacesSupport beta GA rootless-style isolation for pods MultiCIDRServiceAllocator + ServiceCIDRsRollout beta GA expand Service IP ranges via ServiceCIDR and IPAddress objects NFTablesProxyMode beta GA (likely) verify with official release notes PodLifecycleSleepAction beta GA preStop.sleep without exec'ing into the container JobSuccessPolicy beta GA (likely) verify with official release notes TopologyAwareHints GA GA continues to be the underlying mechanism for trafficDistribution

docs.title: Notable deprecations / removals
docs.text:
• The legacy single Service CIDR flag-only configuration is superseded by ServiceCIDR objects — operators should use the API.
  • Various long-beta gates that graduated to GA had their gate options become no-ops (cannot disable anymore).

docs.title: Security
docs.text: • User namespaces GA materially reduces blast radius of container escapes — turn it on where your runtime supports it (containerd ≥ 1.7 on a recent kernel).

docs.title: How to try in-place pod resize
docs.text:
# Edit live:
kubectl patch pod my-app --subresource resize \
  --patch '{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"app","resources":{"requests":{"cpu":"500m"},"limits":{"cpu":"1"}}}]}}'

# The pod's QoS class may NOT change as part of a resize (validation rejects it).
# Memory shrink may be denied by the kernel; CPU resize is generally hot.

spec:

docs.title: Version skew policy (the rules)
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    KCP[kube-apiserver\n1.Y] -->|+/- 1| Other[kube-controller-manager\nkube-scheduler\nCCM\n1.Y or 1.Y-1]
    KCP -->|up to -3| Kubelet[kubelet 1.Y .. 1.Y-3]
    KCP -->|up to -3| Proxy[kube-proxy 1.Y .. 1.Y-3]
    KCP -->|+/- 1| Kubectl[kubectl 1.Y-1 .. 1.Y+1]
  • kube-apiserver: highest version in the control plane.
  • kube-controller-manager / scheduler / CCM: same minor as apiserver, may be one minor older during upgrade.
  • kubelet / kube-proxy: must not be newer than apiserver; up to 3 minors older (relaxed in 1.28).
  • kubectl: within ±1 minor of apiserver.

You must upgrade one minor at a time (no jumps). 1.27 → 1.29 means 1.27 → 1.28 → 1.29.

docs.title: kubeadm upgrade (sketch)
docs.text:
# On the FIRST control-plane node:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y kubeadm=1.YY.x-*
sudo kubeadm upgrade plan
sudo kubeadm upgrade apply v1.YY.x

# Then upgrade kubelet + kubectl on this node:
sudo apt install -y kubelet=1.YY.x-* kubectl=1.YY.x-*
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart kubelet

# On OTHER control-plane nodes:
sudo kubeadm upgrade node

# On WORKER nodes (one at a time):
kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
sudo kubeadm upgrade node
sudo apt install -y kubelet=1.YY.x-* kubectl=1.YY.x-*
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl uncordon <node>

docs.title: Deprecation strategy
docs.text:
• GA APIs are supported for at least 12 months or 3 releases after deprecation, whichever is longer.
  • Beta APIs in *.k8s.io groups removed N+9 months or N+3 releases after deprecation. (The famous PSP removal in 1.25, ingress.networking.k8s.io/v1beta1 removal in 1.22, etc.)
  • Alpha APIs can be removed any release. Never depend on them.

docs.title: Pre-upgrade checklist
docs.text:
• Read the release notes for every minor between source and target.
  • kubectl get apiservices — make sure no APIServices are unhealthy.
  • kubectl get --raw=/metrics | grep apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis — find clients still calling deprecated APIs.
  • Back up etcd (snapshot + offsite).
  • Check CSI drivers, CNI, ingress, mesh, operators for target version support.
  • Test upgrade on a staging cluster of similar shape first.
  • Have a rollback plan (etcd snapshot + previous binaries).

docs.title: Post-upgrade
docs.text:
• kubectl get nodes — all Ready, correct version.
  • kubectl get pods -A — no CrashLoopBackOff / ImagePullBackOff.
  • Smoke-test admission webhooks, autoscaling, ingress.
  • Watch apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis for new warnings.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text:
Concept Manifest kubectl Expected output

Triage starts with classifying the symptom (ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoop, OOMKilled, Pending, networking) then drilling into events and previous-container logs. Ephemeral containers (kubectl debug) attach a debugging toolbox to a running pod without rebuilding the image.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: netshoot
  labels: { app: netshoot }
spec:
  containers:
    - name: netshoot
      image: nicolaka/netshoot:latest
      command: ["sleep", "infinity"]
      securityContext:
        capabilities:
          add: ["NET_ADMIN", "NET_RAW"]
  restartPolicy: Always

kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp -A | tail -20
kubectl describe pod <pod>
kubectl logs <pod> --previous
kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=<container>
kubectl debug node/<node> -it --image=busybox
kubectl top pod

LAST SEEN   TYPE      REASON             OBJECT             MESSAGE
32s         Warning   BackOff            pod/api-7d-abcde   Back-off restarting failed container
20s         Warning   Unhealthy          pod/api-7d-abcde   Readiness probe failed: HTTP 503
State:          Waiting
  Reason:       CrashLoopBackOff
Last State:     Terminated
  Reason:       OOMKilled
  Exit Code:    137

docs.title: Tooling
docs.text: Need Command Inject a debug container into a running pod kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=<container> Debug a node (privileged pod on the host) kubectl debug node/<node> -it --image=busybox Copy a pod for tweaking kubectl debug <pod> --copy-to=debug --container=<c> --set-image=<c>=busybox -- sh Previous container logs kubectl logs <pod> --previous Recent events kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp -A Live resource usage kubectl top pod / kubectl top node Profile control plane kubectl get --raw /debug/pprof/heap > heap.out (with custom profiling endpoints) Audit log apiserver --audit-policy-file + --audit-log-path

docs.title: Ephemeral containers
docs.text:
• Added by kubectl debug against a running pod.
  • Share the pod's PID and network namespace via --target=<container> (so you can nsenter-like inspect the target's process).
  • Cannot be removed — they live for the pod's lifetime.

docs.title: Root-cause cheatsheet
docs.text: Symptom Common root causes ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull Wrong image:tag, private registry without imagePullSecret, rate-limited (Docker Hub anonymous), imagePullPolicy: Always against an offline registry CrashLoopBackOff App crashes on startup (config, missing secret), failing readiness/liveness probe, exit code != 0, missing volume OOMKilled (exit 137) Memory limit too low, leak, JVM/Node heap not aligned with cgroup limit Pending / Unschedulable No node has resources, taint without matching toleration, nodeSelector / affinity does not match, PVC pending (no provisioner) Init:CrashLoopBackOff Init container failing — check its logs explicitly with -c <init-name> Terminating forever Finalizer left by a controller that no longer exists — kubectl patch ... -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}' DNS NXDOMAIN inside pod CoreDNS down, NetworkPolicy blocking egress to kube-dns, wrong dnsPolicy Service has no endpoints Selector typo, all pods Not Ready, headless without subdomain set

docs.title: Audit logs
docs.text:
# audit-policy.yaml
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
omitStages: ["RequestReceived"]
rules:
  - level: Metadata
    resources:
      - group: ""
        resources: ["secrets","configmaps"]
  - level: RequestResponse
    verbs: ["create","update","patch","delete"]
    resources:
      - group: "rbac.authorization.k8s.io"

docs.title: Networking sanity
docs.text:
# DNS
kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -- \
  nslookup kubernetes.default

# Service connectivity
kubectl run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- \
  curl -v http://<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local/

docs.title: Self-assessment checklist
docs.text:
Before claiming mastery, you should be able to:

  • Write a CRD with structural schema, defaulting, and CEL validation rules.
  • Explain storage version vs served version and demonstrate a conversion webhook.
  • Build a controller in Go with kubebuilder that reconciles to status conditions.
  • Diagnose a webhook outage and recover the API server.
  • Choose between ValidatingAdmissionPolicy and a webhook for a given problem.
  • Defend a service mesh adoption plan including SLI, rollback, and cost.
  • Compare Gateway API to Ingress in a multi-team environment.
  • Diagram a multi-cluster topology and identify the failure domains.
  • Justify Cilium vs Calico for a specific workload mix.
  • Explain DRA semantics and why device plugins do not suffice.

docs.title: Common interview traps
docs.text:
• Confusing controller and operator. Operator is a kind of controller bundled with a CRD.
  • Forgetting that mutating webhook order is unspecified.
  • Believing federation is the only multi-cluster pattern.
  • Assuming mesh adds value without observability investment.
  • Treating CRDs as configuration; they are typed APIs with their own contract.

docs.title: Mermaid health check
docs.text: If your mermaid renders blank, the usual causes are: - Unquoted brackets or quotes inside a label. - Use of \n instead of br in HTML form. - Subgraphs without a closing end keyword. - Edges that reference undeclared node IDs.

docs.title: Performance budgets you should memorize
docs.text: Concern Rule of thumb Admission webhook latency under 100 ms p99 Controller workqueue depth under 100 sustained Etcd db size under 8 GB CRD conversion webhook under 30 ms p99 Scheduler bind latency under 1 s p99

docs.title: Closing
docs.text:
The advanced surface area of Kubernetes is large, but most decisions reduce to four levers: who owns the CRD, who runs the controller, where the policy lives, and how the data plane moves bytes. Keep these in mind while reading the rest of this pack.

docs.title: Architect Q&A — Kubernetes Advanced
docs.text: Sixty-plus design questions you should be able to defend in a senior or staff-level review. Read, pause, then read the answer.

docs.title: 1. When do you write your own operator versus consuming an existing one?
docs.text: Write your own when the domain has unique day-2 lifecycle that no community operator models, when you need to embed business invariants, or when the existing operator pulls in a runtime you cannot accept. Consume existing ones for databases, message brokers, and observability stacks where Cloud Native Computing Foundation operators are mature.

docs.title: 2. Operator versus Helm chart — when does the line cross?
docs.text: Helm is enough if the lifecycle is install, upgrade, uninstall and the resource graph is static. The line crosses the moment you need runtime decisions: failover, backup, version-aware migration, or status-driven reconciliation. At that point Helm becomes a deployment artifact for your operator, not the controller itself.

docs.title: 3. CRD versioning — how do you plan it from day one?
docs.text: Pick a single storage version, mark v1alpha1 as served-not-stored once v1beta1 lands, and provide conversion webhooks. Never delete a served version without a deprecation window. Store the canonical version in etcd, convert on read for older clients.

docs.title: 4. What is a CRD storage version and why does it matter?
docs.text: Only one version is persisted in etcd. Conversion webhooks translate between served versions on the wire. If you change storage version, you must rewrite all stored objects via a migration job before retiring the old version, otherwise round-trip data loss occurs.

docs.title: 5. Structural schemas — required for what?
docs.text: Required for v1 CRDs. They enable pruning of unknown fields, defaulting, and proper OpenAPI publishing for kubectl explain. Without them you lose validation guarantees and merge-patch becomes lossy.

docs.title: 6. Subresources — when do you enable status and scale?
docs.text: Enable status whenever your controller owns a status field. It splits RBAC and prevents users from mutating status. Enable scale when the resource is meaningfully replica-counted and you want HPA compatibility.

docs.title: 7. Finalizers — design rules?
docs.text: Finalizers are owned by a single controller. Always namespace them with your domain. Add before creating external state, remove only after external cleanup confirms. Never add a finalizer you cannot remove offline; you will brick deletion.

docs.title: 8. Owner references — when not to use them?
docs.text: Avoid owner references across namespaces or to cluster-scoped owners from namespaced children. Garbage collection assumes same-namespace ownership. Cross-cutting deletion needs a controller, not GC.

docs.title: 9. Reconciler design — level versus edge triggered?
docs.text: Always level-triggered. Read current state, compute desired state, converge. Edge-triggered designs accumulate drift and break on missed events. Use the workqueue for rate-limited retries, not for event ordering.

docs.title: 10. Status conditions — what schema?
docs.text: Use the standard Kubernetes Conditions array with type, status, reason, message, lastTransitionTime, observedGeneration. Tooling, dashboards, and kubectl wait depend on this shape.

docs.title: 11. Generation versus observedGeneration — why both?
docs.text: Generation increments on spec change. observedGeneration is what the controller has reconciled. The gap tells you whether status reflects current spec. Without it, status lies during rollouts.

docs.title: 12. CRD scope — namespaced versus cluster-scoped?
docs.text: Namespaced for tenant-owned resources, cluster-scoped for platform primitives. Mixing them costs you RBAC clarity. When in doubt, namespaced.

docs.title: 13. Mutating versus validating — design pitfalls?
docs.text: Mutating webhooks reorder unpredictably; never assume your sidecar inject runs last. Validating webhooks must be idempotent and side-effect-free. Both must respect timeoutSeconds and failurePolicy.

docs.title: 14. failurePolicy Fail or Ignore?
docs.text: Fail for security policy enforcement. Ignore for advisory mutations like injection on best-effort namespaces. Default Fail, exempt kube-system, exclude your own namespace to avoid bootstrap deadlock.

docs.title: 15. How do you avoid a webhook bringing down the API server?
docs.text: Set timeoutSeconds to 5 or less, scope namespaceSelector and objectSelector tightly, run the webhook in HA with PodDisruptionBudget, exempt the webhook namespace itself, and monitor admission latency as a SLI.

docs.title: 16. Webhook bootstrap dependency loop — how to break?
docs.text: Exclude kube-system and the webhook namespace from selectors. Use cert-manager with a namespace not gated by the webhook. Pre-create the webhook deployment before installing the MutatingWebhookConfiguration.

docs.title: 17. Order of admission — what runs when?
docs.text: Authentication, authorization, mutating admission, schema validation, validating admission, then persistence. Mutating webhooks run in unspecified order; reinvocationPolicy IfNeeded triggers a second pass if any later mutation occurs.

docs.title: 18. CEL ValidatingAdmissionPolicy — when over webhook?
docs.text: For pure validation without external state, prefer CEL. No deployment, no certs, no webhook server. Use webhooks when you need cluster lookups, external API calls, or mutation.

docs.title: 19. Scoping by namespaceSelector and objectSelector?
docs.text: Always set both. Without them you intercept every Pod in every namespace, including system pods. Performance and blast radius depend on tight selectors.

docs.title: 20. SideEffects field — why does it matter?
docs.text: Declares whether your webhook has out-of-band effects. Required for dryRun support. Lying here breaks kubectl diff and apiserver dry-run flows.

docs.title: 21. Scheduler plugin versus extender — choose how?
docs.text: Plugins are in-process, low-latency, type-safe. Extenders are HTTP, language-agnostic, slow. Default to plugins. Extenders only when you cannot ship Go or need to integrate with an external scheduling brain.

docs.title: 22. Scheduling framework extension points?
docs.text: PreFilter, Filter, PostFilter, PreScore, Score, NormalizeScore, Reserve, Permit, PreBind, Bind, PostBind. Pick the latest point that solves your problem; earlier hooks burn cycles on every pod.

docs.title: 23. Multi-scheduler patterns — when to run two?
docs.text: When workload classes have fundamentally different policies: batch versus service, or GPU versus CPU. Use schedulerName to opt-in. Avoid running default scheduler twice.

docs.title: 24. Pod topology spread versus affinity?
docs.text: Topology spread is the modern primitive: skew-aware, declarative, supports zones and nodes uniformly. Use affinity only for hard pinning or anti-co-location with another workload.

docs.title: 25. PriorityClass and preemption — design rules?
docs.text: Define no more than five priority bands. Preemption respects PDBs but can still cause churn. Reserve highest band for system-critical only. Never let user workloads exceed system-cluster-critical.

docs.title: 26. DRA — Dynamic Resource Allocation — what changes?
docs.text: DRA models devices like GPUs as first-class scheduled resources with claims, classes, and lifecycle. Replaces device plugin model for sharable, partitioned, or vendor-rich devices. Plan to migrate over multiple releases.

docs.title: 27. Gang scheduling — how to do it well?
docs.text: Use a coscheduling plugin like Volcano or scheduler-plugins coscheduling. Mark pod groups with a label, the plugin reserves capacity all-or-nothing. Avoid hand-rolled gang via init containers.

docs.title: 28. Mesh adoption — sidecar or sidecarless?
docs.text: Sidecar is mature, predictable, costly. Sidecarless via Istio ambient or Cilium service mesh is cheaper but younger. For greenfield with ops maturity, ambient. For brownfield with strict mTLS and existing skill, sidecar.

docs.title: 29. mTLS — strict, permissive, or off?
docs.text: Permissive during rollout, strict in steady state, never off in shared clusters. Strict at namespace scope first, then mesh-wide. Have an emergency PeerAuthentication rollback ready.

docs.title: 30. Retries and timeouts — where to set them?
docs.text: Per-route at the mesh, with budgets at the destination. Always set both. Unbounded retries amplify outages. Timeouts must be shorter than the upstream client timeout.

docs.title: 31. Mesh observability — what is required before adoption?
docs.text: Distributed tracing with sampling, golden signals dashboards, and access logs at the gateway. Without these, mesh adds latency you cannot explain and failures you cannot debug.

docs.title: 32. Multi-cluster mesh topologies?
docs.text: Primary-remote: one control plane, remote data planes. Multi-primary: control plane in each cluster, federated trust. Replicated: independent meshes joined by gateways. Choose by failure domain isolation needs.

docs.title: 33. East-west gateway — when needed?
docs.text: For multi-cluster mesh when pods cannot route directly across clusters. Adds an extra hop and a mTLS termination point. Avoid if flat L3 is available.

docs.title: 34. WASM filters — production-ready?
docs.text: For specific use cases yes: header rewrite, rate limit, custom auth. Watch for memory leaks and cold-start cost. Compile with strict resource limits, version your filters, ship via OCI.

docs.title: 35. Gateway API versus Ingress — when to migrate?
docs.text: Migrate when you need role separation between platform and app teams, protocol-rich routing, or multi-tenant gateways. Stay on Ingress for simple TLS-terminated HTTP with one team.

docs.title: 36. GatewayClass design?
docs.text: One class per implementation: edge, internal, mesh. Owned by platform. Application teams reference classes, not implementations.

docs.title: 37. HTTPRoute attachment — same versus cross-namespace?
docs.text: Cross-namespace requires ReferenceGrant. Use it for shared gateways. Same-namespace by default for tenant isolation.

docs.title: 38. ParentRefs design?
docs.text: A route can attach to multiple parents. Use this for canary across gateways or for serving the same app on internal and external. Avoid mixing semantics on a single route.

docs.title: 39. TCP, UDP, GRPC routes — when?
docs.text: TCPRoute for opaque L4. UDPRoute for DNS and similar. GRPCRoute for native gRPC matching including method names. Prefer GRPCRoute over HTTPRoute path-matching for gRPC.

docs.title: 40. Policy attachment pattern?
docs.text: Define policies as CRDs that target Gateway, HTTPRoute, or Service. Use the targetRef pattern. Avoid annotation-based policy; it does not survive role separation.

docs.title: 41. Federation versus GitOps fan-out?
docs.text: GitOps fan-out is simpler, scales well, and isolates failure. Federation centralizes control at the cost of a single point of failure and operational complexity. Default to fan-out unless you need cross-cluster placement decisions.

docs.title: 42. Cluster API — when to adopt?
docs.text: When you manage more than five clusters, need declarative provisioning, and want consistent upgrades. The investment pays back at fleet scale, not at one or two clusters.

docs.title: 43. Service discovery across clusters?
docs.text: Multi-cluster Services with ClusterSet, or mesh-based federation. Avoid DNS hacks across clusters; they break health and locality awareness.

docs.title: 44. Cross-cluster failover — design?
docs.text: Active-active with health-weighted DNS or mesh locality routing. Active-passive with explicit promotion controlled by a runbook, never automatic across regions.

docs.title: 45. Workload identity across clusters?
docs.text: SPIFFE IDs federated via SPIRE or mesh trust bundles. Avoid sharing service account tokens; they do not federate cleanly.

docs.title: 46. Policy distribution at fleet scale?
docs.text: Kyverno or OPA policies stored in Git, applied via Flux or Argo per cluster. Policies remain local; reports aggregate centrally.

docs.title: 47. Cilium versus Calico — choose how?
docs.text: Cilium for eBPF datapath, identity-based policy, and integrated mesh-lite. Calico for mature network policy, BGP at scale, and lower learning curve. Both are excellent; the team skill curve usually decides.

docs.title: 48. eBPF kube-proxy replacement — production ready?
docs.text: Yes for Cilium and recent Kubernetes. Removes iptables scaling cliff, improves latency. Validate on your kernel version; eBPF features track kernel.

docs.title: 49. Network policy versus mesh policy?
docs.text: Network policy at L3 or L4. Mesh policy at L7 with identity. Use both: network policy as the floor, mesh policy as the ceiling. Defense in depth.

docs.title: 50. Hubble or Cilium observability — when?
docs.text: When you need flow-level visibility without running a full mesh. Adds modest CPU, gives you dropped-packet attribution and policy hit logs.

docs.title: 51. eBPF tc hooks — what do they replace?
docs.text: iptables NAT, conntrack-heavy paths, and per-packet userspace decisions. Run earlier in the stack, scale linearly, but require kernel-level expertise to debug.

docs.title: 52. Hard versus soft multi-tenancy?
docs.text: Soft: namespaces, RBAC, network policy. Hard: separate clusters or virtual clusters with kube-apiserver isolation. PCI, HIPAA, or hostile tenants need hard.

docs.title: 53. Virtual clusters — when?
docs.text: When you want per-tenant control planes without per-tenant nodes. Capsule, vCluster, or Kamaji. Adds complexity, gains isolation.

docs.title: 54. Quota strategy?
docs.text: ResourceQuota per namespace, LimitRange for defaults, PriorityClass quotas to cap high-priority abuse. Quota at admission time prevents noisy-neighbor scheduling.

docs.title: 55. Tenant scheduling isolation?
docs.text: Node selectors plus taints, with topology spread inside. Avoid dedicated nodes per tenant unless you accept the bin-packing loss.

docs.title: 56. RBAC at scale?
docs.text: ClusterRoles with aggregation labels. Per-tenant Roles via bootstrap operators. Never grant cluster-admin to tenants; use namespace-admin role definitions.

docs.title: 57. Audit logging for tenants?
docs.text: Audit policy with per-namespace metadata level minimum, request level for sensitive verbs. Ship audit to per-tenant sinks where compliance requires.

docs.title: 58. StatefulSet versus operator?
docs.text: StatefulSet for stable identity and ordered rollout. Operator when you need backup, restore, failover, or topology-aware ops. Most databases need both.

docs.title: 59. CSI driver design considerations?
docs.text: Implement Identity, Controller, Node services. Support snapshots if your storage does. Handle volume expansion. Set fsGroupPolicy correctly to avoid permission breakage.

docs.title: 60. Storage classes — how many?
docs.text: One per performance tier and reclaim policy combination. Rarely more than five. Annotate the default; never have two defaults.

docs.title: 61. Topology-aware provisioning?
docs.text: Set volumeBindingMode WaitForFirstConsumer for zonal storage. Without it pods schedule before storage, ending in cross-zone failures.

docs.title: 62. CRD versus aggregated API server?
docs.text: CRD for 95 percent of cases. Aggregated API server when you need custom storage, non-etcd backends, or REST verbs Kubernetes does not model. Aggregated APIs cost you the entire API machinery you must reimplement.

docs.title: 63. Conversion webhook — design?
docs.text: Stateless, fast, idempotent. Round-trip safe: convert v1 to v2 and back must equal original. Test with fuzzing.

docs.title: 64. Defaulting strategy?
docs.text: Prefer CRD schema defaulting over mutating webhook. It runs without network calls, survives webhook outages, and is visible in OpenAPI.

docs.title: 65. Validation strategy?
docs.text: CEL on CRD fields for cross-field rules. ValidatingAdmissionPolicy for cluster-wide rules. Webhooks only when you need external lookups.

docs.title: 66. SLOs for the control plane?
docs.text: P99 admission latency, etcd write latency, scheduler bind latency, controller workqueue depth. Alert on burn rate, not single samples.

docs.title: 67. Etcd sizing and defrag?
docs.text: 8 GB DB size soft limit. Defrag during off-hours. Snapshot every 30 minutes. Three-node minimum, five for fault tolerance.

docs.title: 68. Upgrade strategy?
docs.text: Skew is one minor version. Upgrade control plane first, then nodes. Test in non-prod with same CRDs and webhooks. Always have a rollback path.

docs.title: 69. Disaster recovery for the cluster itself?
docs.text: Etcd snapshots offsite. CRD definitions in Git. Cluster API templates for rebuilding. Practice restore quarterly; untested backups are not backups.

docs.title: 70. Cost levers at scale?
docs.text: Right-size requests via VPA recommendations, bin-pack with node-pool consolidation, use spot for batch, right-tier storage. Operator cost dwarfs node cost above a threshold; consolidate operators.

docs.title: Closing principles
docs.text:
• Reconcile, do not orchestrate.
  • Validate at admission, default at schema, mutate sparingly.
  • Push policy to the platform, not the application.
  • Choose boring technology that has a working operator.
  • Make every extension observable from day zero.
