docs.title: Architect Q&A — Security
docs.text: 60+ Q&A for senior, staff, and architect-level Kubernetes and cloud-native security decisions. Covers multi-tenant boundaries, supply-chain SLSA L3 program, OIDC trust to cloud, secret rotation at scale, runtime detection at scale, zero-trust mesh adoption, compliance program design, and incident response playbooks.

docs.title: Q1. What is the strongest tenant boundary in Kubernetes?
docs.text: A separate cluster. Namespace isolation is a soft boundary — node, kernel, and control-plane are shared. For hostile multi-tenancy, use cluster-per-tenant or vCluster + node pool isolation + gVisor/Kata.

docs.title: Q2. When is namespace-per-tenant acceptable?
docs.text: Cooperative tenants (same company, internal teams). Enforce: NetworkPolicy default-deny, ResourceQuota, LimitRange, RBAC scoped to namespace, no shared CRDs that leak data, PSA restricted.

docs.title: Q3. How do you prevent a tenant from reading another tenant's secrets?
docs.text: RBAC scoped to namespace, no ClusterRoleBindings granting cross-namespace get on Secrets, encrypt-at-rest in etcd with KMS, audit on Secret access, External Secrets per-namespace SA with IRSA scoped to tenant prefix in the secret store.

docs.title: Q4. How do you stop tenants from consuming all node resources?
docs.text: ResourceQuota for cpu/memory/pods, LimitRange defaults, PriorityClass for system workloads, dedicated node pools per tier with taints + tolerations, scheduler with anti-affinity.

docs.title: Q5. What is vCluster and when do you pick it over namespaces?
docs.text: vCluster runs a virtual control plane inside a host namespace. Picks: tenants need cluster-admin for their own scope, want their own CRDs, version skew. Caveat: still shares host nodes — not a hard isolation boundary unless combined with sandbox runtime.

docs.title: Q6. How do you prevent privileged escalation across tenants?
docs.text: Pod Security Admission restricted on tenant namespaces, baseline on system, drop ALL caps, no hostPath, no hostNetwork, no privileged, seccomp RuntimeDefault, read-only root FS. Validate via Kyverno or Gatekeeper as belt-and-suspenders.

docs.title: Q7. How do you isolate tenant traffic east-west?
docs.text: Cilium with cluster-mesh and tenant labels; default-deny NetworkPolicy; per-tenant L7 policies for shared services; egress via per-tenant gateways; mTLS via mesh with SPIFFE IDs that encode tenant.

docs.title: Q8. How do you handle shared cluster-scoped resources like CRDs and webhooks?
docs.text: Platform team owns CRDs. Tenants get RBAC only on namespaced custom resources. Validating webhooks must be tenant-aware via namespace selectors. Conversion webhooks run with platform identity, not tenant.

docs.title: Q9. How do you prevent noisy neighbor in storage?
docs.text: Per-tenant StorageClass with IOPS/throughput limits, CSI quota, ceph/EBS namespace-scoped pools, monitor PVC consumption with quotas.

docs.title: Q10. What is the audit strategy for multi-tenant?
docs.text: Audit policy: log Metadata for all, RequestResponse for tenant Secret/ConfigMap writes. Stream to per-tenant index in SIEM. Retain 1 year. Tenants get read on their slice via API.

docs.title: Q11. What is SLSA L3 in one sentence?
docs.text: Builds run on a hardened, hosted, isolated builder that produces non-forgeable provenance signed by the platform.

docs.title: Q12. What are the L3 hard requirements?
docs.text: Hosted build platform (no self-hosted runners with mutable state), isolated build per invocation, parameterless build entry, hermetic where possible, signed provenance generated by the platform key.

docs.title: Q13. How do you reach L3 with GitHub Actions?
docs.text: Use GitHub-hosted runners (or actions-runner-controller with ephemeral pods), use the SLSA generic generator workflow, sign with sigstore keyless using the GitHub OIDC token, attach in-toto attestation to the OCI registry via cosign.

docs.title: Q14. How do you verify SLSA provenance at admission?
docs.text: Cosign policy controller or Kyverno verifyImages rule with the predicate type slsaprovenance and an issuer/subject regex matching your build platform's OIDC identity.

docs.title: Q15. Where do attestations live?
docs.text: As OCI artifacts referenced by digest in the same registry. cosign download attestation registry/app@sha256:... returns DSSE envelopes containing in-toto statements.

docs.title: Q16. How do you handle base image trust?
docs.text: Pin by digest. Rebuild base images in your own pipeline producing your own provenance. Mirror upstream into a private registry with a verification policy that requires either internal provenance or vendor signature.

docs.title: Q17. What is the rollout plan for SLSA L3 across 200 services?
docs.text: Phase 1: instrument top 10 critical services, pilot signing and verification in staging with --enforce=warn. Phase 2: enforce in staging, warn in prod, build dashboards. Phase 3: enforce in prod for tier 1, expand cohort by cohort. Phase 4: deny unsigned by default.

docs.title: Q18. What gets signed and what gets attested?
docs.text: Sign: container images, Helm charts, OCI artifacts. Attest: SBOM (cyclonedx/spdx), SLSA provenance, vulnerability scan results, test results, custom predicate types (e.g. internal review approval).

docs.title: Q19. How do you prevent dependency confusion?
docs.text: Private registry first in resolver config, scope locks, pin transitive deps, mirror approved deps only, block public installs in CI behind explicit allowlist.

docs.title: Q20. How do you handle SBOM at scale?
docs.text: Generate at build with syft, attach as attestation, push to a central SBOM store (DependencyTrack or Snyk), continuously scan against fresh CVE feeds, alert on new CVEs against deployed digests.

docs.title: Q21. Why use OIDC federation over static cloud keys for K8s workloads?
docs.text: No long-lived secrets in cluster, automatic rotation by IdP, fine-grained policies bound to the workload identity, audit on the cloud side.

docs.title: Q22. How does IRSA work in EKS?
docs.text: EKS issues OIDC tokens to ServiceAccounts. AWS IAM trusts the cluster's OIDC issuer URL. The pod's projected SA token is exchanged via STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. The workload assumes a role scoped via condition keys on sub matching system:serviceaccount:ns:sa.

docs.title: Q23. How do you trust GitHub Actions to deploy to AWS without a static key?
docs.text: Configure AWS IAM OIDC provider for token.actions.githubusercontent.com. Create a role with trust policy conditioning on sub like repo:org/repo:ref:refs/heads/main and aud=sts.amazonaws.com. Use aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4.

docs.title: Q24. What is the equivalent for GCP?
docs.text: Workload Identity Federation. Create a workload identity pool, add provider with the OIDC issuer, bind a service account with principalSet://... condition.

docs.title: Q25. What is the equivalent for Azure?
docs.text: Azure Workload Identity for AKS, federated identity credentials on a managed identity referencing the OIDC issuer URL.

docs.title: Q26. How do you scope tokens minimally?
docs.text: Use audience claim restriction, short TTL (1h max), conditions on sub for exact SA, branch-or-tag restriction in CI, never wildcard repo:org/*.

docs.title: Q27. How do you rotate the cluster OIDC signing key?
docs.text: Managed services rotate automatically on EKS/AKS/GKE. For self-hosted, rotate kube-apiserver --service-account-signing-key-file with overlap window, publish JWKS, update IAM provider thumbprint if needed.

docs.title: Q28. What is the failure mode if OIDC issuer URL is wrong?
docs.text: Workloads cannot assume cloud roles, deployments stall on cloud calls. Mitigation: monitor STS errors, alert on AccessDenied spikes, runbook to verify OIDC provider thumbprint and issuer.

docs.title: Q29. How do you audit OIDC token usage?
docs.text: CloudTrail for AWS STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity events, GCP audit logs for STS token exchanges, correlate on sub claim back to namespace/SA. Forward to SIEM.

docs.title: Q30. How do you prevent token replay across regions or environments?
docs.text: Audience claim per environment, short TTL, IP condition where possible, distinct OIDC issuer per cluster, IRSA roles per env with naming convention.

docs.title: Q31. What is the right secret store for K8s at scale?
docs.text: External Secrets Operator + Vault or AWS Secrets Manager / GCP Secret Manager / Azure Key Vault. Vault wins for dynamic secrets (DB credentials), cloud-native wins for managed simplicity.

docs.title: Q32. How do you rotate a database password without downtime?
docs.text: Two-credential rotation: app uses cred A, rotate to B in store, ESO refreshes secret in K8s, app reloads (sidecar reloader or SIGHUP), invalidate A. Or use Vault dynamic DB secrets with short TTL and lease renewal.

docs.title: Q33. How do you rotate TLS certs at scale?
docs.text: cert-manager with ACME or internal CA, short-lived certs (24h to 90d), reloader watching Secret to roll Deployments, mesh handles workload certs automatically (Istio rotates SVID hourly).

docs.title: Q34. What is the strategy for static secrets that must rotate?
docs.text: Tag with TTL annotation, scheduled job to rotate via API to source store, ESO syncs, application reads via volume mount with subPath, app code retries on auth failure.

docs.title: Q35. How do you prove rotation happened?
docs.text: Audit log on store side, K8s event on Secret update, metric secret_age_seconds exposed by an exporter scraping Secret annotations, alert when > SLA.

docs.title: Q36. What about sealed-secrets — when is it appropriate?
docs.text: Small clusters, GitOps-only, no central store. Caveats: rotation requires re-sealing and committing, the sealing key is a single point of trust. Prefer ESO for anything beyond 10 services.

docs.title: Q37. How do you prevent a secret from being logged?
docs.text: Disable RequestResponse audit on Secrets, redact in app logs, lint pipelines for kubectl get secret -o yaml in scripts, use --token-only flags, ban env vars for highly sensitive secrets — prefer projected volumes.

docs.title: Q38. How do you handle secret access during a Vault outage?
docs.text: Cache last-known value in K8s Secret with ESO, set high refresh interval for non-critical, use Vault Performance Standby, consider regional Vault clusters with replication, fallback to read-only mode in app.

docs.title: Q39. How do you grant least privilege on the secret store?
docs.text: One Vault role per app per env, policies on path secret/data/env/app/*, K8s auth method binding SA to role, audit device on Vault streaming to SIEM, deny * policies.

docs.title: Q40. How do you onboard a new app to External Secrets?
docs.text: Template: Helm chart includes ExternalSecret and SecretStore ref, Vault path computed from {env}/{namespace}/{app}, SA bound to Vault role via Kubernetes auth, CI bootstraps the Vault role via Terraform on first deploy.

docs.title: Q41. Falco vs Tetragon — which to pick?
docs.text: Falco: rule-based, mature, kernel module or eBPF, alerts to falcosidekick. Tetragon: eBPF-native, in-kernel filtering and enforcement, lower overhead at high event volume. Use Tetragon for fleets > 500 nodes or where you need policy enforcement, Falco for mature alerting and community rules.

docs.title: Q42. What rules do you start with?
docs.text: Falco default rules + k8s_audit. Highest value: shell in container, write to /etc, mount of sensitive paths, outbound to non-allowlist destination, exec into kube-system, change to RBAC.

docs.title: Q43. How do you tune false positives?
docs.text: Macro overrides in falco_rules.local.yaml, exception lists per workload label, suppression at falcosidekick before SIEM, weekly review of fired rules with action: tune, delete, escalate.

docs.title: Q44. How do you ship events at scale?
docs.text: Falcosidekick to Kafka, downstream consumers: SIEM (Splunk/Elastic), enrichment service adding pod metadata, deduplication, alert manager. Avoid direct SIEM push from each node.

docs.title: Q45. What is the cardinality risk?
docs.text: Per-event labels (pod, image, command) explode metric cardinality. Use logs not metrics for events, keep metrics aggregated by rule + namespace.

docs.title: Q46. How do you enforce with Tetragon?
docs.text: TracingPolicy with enforcer action — kill, override return value, signal. Example: kill any process opening /etc/shadow outside allowlist. Roll out per-namespace.

docs.title: Q47. Detection coverage map?
docs.text: Map rules to MITRE ATT&CK for Containers. Track coverage per tactic. Aim for detection in: Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Defense Evasion, Credential Access, Discovery, Lateral Movement, Exfiltration.

docs.title: Q48. How do you handle a runtime alert at 3am?
docs.text: Runbook: confirm not noise, isolate pod (NetworkPolicy deny + cordon node if needed), capture forensics (process tree, fd list, /proc/PID/maps), preserve container fs, page IR lead if confirmed, postmortem within 5 days.

docs.title: Q49. What is zero-trust in K8s terms?
docs.text: Every connection authenticated and authorized regardless of network position. Identity is workload-bound (SPIFFE), not IP-bound. Default-deny everywhere.

docs.title: Q50. Istio vs Linkerd vs Cilium for mTLS?
docs.text: Linkerd: simplest, lowest overhead, ambient not yet GA. Istio: most features, ambient mode reduces sidecar cost. Cilium: eBPF mTLS without sidecars, integrates with NetworkPolicy. Pick by org maturity and feature need.

docs.title: Q51. What is the rollout plan?
docs.text: Phase 1: install mesh, enable PERMISSIVE mTLS, observe. Phase 2: enable STRICT per-namespace, fix exceptions. Phase 3: AuthorizationPolicy default-deny per namespace, allowlist intentional traffic. Phase 4: extend to ingress and egress.

docs.title: Q52. What about non-mesh workloads?
docs.text: Mesh egress gateway, sidecar injection by namespace label, accept-no-mesh annotation for legacy with explicit risk acceptance, plan migration with deadline.

docs.title: Q53. How does SPIFFE fit?
docs.text: SPIFFE provides workload identity (SVID) — X.509 or JWT — issued by SPIRE. Mesh uses SVIDs for mTLS. Workloads outside mesh use SPIRE agent to fetch SVID for cross-system auth (e.g. Vault, DB).

docs.title: Q54. How do you authorize at L7?
docs.text: AuthorizationPolicy with method, path, JWT claims. Validate JWT at sidecar via RequestAuthentication. Pass principal to app for fine-grained checks.

docs.title: Q55. What breaks when you turn on STRICT mTLS?
docs.text: Probes from kubelet (allow with PERMISSIVE on probe port or use exec probes), prometheus scraping (use mesh-aware Prom or scrape through sidecar), legacy clients without mTLS, headless services (work but require attention).

docs.title: Q56. How do you observe mesh traffic?
docs.text: Mesh exposes metrics (request rate, error rate, p99) and traces (Jaeger/Tempo). Build SLOs from these. Kiali for topology. Hubble for Cilium.

docs.title: Q57. What is the first step of a compliance program?
docs.text: Scope. Define cardholder data environment (PCI), ePHI systems (HIPAA), or in-scope services (SOC 2). Network segmentation reduces scope dramatically.

docs.title: Q58. How do you implement PCI segmentation in K8s?
docs.text: Dedicated cluster or dedicated namespace + node pool with taints, network policies block all ingress except payment service entry, egress only to PCI-approved endpoints, all logs to a separate SIEM index, all admin via bastion with MFA.

docs.title: Q59. How do you handle HIPAA encryption?
docs.text: At rest: KMS-encrypted etcd, KMS-encrypted PVs, KMS-encrypted object storage. In transit: TLS 1.2+ everywhere, mTLS via mesh, no plaintext intra-cluster.

docs.title: Q60. SOC 2 logging requirements?
docs.text: CC7.2 — monitor system components. Centralized logs with integrity (signed or WORM), retention 1 year, access reviewed quarterly, alerts on detection of unauthorized changes, evidence for auditor.

docs.title: Q61. How do you produce evidence at audit time?
docs.text: Continuous evidence collection: Drata/Vanta/Secureframe pulling from K8s, cloud, IdP, vuln scanner, SIEM. Store as immutable evidence artifacts with timestamps. Auditor gets read-only access.

docs.title: Q62. How do you handle change management for SOC 2?
docs.text: All changes via PR with approval (CC8.1). GitOps enforces this — direct cluster changes denied via RBAC. Emergency change process documented and audited.

docs.title: Q63. What about access reviews?
docs.text: Quarterly: export RBAC bindings, IAM roles, IdP group memberships. Manager attests per direct report. Revoke on no-attestation. Tool: Sailpoint, custom script, or IdP-native review.

docs.title: Q64. How do you prove vulnerability management?
docs.text: Trivy/Snyk in CI, Grype/Trivy continuously against running images, SLA: critical < 7d, high < 30d. Dashboard with MTTR per severity. Auditor sees SLA hit rate.

docs.title: Q65. What are the IR phases?
docs.text: Prepare, Detect, Analyze, Contain, Eradicate, Recover, Lessons Learned. NIST SP 800-61.

docs.title: Q66. What does prepare look like for K8s?
docs.text: Runbooks per scenario, IR team on-call rotation, tabletop exercises quarterly, forensic tooling pre-installed (sysdig capture, kubectl debug, kube-forensics), evidence pipeline tested, legal/PR contacts known.

docs.title: Q67. Compromised pod — playbook?
docs.text: 1) Confirm via Falco/Tetragon evidence. 2) Cordon node. 3) Apply NetworkPolicy deny on pod label. 4) kubectl debug to capture process list, network conns, env. 5) Snapshot container fs. 6) Delete pod, evict node, rotate any creds it held. 7) Hunt for lateral movement via audit log.

docs.title: Q68. Stolen kubeconfig — playbook?
docs.text: 1) Revoke client cert via CSR deletion or rotate cluster CA (worst case). 2) Disable IdP user. 3) Audit log search for user actions. 4) Inventory created/modified resources, treat as compromised. 5) Rotate any secrets accessed. 6) Postmortem on how it leaked.

docs.title: Q69. Cryptojacking detected — playbook?
docs.text: 1) Kill pod, isolate node. 2) Trace image to source — was it pulled from public registry without verification? 3) Block image digest at admission. 4) Check for persistence (DaemonSets, CronJobs, mutating webhooks). 5) Audit all images deployed since the bad pull.

docs.title: Q70. Ransomware on PV — playbook?
docs.text: 1) Snapshot PV before any action. 2) Identify infection vector (vuln, creds, supply chain). 3) Restore from clean backup to new namespace. 4) Validate backup integrity before cutover. 5) Rotate all creds in scope. 6) Notify per legal/regulatory requirements (HIPAA 60d, GDPR 72h).

docs.title: Q71. Public exposure of S3-equivalent / etcd snapshot — playbook?
docs.text: 1) Lock down ACL immediately. 2) Determine what data was exposed and for how long via access logs. 3) Notify legal. 4) Rotate any credentials/PII keys in the exposed data. 5) Postmortem on bucket policy gap, IaC guardrail to prevent recurrence.

docs.title: Q72. How do you measure IR maturity?
docs.text: MTTD (mean time to detect), MTTR (respond), MTTC (contain), tabletop frequency, runbook coverage of scenarios, % of detections with auto-containment, postmortem completion rate.

docs.title: Closing principles
docs.text:
• Default-deny everything: network, RBAC, admission, egress.
  • Identity is the new perimeter: SPIFFE for workloads, OIDC for humans.
  • Sign and verify everything: image, attestation, config bundle.
  • Detect at runtime — preventive controls fail.
  • Practice IR before you need it.
  • Evidence is continuous, not annual.

docs.title: Security for 10-Year-Olds (ELI10)
docs.text: Security stuff explained like you're 10. Each idea has an analogy, the real thing, a tiny diagram, and commands you can actually run.

docs.title: 1. RBAC = different keys for different rooms
Analogy
docs.text: Imagine a school. The art teacher has a key to the art room. The science teacher has a key to the science lab. The principal has a master key. Nobody walks around with every key — that would be dangerous if they lost it.

docs.title: Real thing
docs.text: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) gives each person or robot a small set of permissions. A "Role" is the keyring. A "RoleBinding" hands the keyring to someone.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  U[User]
  RB[RoleBinding]
  R[Role]
  K[API Resources]
  U --> RB --> R --> K

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
# Make a role that can only read pods
kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods -n demo

# Give it to a user
kubectl create rolebinding read-pods --role=pod-reader --user=alice -n demo

# Check what alice can do
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=alice -n demo   # yes
kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as=alice -n demo # no

docs.title: Trap
docs.text: Never make someone cluster-admin "just for now". That's the master key. They'll keep it forever.

docs.title: 2. NetworkPolicy = list of friends who can talk to you
Analogy
docs.text: You're at lunch. You have a rule: only kids from your class can sit at your table. Everyone else has to sit somewhere else. That rule is a NetworkPolicy.

docs.title: Real thing
docs.text: NetworkPolicy says: "pods with this label can receive traffic only from pods with that label, on these ports." Without one, every pod talks to every pod.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  F[Frontend]
  B[Backend]
  D[Database]
  F --> B --> D

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
# Default deny: nobody talks to anyone in the namespace
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny
  namespace: demo
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
EOF

# Allow frontend to call backend
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: front-to-back
  namespace: demo
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app: backend }
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels: { app: frontend }
    ports:
    - port: 8080
EOF

docs.title: Trap
docs.text: You need a CNI that supports NetworkPolicy (Calico, Cilium). On a CNI that ignores it, the rules do nothing — silently.

docs.title: Analogy
docs.text: Your diary has a tiny lock. You write your feelings inside. Your sister can see the diary on the shelf, but she cannot read it without the key. The key is hidden.

docs.title: Real thing
docs.text: A Secret holds passwords or tokens. K8s base64-encodes it (not secure!) and stores it. Encryption-at-rest in etcd is the real lock.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  P[Pod]
  V[Volume]
  S[Secret]
  K[KMS]
  P --> V --> S --> K

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
# Make a secret
kubectl create secret generic db-pass --from-literal=password=hunter2 -n demo

# Mount and read it
kubectl run app -n demo --image=busybox --command -- sleep 3600
kubectl set volume pod/app -n demo --add --name=pwd --type=secret --secret-name=db-pass --mount-path=/etc/db
kubectl exec -n demo app -- cat /etc/db/password

docs.title: Trap
docs.text: Never put a Secret in a git repo as plain YAML. Use SealedSecrets or External Secrets.

docs.title: Analogy
docs.text: Two friends in a club have a secret handshake. When one walks up, they do the handshake. If you don't know the handshake, you don't get in. And both sides check — it's not just a one-way thing.

docs.title: Real thing
docs.text: mTLS (mutual TLS) means both server and client show certificates. The server proves it's the real server. The client proves it's an allowed client. A service mesh does this for every pod-to-pod call automatically.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  A[Pod A]
  SA[Sidecar A]
  SB[Sidecar B]
  B[Pod B]
  A --> SA --> SB --> B

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
# Install Linkerd (simplest mesh)
linkerd install --crds | kubectl apply -f -
linkerd install | kubectl apply -f -

# Inject sidecars into a namespace
kubectl annotate ns demo linkerd.io/inject=enabled

# Roll deployments to pick up the sidecar
kubectl rollout restart deploy -n demo

# See the traffic with mTLS
linkerd viz tap deploy/frontend -n demo

docs.title: Trap
docs.text: Probes from kubelet are not in the mesh. Either use exec probes or allow probe traffic to bypass.

docs.title: 5. Admission webhook = bouncer at the door
Analogy
docs.text: A nightclub has a bouncer. Before you go in, the bouncer checks your ID, your shoes, your shirt. If anything's off, you don't get in. The bouncer can also hand you a wristband (mutate you) before letting you through.

docs.title: Real thing
docs.text: A ValidatingWebhook says yes/no to every API request. A MutatingWebhook can change the request before it's stored. OPA Gatekeeper and Kyverno are popular bouncers.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  K[kubectl apply]
  API[API Server]
  W[Webhook]
  ETC[etcd]
  K --> API --> W --> ETC

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
# Install Kyverno
kubectl create -f https://github.com/kyverno/kyverno/releases/latest/download/install.yaml

# Block any pod without resource limits
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata: { name: require-limits }
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
  - name: check-limits
    match:
      any:
      - resources: { kinds: [Pod] }
    validate:
      message: Containers must set resource limits.
      pattern:
        spec:
          containers:
          - resources:
              limits: { memory: ?*, cpu: ?* }
EOF
kubectl run nolimit --image=nginx   # should fail

docs.title: Trap
docs.text: Webhook down = API server slow or stuck. Always set failurePolicy: Ignore for non-critical, Fail only for must-have.

docs.title: Analogy
docs.text: You buy cookies at the store. The bag has a special seal. If someone opened it and put in something gross, the seal would be broken and you'd see. Also there's a sticker that says which factory made them.

docs.title: Real thing
docs.text: SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) attaches signed proof (provenance) to every build. You can verify "this image was built by our trusted CI from this source commit, nothing else."

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  S[Source]
  CI[CI Builder]
  IMG[Image]
  PROV[Provenance]
  REG[Registry]
  S --> CI --> IMG --> REG
  CI --> PROV --> REG

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
# Sign keylessly with sigstore (uses your OIDC token)
cosign sign registry/myapp:v1

# Generate SBOM and attach as attestation
syft registry/myapp:v1 -o spdx-json > sbom.json
cosign attest --predicate sbom.json --type spdx registry/myapp:v1

# Verify before deploy
cosign verify --certificate-identity-regexp=.*@mycompany.com \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://accounts.google.com registry/myapp:v1

# Scan for known holes
trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL registry/myapp:v1

docs.title: Trap
docs.text: A signature only proves who signed it, not that the contents are good. Pair signing with vuln scanning and policy.

docs.title: Analogy
docs.text: The playground has rules. No running with scissors. No climbing the fence. No bringing matches. Some kids get a pass for the woodshop (they can use sharp things) but the regular playground has strict rules.

docs.title: Real thing
docs.text: Pod Security Admission has three levels: privileged (anything goes — woodshop), baseline (no scissors), restricted (no scissors, no matches, helmet on). Apply per namespace.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  NS[Namespace]
  L[Label]
  PSA[PSA Controller]
  POD[Pod]
  NS --> L --> PSA --> POD

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
# Lock down a namespace
kubectl label ns demo pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

# Try a privileged pod (should be denied)
kubectl run -n demo bad --image=nginx --privileged

docs.title: Trap
docs.text: restricted requires non-root, seccomp, dropped caps. Many off-the-shelf images break. Test before enforcing.

docs.title: Analogy
docs.text: A food inspector visits the bakery and checks every batch for problems before it ships to stores. If they find mold, they don't let it ship.

docs.title: Real thing
docs.text: Trivy or Grype scans container images for known vulnerable libraries (CVEs). You run it in CI to fail bad builds and at runtime to find new problems in already-deployed images.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  IMG[Image]
  SC[Scanner]
  DB[CVE Database]
  REP[Report]
  IMG --> SC --> REP
  DB --> SC

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
trivy image nginx:1.21
grype nginx:1.21
trivy image --severity CRITICAL --exit-code 1 nginx:1.21   # fail CI on critical

docs.title: Trap
docs.text: A scanner can only find what its database knows. Update the DB daily. Zero-day vulns are invisible.

docs.title: Analogy
docs.text: At a big office, every worker wears a badge. The badge has their name, what team they're on, and what floors they can visit. Robots (workloads) need badges too.

docs.title: Real thing
docs.text: SPIFFE gives each workload a verifiable identity (SVID), like spiffe://company/ns/payments/sa/api. SPIRE issues and rotates these automatically.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  W[Workload]
  AG[SPIRE Agent]
  SR[SPIRE Server]
  ID[SVID]
  W --> AG --> SR
  SR --> ID --> W

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: kubectl exec -n demo app -- /opt/spire/bin/spire-agent api fetch x509

docs.title: Trap
docs.text: SPIRE setup is non-trivial. Most teams get SPIFFE for free via Istio or Linkerd.

docs.title: Analogy
docs.text: Your house has motion sensors. If someone breaks a window or sneaks in at night, the alarm goes off. You can't prevent every break-in, but you can know fast.

docs.title: Real thing
docs.text: Falco watches every process, file, and network event in your cluster. Rules say "alert if someone runs a shell inside a container."

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  K[Kernel]
  F[Falco]
  R[Rules]
  AL[Alert]
  K --> F --> AL
  R --> F

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
helm install falco falcosecurity/falco -n falco --create-namespace
kubectl run shell --image=busybox -- sh -c 'sleep 600'
kubectl exec shell -- sh
kubectl logs -n falco -l app.kubernetes.io/name=falco --tail=20

docs.title: Trap
docs.text: Default rules will be noisy. Plan a tuning sprint in week two.

docs.title: What to do next
docs.text:
1. Run all the commands in a throwaway kind/minikube cluster.
  2. Open visual-flows.md to see how requests travel through these pieces.
  3. Read architect-qa.md when you start designing for a real org.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: A reference of common DevOps, Kubernetes, container, and platform terms used throughout this site. Hover any abbreviation in the docs to see its definition (when supported by the browser).

docs.title: Visual Flows — Security
docs.text: 10 simple mermaid flowcharts showing how requests, decisions, and trust flow through Kubernetes and cloud-native security systems. Each chart has a brief explanation, follow-up notes, and the relevant kubectl/cosign commands.

docs.title: 1. kubectl request — authn to authz to admission to etcd
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  U[User]
  AN[Authn]
  AZ[Authz]
  AD[Admission]
  ETC[etcd]
  U --> AN --> AZ --> AD --> ETC

The full path of any kubectl apply. Authn proves who you are (cert, token, OIDC). Authz checks RBAC. Admission validates and mutates. Then store.

Failure modes - Authn fails: 401 Unauthorized - Authz fails: 403 Forbidden - Admission denies: webhook error message - etcd unavailable: 500

Commands 

kubectl auth whoami
kubectl auth can-i create pods -n demo
kubectl get --raw /api/v1/namespaces/demo/pods --v=8

docs.title: 2. RBAC authorization decision
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  REQ[Request]
  RB[RoleBinding]
  R[Role]
  V[Verb Check]
  D[Decision]
  REQ --> RB --> R --> V --> D

Every request maps to subject + verb + resource. RBAC walks every (Cluster)RoleBinding for the subject and unions the rules.

Default: deny. Explicit allow required.

Commands 

kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:demo:app
kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o wide | grep alice
kubectl describe role pod-reader -n demo

docs.title: 3. Admission policy decision (Kyverno or Gatekeeper)
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  AR[AdmissionReview]
  POL[Policy]
  EV[Evaluate]
  RES[Result]
  ETC[etcd]
  AR --> POL --> EV --> RES --> ETC

API server sends AdmissionReview to webhook. Policy engine evaluates against rules. Allow/deny/mutate returned.

Failure policy decides what happens if the webhook is unreachable: Ignore (allow) or Fail (deny).

Commands 

kubectl get clusterpolicies
kubectl get policyreports -A
kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations

docs.title: 4. NetworkPolicy traffic decision
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  SRC[Source Pod]
  CNI[CNI]
  POL[Policy Match]
  DEC[Decision]
  DST[Dest Pod]
  SRC --> CNI --> POL --> DEC --> DST

CNI evaluates ingress/egress rules per pod label. Default = allow if no policy targets the pod, deny if any policy selects it (without matching the rule).

Common pattern: apply default-deny to namespace, then allowlist intentional flows.

Commands 

kubectl get netpol -A
kubectl describe netpol default-deny -n demo
kubectl exec -n demo client -- nc -zv backend 8080

docs.title: 5. Image signing flow (cosign keyless)
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  DEV[CI Build]
  OIDC[OIDC Token]
  FUL[Fulcio CA]
  CRT[Short Cert]
  SIG[Signed Image]
  DEV --> OIDC --> FUL --> CRT --> SIG

CI presents OIDC identity to Fulcio, gets a short-lived signing certificate, signs the image. Signature stored in registry next to image. Rekor logs the event for transparency.

Commands 

cosign sign registry/app:v1
cosign verify --certificate-identity-regexp=.*@company.com \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  registry/app:v1

docs.title: 6. Image admission verification
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  POD[Pod Spec]
  AD[Admission Webhook]
  COS[Cosign Verify]
  REG[Registry]
  DEC[Allow or Deny]
  POD --> AD --> COS --> REG
  COS --> DEC

Sigstore policy controller (or Kyverno verifyImages) intercepts pod creates, fetches signature from registry, verifies against allowed identity, allows only if signed by expected builder.

Commands 

kubectl get clusterimagepolicies
kubectl run unsigned --image=docker.io/random/unverified

docs.title: 7. Secret pull from external store (External Secrets Operator)
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  ES[ExternalSecret]
  SS[SecretStore]
  VLT[Vault]
  K8S[K8s Secret]
  POD[Pod]
  ES --> SS --> VLT --> K8S --> POD

ExternalSecret references a SecretStore which holds connection + auth to Vault/AWS SM/etc. ESO polls or watches, writes a native K8s Secret, pod consumes via volume.

Commands 

kubectl get externalsecrets -A
kubectl describe externalsecret app-creds -n demo
vault kv get secret/demo/app

docs.title: 8. SPIFFE attestation flow
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  POD[Workload]
  AGT[SPIRE Agent]
  ATT[Attest]
  SRV[SPIRE Server]
  SVID[X509 SVID]
  POD --> AGT --> ATT --> SRV --> SVID

Agent on each node attests workload (via k8s_psat selector: namespace, SA, image). Server issues SVID. Workload uses SVID for mTLS or to authenticate to Vault, DB, mesh.

Commands 

kubectl exec -n demo app -- /opt/spire/bin/spire-agent api fetch x509
kubectl logs -n spire spire-server-0

docs.title: 9. OIDC token exchange (workload to AWS via IRSA)
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  POD[Pod with SA]
  TOK[Projected Token]
  STS[AWS STS]
  ROLE[IAM Role]
  CRED[Temp Creds]
  POD --> TOK --> STS --> ROLE --> CRED

Pod has a projected SA token (audience = sts.amazonaws.com). SDK calls AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, AWS validates token signature against cluster OIDC issuer JWKS, returns 1h credentials.

Commands 

kubectl get sa app -n demo -o yaml
aws sts get-caller-identity
aws iam get-role --role-name eks-demo-app

docs.title: 10. Runtime detection alert pipeline
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  K[Kernel Events]
  EBP[eBPF Probe]
  RU[Rule Engine]
  SK[Sidekick]
  SIEM[SIEM Alert]
  K --> EBP --> RU --> SK --> SIEM

Falco/Tetragon hooks kernel via eBPF, evaluates rules in userspace (Falco) or in-kernel (Tetragon), forwards to falcosidekick which routes to SIEM, Slack, PagerDuty.

Commands 

kubectl logs -n falco -l app.kubernetes.io/name=falco --tail=100
tetra getevents -o compact
curl -s http://falcosidekick:2801/healthz

docs.title: How to use these diagrams
docs.text:
• During design reviews, draw the flow for the proposed change. If you can't, the design is incomplete.
  • During incidents, the flow tells you where to look. A 403 means stop at step 2 of flow 1.
  • When teaching, walk left-to-right for each flow before showing YAML.

docs.title: Combined trust chain (everything together)
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  SRC[Source]
  CI[CI Build]
  REG[Registry]
  AD[Admission]
  POD[Pod]
  MESH[Mesh]
  SRC --> CI --> REG --> AD --> POD --> MESH

End-to-end: code goes to CI, CI builds and signs image, registry stores image plus signature plus attestations, admission verifies signature and policy at deploy, pod runs with workload identity and mTLS via mesh.

docs.title: Failure mapping
docs.text: Symptom Likely flow Where to look 401 from kubectl Flow 1 step 2 IdP, kubeconfig, cert expiry 403 from kubectl Flow 2 RBAC bindings for subject Pod denied at create Flow 3 or 6 webhook logs, policy reports Pod cannot reach service Flow 4 netpol describe, CNI logs Image rejected Flow 6 cosign verify locally Secret missing Flow 7 ExternalSecret status, store auth Cannot assume role Flow 9 STS errors, OIDC provider thumbprint No alerts firing Flow 10 falco pod healthy, sidekick reachable

docs.title: Suggested practice
docs.text:
Pick one flow per week. Draw it from memory on a whiteboard. Then run the commands to confirm each step is healthy in your cluster. After ten weeks, you can debug any security incident by mentally walking the flow.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
07 · Terraform & infrastructure-as-code

Twelve concepts that turn a cloud console into a git repo you can trust.

Goal. You stop clicking in the AWS console. You write HCL, run plan, read the diff like a senior reviewer, and ship infrastructure that a stranger can re-create in a different account from a clean checkout. Every concept below is a mechanical skill. Learn it, practise it on the labs in the numbered subfolders, and move on.

docs.title: Declarative vs imperative
docs.text: Desired state is the entire point. Imperative scripts rot; declarative converges.

docs.title: Providers & resources
docs.text: One mental model — provider is a plugin, resource is a noun, data is a lookup.

docs.title: State
docs.text: The source of truth that maps HCL to real-world IDs. Remote backend, locking, surgery.

docs.title: Variables, outputs, locals
docs.text: Inputs, returns, private intermediates. Use each for exactly one job.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text: Functions for infra. Input/output contract. Versioned. Registry-published.

docs.title: Workspaces vs separate state
docs.text: Why workspaces are almost always the wrong answer for dev/staging/prod.

docs.title: Plan discipline
docs.text: Reading a diff at 03:00. Protecting prod from the one-character typo.

docs.title: Drift detection
docs.text: What happens when a human edits the cloud. How Terraform notices and reconciles.

docs.title: Data sources
docs.text: Read, never manage. The cleanest way to cross module and state boundaries.

docs.title: CI/CD for Terraform
docs.text: Atlantis, Terragrunt, environment isolation, OIDC — no more local apply.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: tflint, checkov, terratest. Security-as-code blocks regressions at the PR.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text: sensitive = true is not a secret store. KMS is. State file is plaintext — protect it.

docs.title: 1. Declarative vs imperative
docs.text:
🧭 Reason

Why this exists. At 02:47 on a Friday night, a junior engineer at an ad-tech startup ran a bash script that issued 120 aws ec2 run-instances calls. Halfway through, his laptop lost Wi-Fi. The script had no idempotency — no way to know which instances already existed — so on retry it created 60 duplicates. By 03:30 the on-call had to hand-terminate 180 instances across three regions. The root cause wasn't bash — it was imperative thinking. You tell the machine how. Terraform flips the model. You declare what (the desired state), and Terraform figures out the how — including idempotency, ordering, and retry. Runs are safe to re-execute because the end state is the contract.

🧠 Thinking

Mental model. Imperative gives you a recipe; declarative gives you a photograph.

flowchart LR
  subgraph imperative[Imperative]
    A1[Script step 1] --> A2[Script step 2]
    A2 --> A3[Script step 3]
    A3 --> A4[Hope nothing failed]
  end
  subgraph declarative[Declarative]
    B1["Desired state.tf files"]
    B2["(Current statetfstate)"]
    B3[Real cloud]
    B1 -->|diff| P[Plan engine]
    B2 -->|diff| P
    B3 -->|refresh| B2
    P -->|converges| B3
  end
  • Imperative: every rerun is a new history. Partial failures leave orphans.
  • Declarative: every run converges toward the same end state. Reruns are safe.
  • Terraform is the diff engine. You describe the photograph; it computes the brush strokes.
  • The whole plan/apply loop only makes sense once you accept this reframe.
  • Don't write HCL like a bash script. If you catch yourself reaching for null_resource with local-exec, stop — you've slipped into imperative.

⚡ Execution

Run it yourself.

# Imperative — feels familiar, breaks on retry
for i in 1 2 3; do
  aws s3api create-bucket --bucket "imperative-demo-$i" --region us-east-1
done
# Second run: BucketAlreadyOwnedByYou errors for all three.

# Declarative — same intent, safe to rerun
mkdir -p /tmp/tf-demo && cd /tmp/tf-demo
cat > main.tf <<'HCL'
terraform {
  required_providers {
    random = { source = "hashicorp/random", version = "~> 3.6" }
  }
}
resource "random_pet" "demo" { count = 3 }
output "pets" { value = random_pet.demo[*].id }
HCL

terraform init
terraform apply -auto-approve
terraform apply -auto-approve    # second run — no changes

🔮 Simulation — what you'll see

$ terraform apply -auto-approve
# random_pet.demo[0]: Creating...
# random_pet.demo[1]: Creating...
# random_pet.demo[2]: Creating...
# Apply complete! Resources: 3 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.

$ terraform apply -auto-approve
# No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.
# Apply complete! Resources: 0 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.

✅ Output — state change

→ →

🌍 Real-world use case

At HashiCorp, the company that invented Terraform, the internal platform team runs the same HCL module to provision 40+ customer-facing demo environments every morning. When a demo VM is nuked mid-workshop, a single terraform apply rebuilds only the missing piece — leaving the rest untouched. Before Terraform, the same team kept a 2,000-line bash script that was rewritten every quarter because "it drifted." The declarative rewrite shrank the codebase 6× and cut demo-provisioning incidents to zero.

docs.title: Before
docs.text: imperative bash retries = duplicates

docs.title: During
docs.text: plan engine reconciles intent vs state

docs.title: After
docs.text: idempotent applies rerun = zero changes

docs.title: 2. Providers & resources
docs.text:
🧭 Reason

Why this exists. A platform engineer onboarding at a fintech in Singapore opened the Terraform repo and saw aws_s3_bucket, google_storage_bucket, kubernetes_namespace, and datadog_monitor in the same file — and panicked. Four different clouds, same grammar. The trick: Terraform Core doesn't know AWS. It doesn't know GCP. It ships with zero cloud logic. The knowledge lives in providers — plugins downloaded by terraform init. Every resource in the universe, from an AWS bucket to a Stripe customer to a Cloudflare DNS record, is just a typed object managed by a provider. One mental model scales to every SaaS with a registry entry. The engineer's panic turns into a superpower by lunchtime on day one.

🧠 Thinking

Mental model. Core is the orchestrator. Providers are the translators. Resources are the nouns.

flowchart TB
  subgraph core[Terraform Core]
    PL[plan engine]
    ST[(state)]
  end
  subgraph providers[Providers registry.terraform.io]
    AWS[hashicorp/aws]
    GCP[hashicorp/google]
    K8S[hashicorp/kubernetes]
    DD[DataDog/datadog]
  end
  AWS --> EC2[aws_instance]
  AWS --> S3[aws_s3_bucket]
  GCP --> GCE[google_compute_instance]
  K8S --> NS[kubernetes_namespace]
  DD --> MON[datadog_monitor]
  PL <--> providers
  ST <--> providers
  • Provider = a versioned binary that speaks one cloud/SaaS API. hashicorp/aws v5.70.0 is a pinned contract.
  • Resource = a managed, typed object. Terraform will create, update, or destroy it.
  • Data source = the same typed object, read-only. Lookup, don't manage.
  • Every resource has a schema. terraform providers schema -json dumps every attribute and type.
  • Version providers the same way you version npm dependencies — pessimistic constraints (~> 5.70) with a lockfile (.terraform.lock.hcl) committed to git.

⚡ Execution

Run it yourself.

mkdir -p /tmp/tf-providers && cd /tmp/tf-providers
cat > providers.tf <<'HCL'
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.6"
  required_providers {
    aws        = { source = "hashicorp/aws",        version = "~> 5.70" }
    kubernetes = { source = "hashicorp/kubernetes", version = "~> 2.33" }
    random     = { source = "hashicorp/random",     version = "~> 3.6"  }
  }
}

provider "random" {}                 # no config needed
provider "aws"        { region = "us-east-1" }
provider "kubernetes" { config_path = "~/.kube/config" }

resource "random_id" "suffix" { byte_length = 4 }
HCL

terraform init                         # downloads the three providers
cat .terraform.lock.hcl | head -20     # the lockfile — commit this
terraform providers                    # tree of providers in use

🔮 Simulation — what you'll see

$ terraform init
# Initializing the backend...
# Initializing provider plugins...
# - Finding hashicorp/aws versions matching "~> 5.70"...
# - Installing hashicorp/aws v5.72.1...

# - Installing hashicorp/random v3.6.3...

$ terraform providers
# Providers required by configuration:
# .
# ├── provider[registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws] ~> 5.70
# ├── provider[registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/kubernetes] ~> 2.33
# └── provider[registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/random] ~> 3.6

→ →

🌍 Real-world use case

At Twilio, one Terraform module provisions a new customer environment that spans AWS (VPC + RDS), Datadog (monitors + SLOs), PagerDuty (on-call schedule), and Cloudflare (TLS cert + WAF). Four providers, one apply. The provider abstraction means the platform team ships a single customer_environment module — and when Twilio switches its DNS vendor from Cloudflare to Route53, they swap a 30-line provider block, not a 3,000-line bash runbook.

docs.title: 3. State — the source of truth
docs.text:
🧭 Reason

The Manual State Edit Anti-Pattern

Never manually edit terraform.tfstate or run terraform state rm without a plan. State is Terraform's source of truth. A corrupt state causes plan to recreate every resource — including your production database. Always use terraform state mv, terraform import, or terraform refresh instead. Lock state with -lock=true and enable versioning on your state backend.

Why this exists. Terraform cannot look at a .tf file and know which real-world resources exist. The HCL says "an S3 bucket named app-logs" — but AWS might have ten buckets, none of which Terraform manages, plus the one it created yesterday with a generated suffix. The mapping from HCL address (aws_s3_bucket.logs) to real-world ID (arn:aws:s3:::app-logs-8f2c) lives in the state file. Without it, every plan would have to query the entire cloud, can't know ownership, and couldn't detect drift. At 03:00 a Cruise engineer deleted terraform.tfstate by accident; next plan showed "create 417 resources." The team learned two things the hard way: state is precious, and state belongs in a remote backend with locking — not on a laptop.

🧠 Thinking

Mental model. Three worlds, one mapping.

flowchart LR
  A[".tf filesdesired"] -->|plan| D{diff}
  B["(state filelast-known)"] -->|plan| D
  C["Real cloudactual"] -->|refresh| B
  D -->|apply| C
  subgraph backend[Remote backend]
    B
    L[Lock in DynamoDB]
  end
  U1[Engineer A] -->|acquire lock| L
  U2[Engineer B] -->|wait| L
  • The state file is a JSON map from aws_s3_bucket.logs → { id: "app-logs-8f2c", tags: {...} }.
  • terraform refresh asks the cloud for each resource's current attributes and updates the state.
  • Remote backends (S3 + DynamoDB for AWS, GCS for GCP, Terraform Cloud) give locking, versioning, and shared access.
  • Lock prevents two engineers from applying at the same time and corrupting state.
  • terraform state mv is state surgery — rename a resource's address in state without touching the cloud. Critical when you refactor HCL.

⚡ Execution

Run it yourself.

# Remote backend: S3 for state, DynamoDB for lock
cat > backend.tf <<'HCL'
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket         = "acme-tfstate-prod"
    key            = "platform/app/terraform.tfstate"
    region         = "us-east-1"
    dynamodb_table = "acme-tf-locks"
    encrypt        = true
  }
}
HCL

terraform init                                      # migrates state to S3
terraform state list                                # resources under management
terraform state show aws_s3_bucket.logs             # one resource, all attrs
terraform state pull > /tmp/state-backup.json       # always backup before surgery
terraform state mv aws_s3_bucket.logs aws_s3_bucket.audit_logs
# rename in state only — the bucket itself is untouched
terraform plan                                      # should show "No changes"
AWS GCP 
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "state" {
  bucket = "my-terraform-state"

  versioning {
    enabled = true
  }

  server_side_encryption_configuration {
    rule {
      apply_server_side_encryption_by_default {
        sse_algorithm = "aws:kms"
      }
    }
  }
}

resource "google_storage_bucket" "state" {
  name          = "my-terraform-state"
  location      = "US"
  force_destroy = false

  versioning {
    enabled = true
  }
}

🔮 Simulation — what you'll see

$ terraform state list
# aws_s3_bucket.logs
# aws_s3_bucket_versioning.logs
# aws_kms_key.state

$ terraform state mv aws_s3_bucket.logs aws_s3_bucket.audit_logs
# Move "aws_s3_bucket.logs" to "aws_s3_bucket.audit_logs"
# Successfully moved 1 object(s).

$ terraform plan
# No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.

✅ Output — state change

→ →

🌍 Real-world use case

At Cruise, the self-driving company, a single Terraform monorepo manages 300+ AWS accounts. Every account has its own S3 + DynamoDB backend, encrypted with a per-account KMS key. When engineers refactor a module — say splitting network into vpc + subnets — they write a terraform state mv migration script that runs in CI before the new HCL lands. The discipline is simple: state surgery must ship in the same PR as the code change, and every plan must show "No changes" immediately after the move. This is how Cruise renames resources across hundreds of environments without a single outage.

docs.title: 4. Variables, outputs, locals
docs.text:
🧭 Reason

Why this exists. New Terraform users learn one tool — variable — and then use it for everything. They pass constants as variables. They compute derived values with string interpolation and hold the result in another variable. Readers can't tell what's configurable and what's fixed. Reviewers can't tell what a module exposes and what's private. At Airbnb, a 2020 internal audit found that 60% of declared variables in their platform modules were never set externally — they were just glorified locals. Terraform has three different tools for three different jobs. Learn the distinction once and your HCL reads like a typed function: variable = input parameter, output = return value, local = private let binding.

🧠 Thinking

Mental model. A module is a function.

flowchart LR
  I1[var.region] --> M{Module body}
  I2[var.tags] --> M
  M --> L1[locals.name_prefix]
  L1 --> M
  M --> O1[output.bucket_arn]
  M --> O2[output.endpoint]
  style M fill:#0ea5e9,stroke:#0c4a6e,color:#fff
  • variable — typed input. Can be set via tfvars, CLI, env, or a module call.
  • output — typed return. Read by the root module or by a parent module's module.x.output.
  • local — private let. Computed from variables and other locals. Never visible outside the module.
  • If a value is never overridden externally, it is a local, not a variable.
  • Use sensitive = true on outputs and variables that carry secrets — Terraform masks them in plan output (not a true secret store — see concept 12).

⚡ Execution

Run it yourself.

# variables.tf — declared inputs
variable "env" {
  type        = string
  description = "Deployment environment (dev | staging | prod)"
  validation {
    condition     = contains(["dev", "staging", "prod"], var.env)
    error_message = "env must be dev, staging, or prod."
  }
}

variable "tags" {
  type    = map(string)
  default = {}
}

# locals.tf — private derived values
locals {
  name_prefix = "acme-${var.env}"
  default_tags = merge(
    { Env = var.env, ManagedBy = "terraform" },
    var.tags,
  )
}

# main.tf
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "logs" {
  bucket = "${local.name_prefix}-logs"
  tags   = local.default_tags
}

# outputs.tf — the module's public return
output "bucket_arn"  { value = aws_s3_bucket.logs.arn }
output "bucket_name" { value = aws_s3_bucket.logs.bucket }

terraform apply -var="env=prod" -var='tags={Team="platform"}'
terraform output -json | jq .

🔮 Simulation — what you'll see

$ terraform apply -var="env=staging"
# aws_s3_bucket.logs: Creating...
# aws_s3_bucket.logs: Creation complete after 2s
# Apply complete! Resources: 1 added
# Outputs:
# bucket_arn  = "arn:aws:s3:::acme-staging-logs"
# bucket_name = "acme-staging-logs"

$ terraform apply -var="env=invalid"
# Error: Invalid value for variable
# env must be dev, staging, or prod.

✅ Output — state change

→ →

🌍 Real-world use case

At Airbnb, the platform team enforces a linter rule: every variable block must have a description and a type, and the PR will be rejected if more than 3 modules set the same default to the same value — the signal that the value should be hoisted into a local in a shared module. In the 2020 rewrite, this discipline dropped their variables.tf surface area from ~450 variables to ~120 — each one a real decision the consumer had to make. Reviewers now understand a module in one file instead of three.

docs.title: 5. Modules — reusable contracts
docs.text:
🧭 Reason

Why this exists. Copy-pasting a VPC block across 40 services sounds cheap until you need to change the default enable_flow_logs to true. Now you edit 40 files, and three services have drift. At Gruntwork — the team that literally wrote the Terraform module book — modules replaced copy-paste with function calls: a versioned, documented block of HCL with a clear input/output contract. source = "git::https://github.com/acme/modules.git//vpc?ref=v2.3.1" means every consumer pins the version, the module author can release v2.4.0 safely, and consumers bump when ready. Registry, git tag, local path — the source format is a superpower and a footgun. Pin or perish.

🧠 Thinking

Mental model. Modules compose like functions — inputs in, outputs out, versions pinned.

flowchart LR
  subgraph root[Root module — environments/prod]
    VPC["module.vpcsource = ./modules/vpcversion = 2.3.1"]
    EKS["module.ekssource = registry/eksversion = 19.20.0"]
  end
  VPC -->|output.vpc_id| EKS
  VPC -->|output.subnets| EKS
  subgraph registry[Terraform Registry]
    REG["terraform-aws-modules/eks/awsv19.20.0"]
  end
  EKS -.downloads.-> REG
  • A module is just a folder with variables.tf, main.tf, outputs.tf. That's it.
  • Consumers use module "name" { source = "..." } — source can be local path, git URL, or a registry address.
  • Always pin versions. ref=v2.3.1 for git, version = "~> 19.20" for registry.
  • terraform-aws-modules/* on the registry is the de-facto standard library — vpc, eks, rds, alb.
  • Module versioning follows SemVer: major = breaking change to inputs/outputs, minor = new input with default, patch = bug fix.

📦 terraform-aws-app/ ┣ 📜 main.tf — primary resource definitions ┣ 📜 variables.tf — input variable declarations ┣ 📜 outputs.tf — exported values for other modules ┣ 📜 versions.tf — required_providers + terraform block ┣ 📂 modules/ ┃ ┣ 📂 networking/ — VPC, subnets, security groups ┃ ┗ 📂 compute/ — EKS, EC2, ASG ┣ 📂 environments/ ┃ ┣ 📂 dev/ — terraform.tfvars with dev values ┃ ┗ 📂 prod/ — terraform.tfvars with prod values ┗ 📜 .terraform.lock.hcl — provider version lock file (commit this!)

⚡ Execution

Run it yourself.

# environments/prod/main.tf — the root
module "vpc" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"
  version = "~> 5.13"

  name            = "acme-prod"
  cidr            = "10.0.0.0/16"
  azs             = ["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b", "us-east-1c"]
  private_subnets = ["10.0.1.0/24", "10.0.2.0/24", "10.0.3.0/24"]
  public_subnets  = ["10.0.101.0/24", "10.0.102.0/24", "10.0.103.0/24"]

  enable_nat_gateway = true
  single_nat_gateway = false
  tags = { Env = "prod" }
}

module "eks" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/eks/aws"
  version = "~> 20.24"

  cluster_name    = "acme-prod"
  cluster_version = "1.30"
  vpc_id          = module.vpc.vpc_id
  subnet_ids      = module.vpc.private_subnets
}

terraform init                   # downloads modules to .terraform/modules/
cat .terraform/modules/modules.json | jq '.Modules[] | {Key, Version}'
terraform plan

🔮 Simulation — what you'll see

$ terraform init
# Initializing modules...
# Downloading registry.terraform.io/terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws 5.13.0
# Downloading registry.terraform.io/terraform-aws-modules/eks/aws 20.24.0
# Installed 2 modules

$ terraform plan
# module.vpc.aws_vpc.this[0] will be created
# module.eks.aws_eks_cluster.this[0] will be created
# Plan: 47 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.

✅ Output — state change

→ →

🌍 Real-world use case

At Gruntwork, the team ships the open-source terraform-aws-modules library — downloaded ~300 million times a year from the Terraform Registry. Their rule: every module has a examples/ folder that gets CI-tested on every commit. A breaking change to inputs is a major version bump, documented in the changelog with a migration snippet. Consumers upgrade on their own schedule. This is how a two-engineer team maintains a module used by every Fortune 500 AWS shop — the contract is the versioned API, and the registry is the delivery mechanism.

docs.title: 6. Workspaces vs separate state files
docs.text:
🧭 Reason

Why this exists. New users discover terraform workspace new prod and think they've found the environment-isolation feature. They haven't. Workspaces share the same backend bucket, the same credentials, the same HCL. They only switch the state file name. So a typo in the root module blows up every environment, because every environment runs the same code. At Cruise, an early attempt to use workspaces for dev/staging/prod was abandoned after a terraform apply in dev — with a stale workspace setting — mutated prod. The cure is separate directories, separate backends, separate credentials. Workspaces are for ephemeral experiments (a feature branch, a PR preview), not for the permanent environment boundary.

🧠 Thinking

Mental model. Workspaces are cheap. Separate environments are safe.

flowchart TB
  subgraph wrong[❌ Workspaces for environments]
    W1[terraform workspace select prod]
    W1 --> BE["(single backendprod.tfstate + dev.tfstate)"]
    W1 --> CRED[one IAM role]
  end
  subgraph right[✅ Directory per environment]
    D1[environments/dev/] --> B1[(dev backend)]
    D2[environments/staging/] --> B2[(staging backend)]
    D3[environments/prod/] --> B3[(prod backend)]
    D1 --> C1[dev IAM role]
    D3 --> C3[prod IAM role]
  end
  • Workspaces switch state-file keys — nothing else. Same code, same providers, same credentials.
  • Typos in shared HCL break every workspace simultaneously. There is no blast-radius isolation.
  • Prod and dev should live in separate AWS accounts, with separate backends and separate credentials.
  • Use directory-per-environment: environments/{dev,staging,prod}/main.tf, each with its own backend block and its own terraform.tfvars.
  • Valid uses for workspaces: short-lived per-branch or per-PR preview environments in a non-prod account.

State isolation with workspaces:

  # Bad: single workspace for all environments
  terraform workspace new dev
- # All envs share one state file path
- # Production changes visible alongside dev

  # Good: separate state backends per environment
+ # environments/prod/backend.tf
+ terraform {
+   backend "s3" {
+     bucket = "tf-state-prod"
+     key    = "prod/terraform.tfstate"
+   }
+ }

⚡ Execution

Run it yourself.

# ============ Anti-pattern: workspaces ============
terraform workspace new dev
terraform apply               # writes to dev.tfstate in same bucket
terraform workspace select prod
terraform apply               # same HCL, different state — typo blows up both

# ============ Correct: directory per env ============
tree environments/
# environments/
# ├── dev/      main.tf  backend.tf  terraform.tfvars
# ├── staging/  main.tf  backend.tf  terraform.tfvars
# └── prod/     main.tf  backend.tf  terraform.tfvars

# each directory pins its own backend + account
cat environments/prod/backend.tf
# terraform { backend "s3" {
#   bucket = "acme-prod-tfstate"   # different bucket
#   key    = "platform.tfstate"
#   region = "us-east-1"
# }}

cd environments/prod && terraform init && terraform plan

🔮 Simulation — what you'll see

$ cd environments/prod && terraform init
# Initializing the backend...
# Successfully configured the backend "s3"!

$ aws sts get-caller-identity
# {
#   "Account": "111122223333",       # prod account
#   "Arn": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/tf-prod"
# }

$ cd ../dev && terraform init
# Account: "444455556666",           # dev account — different credentials

✅ Output — state change

→ →

🌍 Real-world use case

At Cruise, after the workspace incident, the platform team standardised on directory-per-environment plus per-account OIDC roles. Each directory has a .github/workflows/ that assumes a role scoped only to that account. A PR to environments/dev/* cannot assume the prod role — the GitHub Actions id-token subject claim doesn't match. The result: dev engineers iterate freely, prod changes require a second reviewer, and workspaces are reserved for ephemeral PR preview stacks that auto-destroy 48h after merge.

docs.title: 7. Plan discipline — reading the diff
docs.text:
🧭 Reason

Why this exists. terraform plan is the single most important output in this whole discipline. It is a diff. Not a prediction, not a suggestion — a contract between the HCL and the cloud. Reading it wrong is how prod dies. At 03:14 a Shopify engineer approved a PR whose plan contained # forces replacement on an RDS instance. She didn't scroll far enough. The apply destroyed the prod database. Recovery: 4h from backup, 2h of lost writes. The fix was cultural, not technical: every prod PR must post the full plan to the ticket, every # forces replacement must be acknowledged in a separate review comment, and -refresh-only is run before every apply to reveal hidden drift. The plan is your last off-ramp before something irreversible happens.

🧠 Thinking

Mental model. Five symbols you must read on sight.

flowchart LR
  subgraph symbols[Plan symbols]
    A[+ create] -->|safe| OK
    B[~ update in-place] -->|safe usually| OK
    C[-/+ destroy + create] -->|DANGER| DANGER
    D[- destroy] -->|DANGER| DANGER
    E[# forces replacement] -->|READ THIS| DANGER
  end
  OK[ship it] -.-> OK_[apply]
  DANGER[stop & review] -.-> HUMAN[two-reviewer rule]
  • + = create a new resource. Usually safe.
  • ~ = update in-place. Safe unless the attribute is immutable.
  • -/+ = destroy then create. Downtime. For an RDS, it means data loss.
  • # forces replacement next to an attribute tells you why it's -/+. Always scroll to find it.
  • Use terraform plan -out=tfplan and terraform apply tfplan — the only way to guarantee the thing you reviewed is the thing that applies.

⚡ Execution

Run it yourself.

# save + show + apply the same plan
terraform plan \
  -var-file="environments/prod/terraform.tfvars" \ # (1)!
  -out=tfplan \                                     # (2)!
  -detailed-exitcode \                              # (3)!
  -lock=true                                        # (4)!
1. -var-file — loads variable values. Stack multiple -var-file flags; last value wins for conflicts. 2. -out=tfplan — saves the plan to a binary file. Pass to terraform apply tfplan for a guaranteed-identical apply. 3. -detailed-exitcode — exits 2 if there are changes (useful in CI: if [ $? -eq 2 ]; then apply; fi). 4. -lock=true — acquires state lock before reading. Default true; set -lock=false ONLY for read-only inspection.

terraform show tfplan                           # human-readable
terraform show -json tfplan | jq '.resource_changes[] |
  {addr: .address, actions: .change.actions}'   # machine-parseable

# catch the killer symbol before apply
terraform show -json tfplan | jq -r '
  .resource_changes[]
  | select(.change.actions | contains(["delete","create"]))
  | "REPLACEMENT: " + .address'

# refresh-only plan to see drift without changing anything
terraform plan -refresh-only

🔮 Simulation — what you'll see

$ terraform plan -out=tfplan
# Terraform will perform the following actions:

#   # aws_db_instance.main must be replaced
# -/+ resource "aws_db_instance" "main" {
#       ~ instance_class = "db.t3.medium" -> "db.m5.large" # forces replacement
#     }

# Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.

$ terraform show -json tfplan | jq -r '.resource_changes[]
  | select(.change.actions | contains(["delete","create"]))
  | .address'
# aws_db_instance.main     <-- PR blocked until human acknowledges

✅ Output — state change

→ →

🌍 Real-world use case

At Shopify, after the RDS incident, every prod Terraform PR runs a CI step called plan-guard that parses the JSON plan for any aws_db_instance, aws_rds_cluster, or aws_elasticache_cluster with a delete+create action pair. If found, the PR status turns red and a label needs-dba-review is attached. Merge is blocked until a database SRE leaves an explicit /approve-replacement comment. The same pattern has since been copied by Stripe and Lyft. Plan discipline is the cheapest, highest-leverage Terraform policy any team can install.

docs.title: 8. Drift detection & reconciliation
docs.text:
🧭 Reason

Why this exists. No matter how strictly you police the console, someone, somewhere, will click. A junior debugging at 02:00 disables a security-group rule. A vendor's support engineer flips a flag to "help." Six months later, terraform apply on an unrelated change tries to reconcile — and reverts the manual fix, or worse, reinstates an attack surface. This is drift: the real cloud diverging from the state-file view. Terraform's answer is a periodic plan -refresh-only that surfaces drift without applying anything. At Netflix and Airbnb, this plan runs hourly in CI against every prod backend — and if drift appears, a ticket fires. You don't manage what you can't see.

🧠 Thinking

Mental model. Three things drift relative to each other. Keep them aligned.

flowchart LR
  HCL["HCLdesired"] -. review .-> STATE
  STATE["(statelast-known)"] -. refresh .-> CLOUD
  CLOUD["Cloudactual"] -. drift .-> STATE
  STATE -. plan .-> DIFF{diff}
  HCL -. plan .-> DIFF
  DIFF -->|apply| CLOUD
  DIFF -->|import| STATE
  • terraform plan compares HCL vs state. It does not automatically refresh the cloud.
  • terraform plan -refresh-only shows state vs cloud — the drift detector.
  • terraform apply -refresh-only accepts the drift (updates state to match cloud) without touching the cloud.
  • terraform import pulls an unmanaged real-world resource into state.
  • Scheduled drift detection in CI catches the console click before the next real change fights it.

⚡ Execution

Run it yourself.

# Simulate a human edit in the AWS console: change a tag manually
aws s3api put-bucket-tagging \
  --bucket app-logs \
  --tagging 'TagSet=[{Key=Owner,Value=manual-edit}]'

# Detect the drift without changing anything
terraform plan -refresh-only
# Output: ~ aws_s3_bucket.logs  Owner: "platform" -> "manual-edit"

# Three responses to drift:
# 1) HCL is right, cloud is wrong -> normal apply reverts the edit
terraform apply

# 2) Cloud is right, HCL was outdated -> update HCL in git, then apply

# 3) You accept reality -> accept drift into state
terraform apply -refresh-only -auto-approve

🔮 Simulation — what you'll see

$ terraform plan -refresh-only
# Note: Objects have changed outside of Terraform
# ~ aws_s3_bucket.logs has been changed
#     tags = {
#       "Owner" = "platform" -> "manual-edit"
#     }

$ terraform apply
# ~ update in-place
# tags.Owner: "manual-edit" -> "platform"
# Apply complete! Resources: 0 added, 1 changed, 0 destroyed.

✅ Output — state change

→ →

🌍 Real-world use case

At Airbnb, every prod Terraform backend is scanned hourly by an internal tool called tfdrift — a thin wrapper that runs terraform plan -refresh-only in each environment directory and posts diffs to a Slack channel. When the e-commerce team migrated their booking service in 2022, drift detection caught 1,200+ console-made tweaks that hadn't been codified. The team resolved 90% by import or HCL updates over three weeks. The remaining 10% were tagged accept and reconciled via -refresh-only apply. Drift detection is the mechanism that turns Terraform from a deployment tool into a source of truth.

docs.title: Before
docs.text: silent drift console edit invisible

docs.title: During
docs.text: refresh-only plan delta visible

docs.title: 9. Data sources — lookup, not manage
docs.text:
🧭 Reason

Why this exists. Not everything in your cloud should be managed by this Terraform root. The account's primary VPC is owned by the networking team's repo. The TLS cert for *.acme.com was bought via ClickOps in 2019 and isn't going anywhere. An AMI's latest ID changes weekly — you want to reference it, not re-declare it. For all of these, the right tool is a data source: a typed, read-only query against the provider. It pulls the current attributes at plan time and exposes them as if they were a resource. It never creates, never mutates, and costs nothing to use. data "aws_ami" "ubuntu" is how a consumer module gets the right AMI without writing "which AMI?" into a hardcoded variable.

🧠 Thinking

Mental model. Two roles: one writer, many readers.

flowchart LR
  subgraph network[Networking repo]
    R[resource aws_vpc.main]
  end
  subgraph app1[App A repo]
    D1[data aws_vpc by_tag]
    D1 --> U1[module.service_a]
  end
  subgraph app2[App B repo]
    D2[data aws_vpc by_tag]
    D2 --> U2[module.service_b]
  end
  R -.tag.-> D1
  R -.tag.-> D2
  • data "aws_vpc" "primary" { tags = { Name = "acme-prod" } } resolves at plan time.
  • Ownership: one module creates the VPC (resource); every other module reads it (data).
  • Data sources are evaluated every plan, so they reflect the current cloud — no staleness risk.
  • For cross-repo wiring, pair a data source with a well-known tag (Name = "acme-prod") — no shared state required.
  • terraform_remote_state is the heavier alternative — reads another module's state directly. Use only when tags aren't enough.

⚡ Execution

Run it yourself.

# main.tf — read the primary VPC from the networking team
data "aws_vpc" "primary" {
  tags = { Name = "acme-prod" }
}

data "aws_subnets" "private" {
  filter {
    name   = "vpc-id"
    values = [data.aws_vpc.primary.id]
  }
  tags = { Tier = "private" }
}

# latest Ubuntu 22.04 AMI — resolved every plan
data "aws_ami" "ubuntu" {
  most_recent = true
  owners      = ["099720109477"]
  filter {
    name   = "name"
    values = ["ubuntu/images/hvm-ssd/ubuntu-jammy-22.04-amd64-server-*"]
  }
}

resource "aws_instance" "worker" {
  ami           = data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id
  subnet_id     = data.aws_subnets.private.ids[0]
  instance_type = "t3.small"
}

output "used_ami_id" { value = data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id }

terraform plan
terraform console <<< 'data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id'

🔮 Simulation — what you'll see

$ terraform plan
# data.aws_vpc.primary: Reading...
# data.aws_vpc.primary: Read complete after 1s [id=vpc-0a1b2c...]
# data.aws_ami.ubuntu:  Read complete after 2s [id=ami-0c55b159c...]
# aws_instance.worker will be created
#   ami       = "ami-0c55b159c..."
#   subnet_id = "subnet-0a1..."

$ terraform console
> data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id
# "ami-0c55b159c..."

✅ Output — state change

→ →

🌍 Real-world use case

At Twilio, each product team owns its own Terraform repo, but they all share a single VPC owned by the networking team. The contract is a tag: Name = "twilio-prod". Every product repo uses data "aws_vpc" "primary" plus data "aws_subnets" to discover the network layout — no shared state, no cross-repo writes, no tight coupling. When networking re-architected into dual-region in 2023, they added a second VPC with Name = "twilio-prod-west". Product teams opted in by flipping a single variable in their data-source filter. Zero breakage, 40 teams migrated in a week.

docs.title: 10. CI/CD for Terraform
docs.text:
🧭 Reason

Why this exists. If a human can run terraform apply from their laptop, your audit trail is "I think so?". Credentials end up in shell history. Two engineers race to apply and corrupt state. Someone forgets to run fmt and the diff is half indentation. The fix is CI/CD: the PR is the only way in, and the CI runs plan, posts it as a comment, and only after approval does a merge trigger apply — with federated credentials (OIDC), no long-lived keys. The tool ecosystem splits into two camps: Atlantis (a dedicated PR-commenting bot) and Terragrunt + vanilla GitHub Actions (a thin DRY wrapper + generic runners). Pick one early. Both end the laptop-apply era.

🧠 Thinking

Mental model. Four gates between a PR and production.

flowchart LR
  PR[Pull request] --> G1[fmt + validate + tflint]
  G1 --> G2["planposted as PR comment"]
  G2 --> G3["checkov / tfsecsecurity gate"]
  G3 --> R[Human review + approve]
  R --> G4["apply on mergevia OIDC role"]
  G4 --> STATE[(remote state)]
  style G3 fill:#f59e0b,stroke:#78350f,color:#000
  style R fill:#10b981,stroke:#065f46,color:#fff
  • Every PR must trigger fmt -check, validate, tflint, plan, and checkov automatically.
  • The plan output is posted back as a PR comment — reviewers see exactly what will change.
  • apply only runs on merge to the environment branch, and only with a short-lived OIDC token.
  • Terragrunt handles the DRY problem: 40 environments × same backend config = one terragrunt.hcl generator.
  • Atlantis runs as a server. Terragrunt + GitHub Actions runs as pure CI. Neither is better — pick on team preference.

⚡ Execution

Run it yourself.

# .github/workflows/terraform.yml
name: terraform
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ['environments/prod/**']
permissions:
  id-token: write      # OIDC
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write
jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults: { run: { working-directory: environments/prod } }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/tf-prod-plan
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
        with: { terraform_version: 1.9.8 }
      - run: terraform fmt -check -recursive
      - run: terraform init
      - run: terraform validate
      - run: terraform plan -out=tfplan -no-color | tee plan.txt
      - uses: bridgecrewio/checkov-action@master
        with: { directory: environments/prod }
      - uses: marocchino/sticky-pull-request-comment@v2
        with: { path: environments/prod/plan.txt }

🔮 Simulation — what you'll see

# On PR:
# ✅ fmt          passed
# ✅ validate     passed
# ✅ plan         posted as comment (47 to add, 0 change, 0 destroy)
# ✅ checkov      no HIGH findings
# ⏸  apply        waits for merge

# On merge:
# ✅ OIDC token for role/tf-prod-apply acquired
# ✅ terraform apply tfplan
# ✅ Apply complete! Resources: 47 added

✅ Output — state change

→ →

🌍 Real-world use case

At HashiCorp, internal teams moved to Terraform Cloud (their managed plan/apply service) in 2019. Before the move: ~30 incidents/year tied to bad local applies. After: zero. The same pattern — PR, plan as comment, human approval, short-lived creds — works identically with Atlantis (open-source) or Terragrunt + GitHub Actions. Gruntwork's Terragrunt approach is the reference for DRY multi-account setups; their public terraform-infrastructure-live template is the single most copied blueprint in regulated industries.
