Architect Q&A — 60+ Senior Distributed Systems Questions
docs.text: Deep questions for Staff/Principal-level interviews. Each entry: question, sharp answer, follow-ups.

docs.title: Q1. What does true active-active multi-region actually mean?
docs.text: Both regions serve writes simultaneously without one being a hot standby. Requires either (a) conflict-free data structures, (b) per-region sharding of write authority, or © consensus across regions paying latency cost.

docs.title: Q2. Most common active-active failure mode?
docs.text: Split-brain on writes after a partition. Both regions accept conflicting writes; reconciliation requires either CRDTs, last-writer-wins (data loss), or human triage.

docs.title: Q3. How do you partition write authority by region?
docs.text: Hash users to "home regions". User U writes only to home; reads can be local with async replication. Failover changes home-region assignment in a control plane.

docs.title: Q4. RTO vs RPO trade-off in active-active?
docs.text: Active-active gets near-zero RTO but RPO depends on replication lag (sync vs async). Sync replication = strong consistency + latency penalty. Async = lower latency + RPO > 0.

docs.title: Q5. When should you NOT go multi-region?
docs.text: If per-user latency is fine from one region, regulatory data residency is single-region, and DR drills can hit < 1 hour RTO. Multi-region triples cost and quadruples complexity.

docs.title: Q6. How do you test multi-region?
docs.text: Quarterly region-out game day: black-hole one region for 30 min, validate failover, data integrity, alerting. If you don't drill, you don't have it.

docs.title: Q7. Why elect a leader at all?
docs.text: To serialize a critical operation (sequence numbers, schema migrations, scheduler). Avoids coordination on every write while keeping a single source of truth.

docs.title: Q8. Three correct ways to elect a leader?
docs.text: (1) Raft/Paxos within a cluster. (2) ZooKeeper/etcd ephemeral nodes. (3) Database row with lease + TTL. Never DIY with timeouts and "first to write wins".

docs.title: Q9. What's the lease lifetime trade-off?
docs.text: Short lease = fast failover, more renewal traffic, more false leader changes. Long lease = slower failover, longer outage if leader dies. Typical: 5-30 sec.

docs.title: Q10. How do you prevent two-leader scenarios (fencing)?
docs.text: Monotonic fencing token issued by the lock service; downstream systems reject operations carrying tokens older than the highest seen. Stops zombie leaders.

docs.title: Q11. What if leader sees split-brain and continues serving?
docs.text: Leader must self-fence: lose lease renewal → stop serving immediately. Heartbeats to lock service are non-negotiable; assume any pause means you lost lease.

docs.title: Q12. Leader election in geo-distributed systems?
docs.text: Cross-region consensus is slow (200ms RTT). Better: region-local leaders with global coordination only for cross-region invariants.

docs.title: Q13. Why is idempotency mandatory?
docs.text: At-least-once delivery is the default in every queue (Kafka, SQS, RabbitMQ). Network blips → redeliveries. Without idempotency, every retry corrupts state.

docs.title: Q14. Three idempotency strategies?
docs.text: (1) Idempotency key + dedup table. (2) Conditional writes (if-not-exists, version match). (3) Natural idempotency (set state to X, not increment by 1).

docs.title: Q15. How long do you keep idempotency keys?
docs.text: Longer than max retry window + clock skew. Typical: 24h-7d. Use TTL store (DynamoDB TTL, Redis EXPIRE) so you don't drown in dedup data.

docs.title: Q16. Exactly-once semantics — real or myth?
docs.text: Real, but only end-to-end with effort. Kafka EOS = transactional producer + idempotent consumer + transactional sink. Cross-system EOS = saga or 2PC. Not free, not magic.

docs.title: Q17. Side-effects (email, payment) idempotency?
docs.text: Wrap the side-effect with an idempotency table commit in the same transaction as the side-effect's local effect. For payments, use Stripe's Idempotency-Key header.

docs.title: Q18. Ordering guarantees in idempotent processing?
docs.text: Per-key ordering via partitioning (Kafka partition by user ID). Global ordering = single partition = no scale. Most domains tolerate per-key ordering only.

docs.title: Section D — CRDT vs Strong Consistency
Q19. When CRDT?
docs.text: Multi-master writes that must converge without coordination: shopping cart, collaborative editor, presence, counters across regions.

docs.title: Q20. CRDT trade-off?
docs.text: You pay in metadata size and "weird" semantics: deleted-then-re-added items resurrect in some CRDTs; counters can over-count under specific failure orderings.

docs.title: Q21. Strong consistency cost?
docs.text: Latency = quorum RTT + leader election overhead. Throughput capped by leader. Required for: financial ledgers, unique constraints, anything with invariants.

docs.title: Q22. Hybrid: which parts strong, which eventual?
docs.text: Strong: identity, money, inventory deduction. Eventual: profile, preferences, recommendations, social graph. Map data to consistency requirement, not vice versa.

docs.title: Q23. CRDT for counters — pitfalls?
docs.text: G-Counter only goes up; PN-Counter for inc/dec but harder to reason about under partition. For exact financial counts, do not use CRDT — use a ledger with replay.

docs.title: Q24. Causal consistency — middle ground?
docs.text: Vector clocks track happens-before. Cheaper than strong, stronger than eventual. Good for collaborative apps where causality matters but global order doesn't.

docs.title: Q25. Estimate storage for 100M users, 1KB profile, 5 years growth at 20%/yr?
docs.text: Year 5 users = 100M * 1.2^5 = ~249M. 249M * 1KB = 249 GB. Add indexes ~3x = ~750 GB. Add replicas (3x) = ~2.25 TB. Add backups (7d daily) = ~16 TB cold storage.

docs.title: Q26. Estimate RPS for 50M DAU, avg 20 actions/day, 80% in 8h peak?
docs.text: 50M * 20 = 1B actions/day. Peak = 0.8 * 1B / (8 * 3600) = ~28k RPS. Burst factor 3x = ~84k peak RPS. Provision for burst.

docs.title: Q27. Bandwidth for 1M concurrent video viewers @ 5 Mbps?
docs.text: 1M * 5 Mbps = 5 Tbps. Way above any single CDN POP. Distribute via CDN with edge caching; origin sees aggregated unique requests, not per-viewer.

docs.title: Q28. Database connection pool sizing?
docs.text: Little's Law: pool_size = throughput * latency. 1k QPS * 50ms = 50 connections. Add headroom 2x = 100. Watch for connection limits on DB (Postgres ~500 default).

docs.title: Q29. Cache size for 95% hit rate on Zipfian access?
docs.text: Cache top ~5% of keys handles ~80% of traffic (80/20). For 95% hit, cache top 20%. For 1B keys with 1KB values, that's 200 GB — probably need tiered cache.

docs.title: Q30. Cost back-of-envelope?
docs.text: Compute: $0.05/vCPU-hr * 24 * 30 = $36/vCPU/month. Storage: S3 $0.023/GB-month, EBS $0.10/GB-month. Egress: $0.09/GB cross-region. Cross-region egress dominates surprise bills.

docs.title: Q31. What is blast radius?
docs.text: Maximum scope of impact when a single component fails. A bad deploy taking down one shard ≠ taking down the whole region. Design caps the blast.

docs.title: Q32. How to reduce blast radius for a multi-tenant service?
docs.text: Cell-based architecture: tenants sharded into cells of N tenants each. Cell failure impacts N, not all. Cells are independent: own DB, own deploys, own queues.

docs.title: Q33. Deploy blast radius?
docs.text: Deploy to one cell first, soak, then waves of cells. A bad deploy hits one cell worth of customers, not 100%. Combine with automatic rollback on SLO burn.

docs.title: Q34. Config change blast radius?
docs.text: Treat config as code: gradual rollout, kill switch, observability per change. Most outages come from config, not code — apply same rigor.

docs.title: Q35. Database blast radius?
docs.text: Per-tenant or per-shard databases mean a corruption/lock event is isolated. Shared DB = single fault domain across tenants.

docs.title: Q36. Network blast radius?
docs.text: Per-cell VPC subnets or accounts. A misrouted security group can't cross cells. AWS multi-account with SCPs is the strongest network isolation.

docs.title: Q37. Define fault domain.
docs.text: A set of resources that fail together. Rack, AZ, region, account, control plane. Spread workloads across fault domains so no single one breaks > X% of capacity.

docs.title: Q38. Common fault-domain mistakes?
docs.text: (1) All replicas in one AZ. (2) Active-passive across regions but failover untested. (3) Shared control plane (one IAM, one DNS, one CI). (4) Same provider for all DR.

docs.title: Q39. Control-plane vs data-plane fault domains?
docs.text: Data plane should keep serving even if control plane is down. Cache config, embed defaults, fail-static. Most cloud providers do this; your services should too.

docs.title: Q40. How many fault domains do I need?
docs.text: Capacity_per_domain * (N - failed) >= peak_demand. For N=3 and 1 failure: each domain sized for peak/2. For N=4: each for peak/3. Trade redundancy cost for resilience.

docs.title: Q41. Cross-fault-domain dependencies?
docs.text: Audit them. A "regional" service that calls a global control plane has a hidden single point of failure. Map all dependencies as part of design review.

docs.title: Q42. What is a deploy lane?
docs.text: A pipeline that deploys to a subset of fleet (cell, region, persona) before others. Lanes serialize risk; a regression in lane 1 never reaches lane 5.

docs.title: Q43. Canary vs blue-green vs rolling vs cell-based?
docs.text: Canary: small % of traffic. Blue-green: instant cutover, easy rollback, 2x cost. Rolling: in-place per instance, no extra cost, slower rollback. Cell: per-tenant group; combines isolation + gradual exposure.

docs.title: Q44. Auto-rollback signals?
docs.text: SLO burn rate (fast burn = 14.4x in 1h triggers rollback), error rate spike, latency p99 above threshold, downstream alert. Rollback should be one-button.

docs.title: Q45. Database migrations in lanes?
docs.text: Schema changes are forward-compatible (expand-then-contract pattern). New code works against old schema; deploy code → migrate → deploy code that uses new schema.

docs.title: Q46. Feature flags vs deploy lanes?
docs.text: Deploy lanes deploy code; flags toggle behavior. Combined: deploy dark, then ramp flag per cell. Decouples deploy risk from feature risk.

docs.title: Section I — Change Management at Scale
Q47. Why most outages are change-induced?
docs.text: ~70% of incidents trace to a recent deploy or config change. Stable systems break when humans change them. Discipline change cadence and you cut MTBF dramatically.

docs.title: Q48. Change advisory boards — useful?
docs.text: For high-risk changes (network, IAM, data migrations) yes. For app deploys, no — slows down iteration. Tier changes by risk; board only on high-tier.

docs.title: Q49. Freeze windows?
docs.text: Risk windows (Black Friday, end of quarter): full code freeze except security. Reduces compounding incidents during high-revenue periods.

docs.title: Q50. Reverting vs rolling forward?
docs.text: Default to revert. Roll forward only if revert is impossible (data migration). Time-to-recover beats elegant fix; investigate after revert restores service.

docs.title: Q51. Change failure rate (CFR) — DORA metric?
docs.text: % of deploys causing prod incident. Elite teams < 5%, low performers 60%+. Track per service; high CFR signals missing tests or coupled architecture.

docs.title: Q52. What makes on-call sustainable?
docs.text: < 2 actionable pages per shift, runbooks for top 10 alerts, clear escalation, post-incident actions tracked, rotation respects timezones.

docs.title: Q53. Page volume KPI?
docs.text: Median pages per on-call shift. > 5 = burnout territory. > 10 = quit risk. Reduce by deleting noisy alerts and fixing root causes of repeat pages.

docs.title: Q54. Alert fatigue — root cause?
docs.text: Alerts on causes (CPU > 80%) instead of symptoms (user-facing latency). Alert on SLO burn, not metrics. Page only when human action required.

docs.title: Q55. Follow-the-sun vs single-region on-call?
docs.text: Follow-the-sun: lower individual burden, requires runbook discipline + handoff process. Single region: easier coordination, brutal nights. Pick by team size.

docs.title: Q56. Runbook quality test?
docs.text: A new hire can resolve a known incident in < 15 min using only the runbook. If not, rewrite. Stale runbooks are worse than none — false confidence.

docs.title: Q57. Top 5 platform KPIs?
docs.text: (1) Lead time for change. (2) Deploy frequency. (3) MTTR. (4) Change failure rate. (5) Developer NPS / time-to-first-deploy for new service.

docs.title: Q58. Self-service maturity?
docs.text: Level 1: tickets. Level 2: portal with approvals. Level 3: API/CLI self-service. Level 4: declarative GitOps. Aim for 4; not all paths get there.

docs.title: Q59. Golden path vs golden cage?
docs.text: Golden path: opinionated easy way that handles 80% of needs; teams can deviate. Cage: forced compliance, no escape hatch — kills innovation.

docs.title: Q60. How to measure platform value?
docs.text: Engineer-hours saved per month vs platform-team cost. Adoption rate (services on platform / total). Time-to-recover platform incidents (you're now critical infra).

docs.title: Q61. Platform funding model?
docs.text: Centrally funded — never charge back per call early. Once mature, optional showback helps teams understand cost. Mandatory chargeback creates perverse incentives.

docs.title: Q62. When platform team becomes a bottleneck?
docs.text: Approval queues > 1 day, ticket SLA missed, teams building shadow platforms. Fix by automating approvals, decentralizing ownership, expanding self-service.

docs.title: Q63. Cap a runaway query in production?
docs.text: Query timeout at app + DB. pg_stat_activity + pg_cancel_backend(pid). Long term: RLS or per-tenant connection limits, query plan caching, kill long-runners by SLO.

docs.title: Q64. Hot partition in Kafka?
docs.text: Repartition by composite key (userid + bucket). Add more partitions (only future data benefits). Producer-side load shedding for the hot key. Identify upstream cause.

docs.title: Q65. Designing for 10x growth — what bends first?
docs.text: Database writes (single leader). Hot keys in cache. Egress bandwidth. On-call. Plan: shard early, async-ify, add CDN, hire ahead of load.

docs.title: Q66. Migrate from monolith — strangler fig?
docs.text: Front the monolith with a router. New endpoints land in new service. Migrate one endpoint at a time, dual-write during cutover, retire old code. Years not weeks; stay disciplined.

docs.title: Q67. Most common architecture mistake at $500M ARR companies?
docs.text: Distributed monolith — services share a DB, deploy in lockstep, fail together. All cost of microservices, none of the benefit. Decouple data first.

docs.title: Q68. Backpressure end-to-end?
docs.text: Every async hop has bounded queue + reject policy. Drop oldest, drop newest, or shed by priority. Without backpressure, slow consumer = OOM somewhere upstream.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: A reference of common DevOps, Kubernetes, container, and platform terms used throughout this site. Hover any abbreviation in the docs to see its definition (when supported by the browser).

docs.title: Cloud Mastery — 40+ Q&A on AWS, GCP, and Azure Patterns
Cloud Mastery — 40+ Q&A on AWS, GCP, and Azure Patterns
docs.text: Architectural Q&A spanning the three major clouds. Cross-cloud parity included where relevant.

docs.title: Section A — VPC and Network Design
Q1. Three-tier VPC layout — what subnets do you create?
docs.text: Public (ALB, NAT gateway, bastion), private app (compute, no internet egress except via NAT), private data (DB, no NAT). One subnet per AZ per tier = 9 subnets minimum across 3 AZs.

docs.title: Q2. Why /20 over /24 for VPC subnets?
docs.text: A /24 = 256 addresses, ~250 usable (cloud reserves 5). EKS pods can burn through that fast (one IP per pod with VPC CNI). /20 = 4096 addresses; future-proofs for pod density.

docs.title: Q3. NAT gateway vs NAT instance?
docs.text: NAT gateway: managed, scales to 45 Gbps, $0.045/hr + $0.045/GB. NAT instance: cheap but you operate it, single point of failure unless HA-pair. Default to NAT gateway in production.

docs.title: Q4. VPC peering vs Transit Gateway?
docs.text: Peering: 1:1, no transitive routing, simple, free between VPCs (pay for cross-AZ traffic). TGW: hub-and-spoke, transitive, supports thousands of VPCs, $0.05/hr/attachment + $0.02/GB. TGW for >5 VPCs.

docs.title: Q5. Cross-region VPC connectivity options?
docs.text: TGW peering (regional TGWs peered), VPC peering across regions, AWS Cloud WAN (newer, simpler for many regions), or VPN/Direct Connect over private backbone.

docs.title: Q6. GCP equivalent of TGW?
docs.text: Shared VPC + Network Connectivity Center (hub-spoke). GCP global VPCs simplify multi-region inside one VPC (unique to GCP — AWS/Azure are regional).

docs.title: Q7. Azure equivalent?
docs.text: Virtual WAN (hub-and-spoke at scale) or VNet peering (pairwise). Azure VNets are also regional like AWS.

docs.title: Q8. What's an egress-only Internet Gateway?
docs.text: IPv6-only outbound; blocks inbound. AWS-specific. For IPv4 you need NAT GW. GCP/Azure handle similarly with default-deny inbound on private subnets.

docs.title: Q9. PrivateLink / Private Service Connect / Private Endpoint?
docs.text: Three names for same idea: connect to managed services (S3, BigQuery, Storage Account) via private IPs in your VPC. Avoids public internet, satisfies compliance, often cheaper egress.

docs.title: Q10. Pitfall: VPC endpoint costs?
docs.text: Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) cost $0.01/hr/AZ + $0.01/GB. Multiplied across services and AZs, can exceed NAT GW cost. Gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB only) are free — use those first.

docs.title: Q11. AWS IAM principals?
docs.text: Users (humans, long-lived creds), roles (assumable, temporary creds), service-linked roles (managed by AWS), federated identities (SSO/OIDC). Prefer roles + federation; ban IAM users in prod.

docs.title: Q12. GCP IAM model differences?
docs.text: GCP uses service accounts (not roles). Permissions granted via predefined or custom roles bound to principals at project, folder, or org level. Workload Identity = OIDC for GKE workloads.

docs.title: Q13. Azure RBAC model?
docs.text: Scope (mgmt group → subscription → RG → resource), role definitions (built-in or custom), assignments. Azure AD identities. Managed Identities = service-account equivalent.

docs.title: Q14. Least privilege how — practically?
docs.text: Start from CloudTrail / Cloud Audit Logs / Activity Log. Generate policy from actual API calls (AWS Access Analyzer, GCP Policy Analyzer). Deny by default; allow per-action; review quarterly.

docs.title: Q15. AWS SCPs vs IAM policies?
docs.text: SCPs (Service Control Policies) attach at OU/account level, set the ceiling — even root can't exceed. IAM policies grant within the ceiling. Use SCPs for guardrails (e.g., "no us-east-1 outside DR account").

docs.title: Q16. GCP Org Policies?
docs.text: Constraint-based: deny VM external IPs, require uniform bucket access, restrict allowed regions. Hierarchical inheritance. Equivalent strength to SCPs.

docs.title: Q17. Cross-account access pattern?
docs.text: Principal in account A assumes a role in account B via STS:AssumeRole. Trust policy on B specifies who can assume. ExternalID for third-party access (deputy confused problem).

docs.title: Q18. Secrets — where?
docs.text: AWS Secrets Manager (rotation), GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault. Never in env vars, code, or container images. Mount via CSI driver or fetch at startup. Rotate quarterly minimum.

docs.title: Q19. AWS Organizations baseline structure?
docs.text: Mgmt account (consolidated billing, no workloads), Security OU (audit, log archive), Workload OUs by environment (dev, stage, prod) and/or business unit. Control Tower automates baseline.

docs.title: Q20. Why one account per environment?
docs.text: Hard isolation: blast radius capped, IAM boundaries clear, billing per environment, easy to delete. Single-account "we'll use tags" inevitably leaks.

docs.title: Q21. GCP equivalent — projects and folders?
docs.text: Org → Folders (e.g., dept) → Projects (one per env per service). Project = primary isolation boundary. Hundreds of projects normal at scale.

docs.title: Q22. Azure subscriptions vs management groups?
docs.text: Subscriptions = billing + RBAC boundary. Management groups = hierarchical org. Mirror your AWS OU structure with mgmt groups + subscriptions per env.

docs.title: Q23. Centralized logging across accounts?
docs.text: AWS: CloudTrail org trail → central S3 bucket in log-archive account. GCP: aggregated sink at org level → BigQuery. Azure: Log Analytics workspace at hub.

docs.title: Q24. Cross-account networking — best practice?
docs.text: Centralized network account owns TGW, shared VPC endpoints, central egress. Workload accounts attach to TGW. Reduces NAT/endpoint costs and simplifies governance.

docs.title: Q25. When Lambda over ECS/EKS?
docs.text: Bursty/sporadic workload (< 25% utilization), event-driven (S3, SQS, EventBridge), no long-running connections, cold-start tolerable. Cost crossover ~250ms * X requests/month vs 1 container.

docs.title: Q26. When containers over Lambda?
docs.text: Sustained traffic, > 15 min jobs, custom runtimes, websocket servers, ML inference with GPU, predictable cost at scale, multi-process needs.

docs.title: Q27. Lambda cold start — mitigations?
docs.text: Provisioned concurrency (defeats the cost model for low traffic), SnapStart for Java, smaller packages, init outside handler, ARM (Graviton) faster cold start. Or stop fighting and use Fargate.

docs.title: Q28. GCP Cloud Run vs Cloud Functions?
docs.text: Cloud Functions = single-purpose, event-driven, smaller package. Cloud Run = container, scales to zero, websockets supported, longer timeout (60 min). Cloud Run is the modern default.

docs.title: Q29. Azure Functions vs Container Apps?
docs.text: Functions = event-driven serverless. Container Apps = managed Kubernetes-light with KEDA scaling. Container Apps is closer to Cloud Run; AKS for full K8s.

docs.title: Q30. Step Functions / Workflows / Logic Apps — when?
docs.text: Orchestrating multi-step workflows with retry, branching, human approval. Saves you writing state machine code. Pricier per state transition; use for low-volume, complex flows.

docs.title: Q31. Top 5 AWS cost levers?
docs.text: Savings Plans / Reserved Instances (1-3 year commit), Spot for stateless workloads (90% off), right-sizing (CloudWatch + Compute Optimizer), S3 Intelligent-Tiering, gp3 over gp2 EBS (20% cheaper, faster).

docs.title: Q32. Cross-region egress trap?
docs.text: $0.02/GB AWS, $0.08-0.12/GB cross-continent. A chatty service replicating logs to a central account in another region can dominate the bill. Aggregate locally, ship summaries.

docs.title: Q33. NAT gateway data transfer cost?
docs.text: $0.045/GB through NAT. A pull-image-on-every-restart anti-pattern costs more in NAT than ECR pulls themselves. Use VPC endpoints (free for S3/ECR gateway endpoints).

docs.title: Q34. GCP cost-optimization patterns?
docs.text: Committed Use Discounts (CUDs), preemptible/Spot VMs, regional persistent disks, BigQuery flat-rate vs on-demand, lifecycle policies on GCS, sustained-use discounts (automatic).

docs.title: Q35. Azure cost levers?
docs.text: Reserved Instances, Azure Hybrid Benefit (BYOL Windows/SQL), Spot VMs, Cosmos autoscale RU/s, lifecycle on Storage, Cost Management + Advisor recommendations.

docs.title: Q36. Showback vs chargeback?
docs.text: Showback: visibility, no penalty (early stage). Chargeback: actual billing to teams (mature). Tag everything (cost center, env, owner) — untagged spend is mystery spend.

docs.title: Q37. Right-sizing approach?
docs.text: Trailing 30-day utilization. Resize when sustained < 40% CPU/memory. Cloud-native tooling: AWS Compute Optimizer, GCP Recommender, Azure Advisor. Reduce 30%, monitor 1 week, repeat.

docs.title: Q38. Common surprise bill cause?
docs.text: (1) NAT egress from container pulls. (2) Cross-AZ data transfer in chatty microservices. (3) Idle Load Balancers (~$20/mo each, multiplied). (4) Snapshots never deleted. (5) Forgotten dev env left running.

docs.title: Q39. AWS Well-Architected — six pillars?
docs.text: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, Sustainability. Use the Well-Architected Tool to self-assess; quarterly review.

docs.title: Q40. GCP Architecture Framework pillars?
docs.text: System design, Operational excellence, Security/privacy/compliance, Reliability, Cost optimization, Performance optimization. Almost identical to AWS.

docs.title: Q41. Azure Well-Architected Framework?
docs.text: Cost, Operational Excellence, Performance Efficiency, Reliability, Security. Five pillars; same intent. Azure Advisor cross-references.

docs.title: Q42. Top reliability tenet across all three?
docs.text: Design for failure: multi-AZ minimum, multi-region for tier-1, automated failover tested in drills, RPO/RTO defined per workload, chaos engineering discipline.

docs.title: Q43. Top security tenet?
docs.text: Identity at the perimeter (zero-trust), least privilege, encrypt in transit + at rest, log everything to immutable storage, automated detection (GuardDuty, SCC, Defender).

docs.title: Q44. Sustainability — real or marketing?
docs.text: Real: measure carbon (AWS Customer Carbon, GCP Carbon Footprint, Azure Emissions), pick low-carbon regions (Iowa, Frankfurt, Sweden), schedule batch in low-carbon hours, right-size relentlessly.

docs.title: Q45. S3 bucket — security baseline?
docs.text: Block Public Access org-wide, encryption with KMS CMK, bucket policy enforcing TLS, versioning + MFA delete for critical, Object Lock for compliance, access logs to separate bucket.

docs.title: Q46. RDS HA architecture?
docs.text: Multi-AZ deployment (sync standby in another AZ), read replicas in same/other regions, automated backups + PITR, parameter group tuned, performance insights enabled.

docs.title: Q47. DynamoDB partition key design?
docs.text: High cardinality, evenly accessed. Avoid hot keys (timestamp prefix bad). Use composite keys (PK = userid, SK = timestamp). Use adaptive capacity but don't rely on it.

docs.title: Q48. GCP Spanner vs BigQuery?
docs.text: Spanner = transactional, global SQL, strong consistency, $$$. BigQuery = analytical, columnar, serverless, cheap. Spanner for OLTP at planetary scale; BQ for analytics.

docs.title: Q49. Azure Cosmos DB — consistency models?
docs.text: Five levels: Strong, Bounded Staleness, Session (default), Consistent Prefix, Eventual. Pick the weakest that meets requirement; cheaper and faster.

docs.title: Q50. CloudFront / Cloud CDN / Azure Front Door — common patterns?
docs.text: Edge cache static, origin shield to reduce origin load, signed URLs for private content, Lambda@Edge / Cloud Run / Front Door rules for header manipulation, WAF integration.

docs.title: Q51. EKS vs GKE vs AKS — biggest difference?
docs.text: GKE Autopilot is most managed (no node ops). EKS = most flexible, weakest defaults. AKS = best Windows + Active Directory integration. All converge on the K8s API.

docs.title: Q52. Pod IP exhaustion — common in AWS?
docs.text: VPC CNI assigns ENI IPs to pods. /24 subnet = 250 IPs = ~200 pods per node. Use prefix delegation, larger subnets, or custom CNI (Calico).

docs.title: Q53. Cluster autoscaling — cost trap?
docs.text: Karpenter (AWS) provisions right-sized nodes per pod requests. Without it, you over-provision. Set conservative pod requests, use Karpenter to consolidate, scale down empty nodes fast.

docs.title: Q54. Multi-region K8s — yes or no?
docs.text: Federation is mostly dead. Better: independent clusters per region, GitOps push same manifests, global load balancer routes. Don't try to "one cluster across regions".

docs.title: Q55. Pod security baseline?
docs.text: Non-root user, read-only root FS, drop all capabilities, NetworkPolicy default-deny, PodSecurity admission restricted profile, resource limits always set, image scanning in CI.

docs.title: Q56. Four DR strategies (AWS terminology)?
docs.text: Backup & Restore (cheapest, RTO hours), Pilot Light (minimal infra running, RTO 10s of minutes), Warm Standby (scaled-down full env, RTO minutes), Multi-Site Active-Active (RTO seconds).

docs.title: Q57. RPO vs RTO — how to choose?
docs.text: Driven by business impact. Banking transactions: RPO seconds, RTO minutes. Marketing site: RPO hours, RTO hours. Each tier has cost; do not over-engineer tier-3 systems.

docs.title: Q58. DR drill cadence?
docs.text: Quarterly minimum for tier-1, annually for tier-2. Untested DR is documented hope. Drill includes: failover, validate, fail back, write postmortem.

docs.title: Q59. Backup pitfalls?
docs.text: Backups in same region as data (region failure = no backups). Backups never restore-tested. Encryption keys lost = data lost. Retention misaligned with compliance (GDPR).

docs.title: Q60. Multi-cloud DR — worth it?
docs.text: Rarely. Adds complexity for theoretical resilience to a multi-decade-rare provider failure. Better: multi-region + disciplined backups. Multi-cloud only if compliance mandates or data sovereignty.

docs.title: Cross-Cloud Service Mapping
docs.text: Need AWS GCP Azure Object storage S3 GCS Blob Storage Managed K8s EKS GKE AKS Serverless functions Lambda Cloud Functions Functions Container serverless App Runner / Fargate Cloud Run Container Apps Managed SQL RDS / Aurora Cloud SQL / Spanner SQL DB / Cosmos NoSQL DynamoDB Firestore / Bigtable Cosmos DB Event bus EventBridge Eventarc / Pub/Sub Event Grid Queue SQS Pub/Sub Service Bus Streaming Kinesis / MSK Pub/Sub / Dataflow Event Hubs Secrets Secrets Manager Secret Manager Key Vault CDN CloudFront Cloud CDN Front Door / CDN Identity IAM + IAM IdC Cloud IAM Entra ID + RBAC Org guardrails SCP + Control Tower Org Policy Mgmt Groups + Policy

docs.title: Decision Frameworks
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  W[Workload type?] --> EV[Event driven]
  W --> ST[Steady state]
  W --> BU[Bursty]
  EV --> SF[Functions or Cloud Run]
  ST --> CO[Containers or VMs]
  BU --> SE[Serverless]
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  D[Data type?] --> RE[Relational]
  D --> KV[Key value]
  D --> AN[Analytics]
  RE --> RDS[RDS or Spanner]
  KV --> DD[DynamoDB or Firestore]
  AN --> BQ[BigQuery or Snowflake]

docs.title: Anti-Patterns (Cloud Edition)
docs.text: Anti-Pattern Cost / Risk Public S3 bucket "by accident" Data breach IAM user with admin in prod Credential leak = takeover Single region for tier-1 Region outage = business outage No tagging No cost attribution, mystery bill Snapshots never expired Slow storage growth, surprise bill Cross-region chatty calls Egress dominates compute cost One giant cluster, all tenants Blast radius = whole business Manual click-ops in prod Audit gap, no rollback Plain-text secrets in env vars Leaked in logs/dumps LB per microservice $20/mo x 100 services = $24k/yr

docs.title: 12-Step Cloud Architecture Review
docs.text:
1. Map every account/project/subscription.
  2. Diagram VPC/VNet/Networks with fault domains.
  3. Inventory IAM principals, roles, key bindings.
  4. List all data stores: type, region, encryption, backup.
  5. Identify tier-1 workloads and their RPO/RTO.
  6. Map cross-region/cross-cloud dependencies.
  7. Audit security baseline (encryption, public exposure).
  8. Cost report by account/service, top 10 spenders.
  9. Tag coverage and untagged spend.
  10. DR drill last-completed dates per workload.
  11. On-call coverage and runbook coverage.
  12. Open compliance gaps (SOC2, HIPAA, PCI as relevant).

docs.title: Closing Notes
docs.text:
Cloud architecture is mostly about trade-offs and discipline, not magic services. The companies that win on cloud have boring architecture, ruthless tagging, drilled DR, and tight cost reviews. The ones that lose chase shiny services and pay 3x for it.

Pick one cloud as primary, get deep, learn the others by mapping equivalents.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: A reference of common DevOps, Kubernetes, container, and platform terms used throughout this site. Hover any abbreviation in the docs to see its definition (when supported by the browser).

docs.title: ELI10 — Distributed Systems for 10-Year-Olds
docs.text: Each concept has: simple analogy, real meaning, mermaid diagram, sample command/snippet.

docs.title: 1. Replication
docs.text:
Analogy: Every kid in the classroom has their own copy of the homework sheet. If one kid loses theirs, the others still have it. The teacher can ask any kid for the answer.

Real: Data is copied across multiple servers (called replicas). If one server dies, others still have the data. Reads can hit any replica for speed.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  T[Teacher write] --> P[Primary]
  P --> R1[Replica 1]
  P --> R2[Replica 2]
  P --> R3[Replica 3]

Snippet: 

# Postgres streaming replication setup (primary side)
echo "wal_level = replica" >> postgresql.conf
echo "max_wal_senders = 5" >> postgresql.conf

docs.title: 2. Sharding
docs.text:
Analogy: Every kid only carries part of the toy collection home. Sara has all the dolls, Sam has all the cars, Lin has all the puzzles. To find a toy, you ask the right kid.

Real: Data is split (sharded) across servers based on a key. Each server only stores its slice. To find data, the router computes which shard to ask.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  C[Client] --> RT[Router]
  RT --> S1[Shard A-H]
  RT --> S2[Shard I-P]
  RT --> S3[Shard Q-Z]

Snippet: 

def shard_for(user_id, num_shards=4):
    return hash(user_id) % num_shards

docs.title: 3. Eventual Consistency
docs.text:
Analogy: When the principal makes an announcement, every classroom hears it within a few minutes — not all at the exact same second. Eventually everyone knows.

Real: A change made on one server takes a tiny bit of time to spread to the others. For a moment, different servers may show different answers. Eventually they all agree.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  W[Write to N1] --> N1[Node 1 fresh]
  N1 -.async.-> N2[Node 2 stale]
  N1 -.async.-> N3[Node 3 stale]
  N2 --> OK[All agree]
  N3 --> OK

Snippet: 

# DynamoDB eventually consistent read default
aws dynamodb get-item --table users --key '{"id":{"S":"u1"}}'
# strongly consistent read costs more
aws dynamodb get-item --table users --key '{"id":{"S":"u1"}}' --consistent-read

docs.title: 4. Quorum
docs.text:
Analogy: Class wants to pick a snack. With 5 kids, you need at least 3 to vote yes for it to count. Majority wins. Even if 2 kids are absent, the vote is still valid.

Real: A quorum is the minimum number of nodes that must agree before an operation is considered done. For 5 nodes, quorum = 3 (majority). Survives 2 failures.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  W[Write request] --> N1[Node 1 yes]
  W --> N2[Node 2 yes]
  W --> N3[Node 3 yes]
  W --> N4[Node 4 down]
  W --> N5[Node 5 down]
  N3 --> OK[Quorum reached - commit]

Snippet: 

# etcd cluster of 5 - tolerates 2 failures
# quorum = (5/2) + 1 = 3
etcd --initial-cluster=n1=...,n2=...,n3=...,n4=...,n5=...

docs.title: 5. Circuit Breaker
docs.text:
Analogy: If the slide on the playground is broken, kids stop trying it for a while. Every 5 minutes one kid checks if it's fixed. If yes, everyone uses it again.

Real: When a downstream service keeps failing, the client stops calling it for a cooldown period. Saves resources and gives the broken thing time to recover. Periodically retries.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  A[App] --> CB[Circuit Breaker]
  CB -->|closed| S[Service ok]
  CB -->|open| F[Fail fast]
  CB -->|half-open| T[Test 1 call]

Snippet: 

from pybreaker import CircuitBreaker
cb = CircuitBreaker(fail_max=5, reset_timeout=30)

@cb
def call_payment_api():
    return requests.post("https://pay/charge")

docs.title: 6. Leader Election
docs.text:
Analogy: In a relay race, only one kid is the team captain at a time. The captain decides who runs which leg. If the captain leaves, the team votes for a new captain.

Real: In a cluster, one node is chosen to be the leader (handles all writes or makes decisions). If the leader dies, the others run an election to pick a new one.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  N1[Node 1 leader] --> Y[Serves writes]
  N1 -.dies.-> X[Election starts]
  X --> N2[Node 2 candidate]
  X --> N3[Node 3 candidate]
  N2 --> NL[Node 2 new leader]

Snippet: 

# kubectl shows leader election in kube-controller-manager
kubectl get lease -n kube-system kube-controller-manager -o yaml

docs.title: 7. Load Balancing
docs.text:
Analogy: When 30 kids show up to the ice cream truck, the worker waves them into 3 lines so each line stays short. No one line gets all the kids.

Real: A load balancer spreads incoming requests across multiple servers so no single server gets overwhelmed. Common strategies: round-robin, least-connections, hash-based.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  C[Clients] --> LB[Load Balancer]
  LB --> S1[Server 1]
  LB --> S2[Server 2]
  LB --> S3[Server 3]

Snippet: 

upstream backend {
    least_conn;
    server app1:8080;
    server app2:8080;
    server app3:8080;
}

docs.title: 8. Caching
docs.text:
Analogy: You keep your favorite snack in your desk drawer instead of walking to the kitchen every time. Faster to grab from the drawer (cache) than the kitchen (database).

Real: Frequently-read data is stored close to the consumer (in memory) so we don't have to hit the slow database every time. Cache hit = fast; cache miss = fetch and store.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  A[App] --> C[Cache check]
  C -->|hit| R[Return fast]
  C -->|miss| DB[Query DB]
  DB --> ST[Store in cache]
  ST --> R

Snippet: 

import redis
r = redis.Redis()
val = r.get("user:42")
if not val:
    val = db.fetch_user(42)
    r.setex("user:42", 300, val)

docs.title: 9. Message Queue
docs.text:
Analogy: When you give the lunch lady your order, she writes it on a ticket and puts it in a line. Cooks pick up tickets one at a time and make the food. You don't wait at the counter.

Real: Producers send messages to a queue. Consumers pick them up and process them asynchronously. Decouples sender from receiver; smooths bursts.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  P1[Producer] --> Q[Queue]
  P2[Producer] --> Q
  Q --> C1[Consumer 1]
  Q --> C2[Consumer 2]

Snippet: 

# RabbitMQ basic publish
rabbitmqadmin publish exchange=amq.default routing_key=orders payload="order123"

docs.title: 10. Rate Limiting
docs.text:
Analogy: The cafeteria gives each kid 2 cookies max. If you ask for a 3rd, the lunch lady says "no, come back tomorrow". Stops one greedy kid eating all the cookies.

Real: Limit how many requests a client can make per time window. Protects the system from abuse and noisy neighbors. Common: token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed window.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  C[Client] --> RL[Rate Limiter]
  RL -->|under limit| API[API]
  RL -->|over limit| R[429 reject]

Snippet: 

# nginx rate limit
# limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=api:10m rate=10r/s;
# location /api { limit_req zone=api burst=20 nodelay; }

docs.title: 11. CDN
docs.text:
Analogy: Instead of one ice cream truck for the whole town, there are little freezers in every neighborhood. Closer = faster ice cream. The factory only makes new flavors.

Real: A Content Delivery Network caches static content at edge locations close to users. Origin server only handles cache misses and dynamic content.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  U1[User EU] --> E1[Edge Frankfurt]
  U2[User US] --> E2[Edge Virginia]
  E1 -->|miss| O[Origin]
  E2 -->|miss| O

Snippet: 

# CloudFront cache headers from origin
Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400, s-maxage=31536000

docs.title: 12. Retry with Backoff
docs.text:
Analogy: If you knock on the door and no one answers, you wait a minute and knock again. Then 2 minutes. Then 4. You don't keep banging — you give them time to come.

Real: When a request fails, retry after a delay that grows (exponential backoff) plus randomness (jitter) to avoid all clients retrying at the same instant.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  T[Try] -->|fail| W1[Wait 1s]
  W1 --> T2[Try 2]
  T2 -->|fail| W2[Wait 2s]
  W2 --> T3[Try 3]
  T3 -->|ok| OK[Done]

Snippet: 

import time, random
for i in range(5):
    try: return call_api()
    except: time.sleep((2 ** i) + random.random())

docs.title: 13. Heartbeat
docs.text:
Analogy: Every minute the teacher says "raise your hand if you're here". If a kid doesn't raise their hand for 3 minutes, the teacher marks them absent.

Real: Nodes periodically send "I'm alive" signals to a coordinator. Missing N consecutive heartbeats marks the node as dead and triggers failover.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  N[Node] -->|every 5s| M[Monitor]
  M -->|3 missed| D[Mark dead]
  D --> F[Failover]

Snippet: 

# Kubernetes liveness probe
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 3

docs.title: 14. Idempotency
docs.text:
Analogy: Pressing the elevator button 5 times doesn't make the elevator come 5 times. The button only registers once. Same outcome whether you press it once or many.

Real: An operation is idempotent if doing it multiple times has the same effect as doing it once. Critical for retries — without it, retries cause duplicates.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  R1[Request id-42] --> S[Server]
  R2[Retry id-42] --> S
  S -->|same id seen| OK[Return cached result]

Snippet: 

# Stripe idempotency key
curl -X POST https://api.stripe.com/v1/charges \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: order-12345" \
  -d amount=2000

docs.title: 15. Sharding vs Replication (Together)
docs.text:
Analogy: Class splits into 3 reading groups (sharding). Each group has 3 kids who all read the same chapter (replication). Group A reads ch.1, group B ch.2, group C ch.3.

Real: Real systems combine both: shard for horizontal scale, replicate each shard for fault tolerance. A 9-node cluster might have 3 shards x 3 replicas.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  D[Data] --> SA[Shard A x3 replicas]
  D --> SB[Shard B x3 replicas]
  D --> SC[Shard C x3 replicas]

Snippet: 

# MongoDB sharded replica set summary
shardA: { primary: a1, secondary: [a2, a3] }
shardB: { primary: b1, secondary: [b2, b3] }
shardC: { primary: c1, secondary: [c2, c3] }

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text:
Concept Kid Analogy When to Use Replication Everyone has homework copy Survive node loss Sharding Each kid carries some toys Scale horizontally Eventual Consistency Announcement spreads in minutes Tolerate slight staleness Quorum Class majority vote Decide under failure Circuit Breaker Skip broken slide Protect from cascading failure Leader Election Team captain Single source of truth Load Balancer Lines at ice cream truck Spread traffic Cache Snacks in desk Speed up frequent reads Queue Lunch ticket line Decouple producer/consumer Rate Limit Max 2 cookies Stop abuse CDN Local freezers Reduce latency globally Retry+Backoff Knock and wait Handle transient failures Heartbeat Teacher attendance Detect dead nodes Idempotency Elevator button Safe retries

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: A reference of common DevOps, Kubernetes, container, and platform terms used throughout this site. Hover any abbreviation in the docs to see its definition (when supported by the browser).

docs.title: Visual Flows — 12 Mermaid Diagrams
docs.text: Whiteboard-ready diagrams for core distributed-system patterns. Redraw 3 from memory before any system design interview.

docs.title: 1. Multi-Region Edge → App → DB Request Flow
docs.text:
User requests routed to nearest region; cross-region only on home-region miss.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  U[User] --> DNS[GeoDNS]
  DNS --> E[Edge POP]
  E --> APP[Regional App]
  APP --> DB[Regional DB]
  DB --> X[Cross-region async replicate]

Notes: Edge terminates TLS. App reads local DB. Writes either go to home region or replicate via async stream. RTT user-to-edge < 50ms, edge-to-app < 10ms.

docs.title: 2. Retry With Exponential Backoff and Jitter
docs.text:
Failed requests are retried with growing delays plus random jitter to avoid thundering herds.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  C[Client] --> T1[Try 1]
  T1 -->|fail| W1[Wait 1s + jitter]
  W1 --> T2[Try 2]
  T2 -->|fail| W2[Wait 2s + jitter]
  W2 --> T3[Try 3]
  T3 -->|ok| OK[Done]

Notes: Cap at max retries (5) and max delay (30s). Jitter = random 0..backoff. Without jitter, all clients retry in lockstep and re-DDoS the dependency.

docs.title: 3. Saga (Compensation-Based Transaction)
docs.text:
Distributed transaction without 2PC: each step has a compensating action on failure.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  S[Order placed] --> R[Reserve inventory]
  R --> C[Charge card]
  C --> SH[Ship]
  SH --> D[Done]
  C -->|fail| RR[Release inventory]

Notes: Compensations must be idempotent. State machine tracks step. Saga orchestrator coordinates; alternative is choreography (each service emits events).

docs.title: 4. CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)
docs.text:
Writes go through commands; reads served from optimized read models.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  U[User] --> CMD[Command API]
  CMD --> WDB[Write DB]
  WDB --> EV[Event stream]
  EV --> RM[Read Model]
  U --> Q[Query API reads RM]

Notes: Read model can denormalize, materialize, or join. Eventual consistency between command and query. Used heavily with event sourcing.

docs.title: 5. Event Sourcing
docs.text:
Store every state change as an append-only event log; rebuild state by replay.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  C[Command] --> A[Aggregate]
  A --> E[Append event]
  E --> ES[Event Store]
  ES --> P[Projection]
  P --> RM[Read Models]

Notes: Snapshots speed up replay for hot aggregates. Versioning events is forever-painful — design event schemas carefully. Audit log free.

docs.title: 6. Rate Limiting (Token Bucket)
docs.text:
Each client has a bucket of tokens; each request consumes one; bucket refills at fixed rate.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  R[Request] --> B[Token Bucket]
  B -->|has token| API[Forward to API]
  B -->|empty| RJ[429 Too Many]
  TR[Refill timer] --> B

Notes: Bucket size = burst tolerance. Refill rate = sustained limit. Distributed implementations use Redis with Lua scripts for atomicity.

docs.title: 7. Bulkhead (Resource Isolation)
docs.text:
Partition resources so one slow dependency cannot exhaust all threads/connections.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  APP[App] --> B1[Pool A 20 threads]
  APP --> B2[Pool B 20 threads]
  APP --> B3[Pool C 20 threads]
  B1 --> SA[Service A slow]
  B2 --> SB[Service B ok]
  B3 --> SC[Service C ok]

Notes: A's slowness only saturates pool A. B and C keep serving. Without bulkheads, all 60 threads block on A. Hystrix/Resilience4j patterns.

docs.title: 8. Cache Stampede Prevention
docs.text:
When a hot key expires, only one fetch goes to the DB; others wait.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  R[Many requests] --> C[Cache check]
  C -->|hit| OK[Return]
  C -->|miss| L[Lock single fetcher]
  L --> DB[DB fetch]
  DB --> ST[Store + unlock]
  ST --> OK

Notes: Use distributed lock (Redis SETNX) or "request coalescing" / singleflight pattern. Alternative: probabilistic early refresh before TTL expires.

docs.title: 9. Pub/Sub Fan-Out
docs.text:
One event published; many independent consumers process it asynchronously.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  P[Producer] --> T[Topic]
  T --> S1[Email service]
  T --> S2[Analytics]
  T --> S3[Audit log]
  T --> S4[Search index]

Notes: Each consumer has own offset; failures isolated. Add new consumers without touching producer. Backpressure handled per consumer queue.

docs.title: 10. Circuit Breaker State Machine
docs.text:
Three states: closed (normal), open (failing fast), half-open (probing recovery).

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  CL[Closed] -->|N failures| OP[Open]
  OP -->|cooldown| HO[Half-Open]
  HO -->|success| CL
  HO -->|fail| OP

Notes: Closed = pass-through. Open = reject immediately, no call. Half-open = let one through to test. Failure threshold tunable per dependency.

docs.title: 11. Read-Through Cache
docs.text:
App always reads from cache; cache pulls from DB on miss.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  A[App] --> C[Cache]
  C -->|hit| R[Return]
  C -->|miss| DB[Fetch DB]
  DB --> CW[Cache write]
  CW --> R

Notes: Simpler than cache-aside (app handles miss). Variants: write-through (DB on write), write-behind (async DB write). TTL or LRU eviction.

docs.title: 12. Outbox Pattern (Reliable Event Publishing)
docs.text:
Write business state and event in same transaction; relay publishes events from outbox.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  TX[Transaction] --> ST[State update]
  TX --> OB[Outbox row]
  OB --> RL[Relay process]
  RL --> K[Kafka]
  RL --> M[Mark sent]

Notes: Solves dual-write problem (DB + Kafka can't be atomic). Relay is at-least-once → consumers must be idempotent. Debezium CDC is a common relay.

docs.title: Pattern Selection Cheatsheet
docs.text: Need Pattern Cross-service transaction Saga Reliable event publish Outbox Slow dependency isolation Bulkhead Failing dependency Circuit Breaker Read scale Cache + Read Replicas Write scale Sharding + CQRS Audit trail / replay Event Sourcing Spike protection Rate Limit + Backpressure Burst smoothing Queue Latency to global users CDN + Multi-Region

docs.title: Composite Flow — End-to-End Order
docs.text:
How patterns compose for a real user order. (Simplified to 6 nodes.)

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  U[User] --> EDGE[Edge + Rate limit]
  EDGE --> API[API Gateway]
  API --> SAGA[Saga orchestrator]
  SAGA --> Q[Outbox - Kafka]
  Q --> DS[Downstream services]

docs.title: Failure-Mode Drawing
docs.text:
When asked "what happens if X breaks?", draw the X with a red mark and trace the impact.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  C[Client] --> LB[LB ok]
  LB --> S1[Server1 ok]
  LB --> S2[Server2 dead]
  S1 --> DB[DB ok]
  LB -.skip dead.-> S2

Drawing rules: - Use dead, slow, partition labels on nodes. - Draw the affected request path; what does the user experience? - Then draw the recovery path: health check fails, LB removes, traffic shifts.

docs.title: Tips for Whiteboard Sessions
docs.text:
1. Always start with one box for the user, one for the system. Then expand.
  2. Label arrows with protocol + sync/async (e.g. "HTTP sync", "Kafka async").
  3. Mark fault domains explicitly (AZ1, AZ2, region boundaries).
  4. After happy path, ask interviewer "want me to draw failure modes?"
  5. Keep diagrams to ≤ 6 nodes per view; use sub-diagrams for depth.
  6. Use the same node names across diagrams so the audience tracks state.

docs.title: Interview Q&A Index
docs.text: # Question One-line Answer 1 What does set -euo pipefail do? Exit on error (-e), unset var error (-u), propagate pipe failures (-o pipefail) 2 When should you use [[ ]] vs [ ]? Always [[ ]] in bash — no word splitting, regex support, no quoting bugs 3 How do you safely run shell commands from Python? subprocess.run(["cmd", "arg"], check=True) — never shell=True with user input 4 What's the difference between $() and backticks? $() is nestable and readable; backticks are legacy — always use $() 5 How do you pass secrets to scripts without env vars? Named pipes, /dev/stdin, or a secrets manager SDK — never command-line args 6 What's the purpose of local in bash functions? Prevents variable leakage into the global scope; without it all vars are global 7 How does xargs -P work? Runs N processes in parallel; combine with -n1 to process one arg per process 8 What is trap used for? Registering cleanup handlers for signals: trap 'cleanup' EXIT ERR INT TERM 9 How do you do retries in Python? tenacity library or manual exponential backoff with time.sleep(2**attempt) 10 What's a Kubernetes operator/controller? A control loop watching CRDs and reconciling actual vs desired state — kopf in Python
